# Protocol (frontend/backend contract)

Last reviewed: 2026-10-31, against the routes, event emission and database records in `server/internal/hub/` at commit `f3a13fdb7672927197cb8ac38bccb9c65671677b`. The timeouts, retention periods and count limits below are protocol or configuration values; actual performance was not measured.

All JSON fields are snake_case. Times are RFC3339 (UTC). HTTP `listen` defaults to `:18660`; TLS is turned on explicitly with `public.tls_listen` and serves HTTPS / WSS. Over the public internet IPv6 is preferred; see [network.md](../operations/network.md) for configuration and firewall rules.


### 客户端密码登录

管理员在「管理端 › 设备 › 客户端密码登录」设置连接密码并开启。连接密码与管理员密码分开，使用 RFC 9807 OPAQUE；
密码只在输入它的浏览器中参与计算，注册和登录接口均拒绝 `password` 字段。服务端保存 OPAQUE 注册记录和服务器密钥材料，
不保存密码原文或可直接用来登录的固定密码哈希。客户端密码长度规则由设置页面检查，服务端无法从盲化消息检查密码强度。

服务端与浏览器 WebAssembly 共用 `github.com/bytemare/opaque` 的固定配置，协议标识
`opaque-ristretto255-sha512-argon2id-v1`，上下文 `persona/client-password-login/v1`，客户端身份 `persona-client`，
服务端身份 `persona-hub:<hub_id>`。浏览器在一次性 Worker 内计算，结束后销毁 Worker；密码不进入 URL、存储或网络请求。
网页登录成功后继续使用浏览器设备 token。此功能只在中心 hub 提供，成员返回 `409 member_hub`，请连接中心的 HTTPS 地址。

公开接口前缀 `/api/v1/auth/password`，需要 TLS，回环连接允许本地开发或本机 TLS 终止代理；不信任调用方传入的 `X-Forwarded-*`。
写接口只接受同源 JSON，响应禁止缓存。每个来源及全局都限制登录发起次数，避免错误密码只在客户端被发现时绕过限流。

| 接口 | 请求与响应 |
| --- | --- |
| `GET /state` | `{enabled,suite,hub_id,hub_name}` |
| `POST /start` | `{message,name,kind,challenge?}`，`message` 为 base64 KE1；返回 `{session,message,identity,suite}`，响应消息为 KE2 |
| `POST /finish` | `{session,message}`，消息为 base64 KE3；成功返回 `{token,id,hub_id,name}`，或移动端的 `{code}` |
| `POST /exchange` | `{code,verifier}`，验证 RFC 7636 S256 PKCE 后返回设备凭据 |

移动端先输入 HTTPS hub 地址，再在系统浏览器登录。`/login/device` 的 URL fragment 携带随机 `state`、PKCE `challenge`、
设备 `name` 和 `kind`；`verifier` 只留在 App 内存。浏览器登录成功后通过 `persona://password-login?code=…&state=…` 返回，
App 核对 state 并向原 HTTPS 地址兑换 code，禁止重定向。跳转链接不包含设备 token；Android 从经过系统证书验证的兑换连接取得公钥指纹，
之后沿用现有钉扎连接。自签名证书部署仍使用扫码配对。

验证状态与授权码只在内存保留，协议有效期为 5 分钟，重启即失效；不论验证成功还是失败都消耗一次。
状态总量上限为 128 条。这些是协议和资源限制，实际性能未实测。
改密码、开关登录均更换配置版本，旧验证流程与授权码不能继续签发设备凭据。关闭登录保留已有设备；管理员可同时撤销所有设备，
事务提交后清鉴权缓存并断开已有连接。签发设备凭据与修改配置通过数据库行锁协调，避免旧密码在撤销后并发签发新凭据。

管理接口沿用管理员会话与 CSRF 检查，前缀 `/api/v1/admin/password-login`：

| 接口 | 请求与响应 |
| --- | --- |
| `GET /api/v1/admin/password-login` | `{enabled,configured,revision}`，不返回注册记录或密钥 |
| `POST /register/start` | `{message,revision}`，注册盲化请求；返回 `{session,message,identity,suite}` |
| `POST /register/finish` | `{session,message,revoke_devices}`，保存注册记录并开启登录；仅发起注册的管理员会话可完成 |
| `PUT /api/v1/admin/password-login` | `{enabled,revision,revoke_devices}`，切换登录或同时撤销设备 |

设置版本不匹配返回 `409 stale_settings`；错误密码、过期或重复验证返回 `401 bad_password`；未开启返回 `403 password_login_disabled`。

## Authentication

- Prefer `Authorization: Bearer <token>`. The current implementation has not locked down URL tokens: when there is no Authorization value, every authenticated API (WebSocket included) still falls back to `?token=`, not only on loopback or for WS. Clients should use the header so credentials stay out of URLs.
- The workspace board (#1646) adds GET `/api/v1/workspace-board` and `/api/v1/workspaces` to the `answer` read allowlist; changing the board still requires `full`. See "Workspace board".
- The watch's Milk Frog (#4869) adds GET `/api/v1/personas/nwverse/pet/<file>` (a plain `.json` or `.png` name) to the `answer` read allowlist, for its row and watch face ([persona.md](../apple/persona.md) "The Milk Frog on the watch"); no other persona file, package or upload is readable with an `answer` token.
- The `token` in hub.json is the master token. It is accepted only from trusted sources such as loopback / LAN; from the public internet it returns `403 master_token_local_only` even over TLS. Public clients should use a temporary pairing token or a device token. Plaintext API over the public internet is rejected by default with `403 tls_required`; the only exception is `GET /api/v1/health`.
- Per-device credentials: `POST /api/v1/auth/tokens {"name":"<device name>","kind":"phone"}` → `{id,token,role,name}`. Device tokens start with `jd_`; the hub stores only a hash. `kind: watch` gets `answer`, every other kind gets `full`. The stored kind is `phone`, `watch`, `web` or `link`; anything else is stored as `other`.
The web client may send `"replaces":"<this browser's previous device id>"`: once the new credential is created, the hub revokes that one (only if it is a `kind: web` credential not yet revoked; other kinds and unknown ids are left alone, and the new credential is issued either way), and the response gains `"replaced":"<id>"`. Logging in again from the same browser no longer piles up devices (#3356). Web devices stored as `other` before the upgrade are not replaced and must be revoked by hand. `full` can create device tokens. `answer` can only do what the watch needs (an allowlist, `devicetokens.go`); everything else is 403, GET included. Allowed: reading machines, sessions, chat content, interactions and the Inbox list; answering interactions; sending messages; marking read / interrupting; marking Inbox items done, drafting, replying. Files, launchers, device registration and WebSocket are not allowed. When answering a screen card it can only pick an option or press `1`–`9`, `esc`, `enter`; it cannot type, and cannot pick the free-input option ("Type something", which needs text; this is rejected before the card is claimed, so the card stays for the phone). It can only send messages to sessions in the list, text only (control characters stripped), with no launcher or model choice and no images. Inbox replies cannot carry document state changes, and cannot send `/agent` when `lark_agent` is on. Sending messages and approving plans are capabilities it has by design, so a lost watch still needs to be revoked. A newly paired App immediately exchanges for its own token and uses only that from then on. A paired watch exchanges for a separate `kind: watch` one and the watch only ever gets that. Until the exchange succeeds (request failed, old hub) the watch gets no credential at all and shows "No watch credential yet"; tapping "Sync from iPhone" makes the phone exchange again (#1185: it used to borrow the phone's `full` token for the time being, which defeated the restriction from #1128).
- `GET /api/v1/auth/tokens` returns `{tokens,current,push}`; `push` maps a credential id to the push way of the device it registered last (`docs/operations/push-relay.md` "Which way a device is pushed"). `DELETE /api/v1/auth/tokens/{id}` revokes a credential, clears the cache (authentication results are cached for 30 seconds and cleared on revoke) and disconnects every long-lived connection opened with that credential: the main WebSocket, live screen, forwarded ports, dev server previews and extension relays. The node-side streams close too, ending screen input and releasing any keep-awake hold for those screen connections. Connections opened with other credentials stay connected. The App manages these in **Settings › Devices**. When an old hub lacks this API, old clients keep using credentials through the original pairing flow.
- Credentials for a computer's link ([link.md](../operations/link.md)): `POST /api/v1/auth/tokens {"kind":"link","machine":"<a machine in hub.json with kind link>"}` → `role: link`,
  which can only open `/api/v1/link` and `/api/v1/link/stream`; every other API is 403. The list includes `machine_id`. When redeeming a pairing code generated for that computer (`{"machine"}` below),
  kind and machine are set by the pairing code; naming a different machine in the request returns 403.
- Extension tokens (starting with `pext_`, #1855): the hub issues them for the scopes the extension was granted (`permissions.hub`). They open only the routes registered for those scopes; everything else is 403 `permission_denied` (with `scope` when a scope is missing),
  and only requests from the local machine are accepted, unless they carry their manager's proof that they came through it (`X-Persona-Manager-Proof`, a relayed manager's extensions: [managers.md](../assistant/managers.md) "Extensions and the hub's API"). See [extensions.md](../extensions/extensions.md) ("Permissions", "Hub API: scopes").
- Linked hubs ([mesh.md](../server/mesh.md)): another hub's credential has kind / role `peer` (`machine_id` is the other side's hub_id) and can only open `GET /api/v1/peer`;
  a link code `jx_…` can only `POST /api/v1/peer/pair`; every other API is 403. In a group only the **primary hub** accepts App credentials: a member forwards App requests unchanged (with `Authorization`)
  to the primary, and when it joins it hands the credentials it has issued (hashes) to the primary, so devices paired with the member keep working. When the primary is unreachable, the member returns
  `503 {"code":"center_unreachable","center":{"hub_id","name"}}`.
- Public authentication failures are counted per IPv4 address and per IPv6 /64, and the ban check runs before the database lookup; `429 rate_limited` carries `Retry-After` in seconds. LAN / VPN is not counted. Parameters are in [network configuration](../operations/network.md#hubjson-网络配置).
- Services (separate processes such as the assistant) connect to the hub's bus with a different token (`jb_…`), which can only open `GET /api/v1/bus`. See "Bus" below.
- Requests may send `Accept-Language: zh-Hans|en|ja` (the full list a browser sends is also accepted; the first entry is taken and falls back per [i18n.md](i18n.md)): human-readable text in that response (`error`, status descriptions) uses that language. `code` does not change; clients still branch on `code`. Without it, the user's language is used (see `client_hello.locale` in "Client capabilities and heartbeat").
- Every response carries `X-Request-Id`. A request may send `X-Client-Request-Id` (4–32 hex characters / `-`), and the hub then uses it (`docs/server/server.md`, "Operations").

### Agent session sharing

The trusted ownership, catalog/selection/preview, one-time capability, tokenless
management and independent anonymous HTTP contract is in
[Agent session sharing](../server/agent-sharing.md). Manager hello capability
`agent_sharing.v1` negotiates these routes; node capabilities `share_projection.v1`
and `creation_receipt.v1` negotiate complete source projection and durable new-start
receipts. Unlike ordinary legacy API routes, sharing management never accepts URL
tokens or a default manager, and the public route never inherits login credentials.
An explicitly configured independent HTTP **or** HTTPS origin is supported; HTTP
requires the localized transport warning and explicit risk acknowledgement.

### Agent session archives

Hubs advertising `agent_session_archives` in hello / health relay recoverable archives for Agent sessions to their owning manager: every runtime the lists show (Claude Code, Codex, the Codex App, Orca, Paseo, DSH, opencode, pi…), since the record is the manager's own. Persona's own conversations use their existing assistant API. Archiving does not move or delete the source transcript.

| Request | Response | Permission |
|---|---|---|
| `GET /api/v1/sessions/archived?machine_id=` | `{ "sessions": [Session] }`, newest activity first within each manager; clients sort merged results; machine filter optional | full, answer; extensions with agents.read see only their manager's machines |
| `POST /api/v1/sessions/{mid}/{sid}/archive` | `{ "ok": true, "native"?: NativeArchive }` ("Native archive", below) | full |
| `POST /api/v1/sessions/{mid}/{sid}/archive?close=1` | `{ "ok": true, "archived": true, "close": { "closed": bool, "outcome": "closed" \| "not_running" \| "refused" \| "offline" \| "failed", "reason"?: string, "detail"?: string }, "native"?: NativeArchive }` ("Archive and close", below) | full |
| `POST /api/v1/sessions/{mid}/{sid}/archive?force=1` | `{ "ok": true, "archived": true, "close": { "closed": true, "outcome": "closed" } }`: cancel a confirmation-blocked Agent, close it, then archive it | full |
| `POST /api/v1/sessions/{mid}/{sid}/unarchive` | `{ "ok": true, "native"?: NativeArchive }` | full |

Archived rows carry `Session.archived=true` and are excluded from normal whole lists, WebSocket lists/deltas and paginated indexes. Successful writes refresh normal lists; clients refresh the archive list separately and retain errors. Clients hide archive controls when the feature is absent. A manager announces `agent_session_archives` in its bus hello; the Hub advertises the fleet-wide feature only when every relevant owner is connected and supports it. Mixed manager versions conservatively hide controls. Direct requests to an old manager return 501 `agent_archives_unsupported`; an offline owner returns 503 `assistant_offline`. The combined archive list fails explicitly when an owner is unavailable rather than pretending a partial list is complete. Unknown sessions return 404, assistant conversations return 400, and busy sessions cannot be archived (409 `agent_busy`): starting, working, waiting for an answer (a card), background work, running subagents or workflows. A finished turn awaiting the user's reply (`awaits_reply`) is idle and can be archived, as "Delete chat" could. Read-only credentials cannot mutate archives (403). Storage failures return 500 without reporting success. Repeating either operation preserves the requested visibility.

The owning manager persists records keyed by machine and session IDs without expiry. Clients must use the session's Hub, which routes mutations by machine ownership and merges manager archive lists. Mesh requests follow the existing center routing. The manager retains a minimal offline, read-only snapshot when a source inventory ages out, including after restoration and restart. Live inventory takes precedence. Reading still requires the original transcript to exist on a reachable computer; restoring does not recreate files. The manager reports `archive_changed_at` so the Hub can apply the same legacy deletion projection to normal and archived lists. A later explicit archive/restore supersedes an earlier deletion. Existing Hub deletion timestamps no longer expire: this preserves deletion across manager restarts and long-lived fallback snapshots. This deliberately trades bounded tombstone storage for preventing old conversations from unexpectedly reappearing; no new Hub business store is introduced.

New source activity (an advancing update timestamp, running or waiting for input) permanently restores the session; becoming idle again does not re-hide it. Only a list read after the archive was written counts: one read before it (a list publish or another request that read the session while it still worked or waited for the user, then waited for the archive's lock) cannot restore it. Failed automatic restores are retried without committing the failed write in memory. Archive storage and lock waits have a three-second deadline, bounded further by the request context. Opening an unchanged archive list does not rebuild or broadcast normal inventories.

The manager also archives closed sessions by itself once they have been idle for `archive_closed_days` and no open to-do counts on them, through the same record (`server/internal/assistant/agent_archive_auto.go`; [todos.md](../assistant/todos.md) "Closed sessions archive themselves"). Such a session is restored like any other.

Archives made only in the tool (archiving in the Codex App) are not listed here; existing source-discovery rules still apply. Every runtime uses the same manager-owned archive semantics. In the manager, ordinary archive callers (these routes, "Archive and close", the assistant's tools) go through `setAgentArchive` (`server/internal/assistant/agent_archives.go`); the native archive below follows from the record it saves (`noteAgentArchive`).

**Cancel a stuck confirmation** (`?force=1`, main-chat `agent_archive` with `force: true`): only a currently blocked Agent without other active work is eligible. The manager and node recheck the state. The node closes its terminal with Ctrl-C and closes the pane, or asks its runtime to close; Paseo uses the same archive request as its CLI's `archive --force`, which closes the provider and rejects outstanding permissions. No permission or plan is approved. Permission/plan cards are rejected, screen cards cancelled, and the transcript is kept. Working, starting, background work, running children/workflows, loops, queued messages, and serving ports remain protected. Questions and forms are not confirmation overrides. Before closing, the manager persists the archive with a future close timestamp in one write, then replaces it with the actual close time on success. A failed close removes that provisional archive and leaves the session and cards visible. The web screen card offers **Close Agent**, explains the cancellation, and asks for **Close and archive** or **Cancel**; the existing archive toast offers Undo. The cached blocked snapshot from before a successful close cannot restore the archive; new activity still can. Ordinary archive and archive-and-close keep their existing busy restrictions.

**Archive and close** (`?close=1`, hello / health feature `agent_session_archive_close`): archives the session, then closes its agent and its terminal on its computer, since the user asked for it (node `session.retire` with `close_terminal`, `docs/assistant/todos.md`): the tab and the agent process go, the transcript and how it was started stay; it is read-only from then on, and Resume on its terminal page brings it back (`claude --resume`, `codex resume`). Restoring it reopens nothing. Implemented by `archiveAndCloseAgentSession` (`server/internal/assistant/agent_archive_close.go`).

- A busy agent is refused before anything changes (409 `agent_busy`): the archive's busy rules, plus a `/loop`, queued messages or a server it runs (`ports`), since closing would stop what the user may be using.
- The archive comes first and is never undone by the close. When the close does not happen, the answer is still 200 with `closed: false`, the session stays archived and still open on its computer, and `reason` says why in the request's language (`detail`: the node's own words): `not_running` (it was not running: nothing to close, no reason), `refused` (the node will not close it: its engine or another tool keeps it, a runtime's or the Codex App's session, Codex started outside Persona so its launcher is unknown, the agent turned busy, a node from before `session.retire`), `offline` (its computer is not connected), `failed` (the call failed). The user can close it from the computer or restore it.
- Only an agent of a terminal engine (herdr, Herdr App, Orca, Tern) that is still is closed: Claude Code, Codex or a compatible CLI, not another tool's session or one of an engine that runs Agents itself. Clients offer the action only for those; the node decides.
- Activity the agent writes while it is being closed does not restore the archive: the record keeps `closed_at`, and only activity after it counts.
- The hub forwards `?close=1` only to a manager that names `agent_session_archive_close` in its hello; an older one would archive and leave the agent open, so the hub answers 501 `agent_archive_close_unsupported` instead, and advertises the feature only when every owner has it.

**Native archive.** After Persona's own record is saved, the manager also asks the tool that owns the session to archive (or restore) it with the tool's own reversible archive, through the node's `session.archive` / `session.unarchive` ("hub ↔ node RPC"). Persona's archive is the source of truth: it succeeds whatever the tool answers, and nothing is ever deleted. `native` (`NativeArchive`: `{archived, state, error?}`) is what the tool has: `state` `done` (the tool has it the same way), `pending` (not yet: the machine offline, the Agent working, Codex still open in a terminal, the last error in `error`, diagnostic text that is not localized: clients word the state themselves; the manager tries again whenever that machine's session list arrives, backing off from 1 to 30 minutes), or `unsupported` (the tool has no archive Persona can drive, such as Claude Code, or the node is older: the archive is Persona's alone, and `error` may say why). The request waits a few seconds for the tool before answering `pending`. Archived rows from `GET /api/v1/sessions/archived` carry the same object as `native_archive`; it is absent when the tool was never asked (sessions archived before this existed). The manager keeps these records in the setting `sessions.archived.native`, beside `sessions.archived`.

What each tool does: Codex threads are archived with the app-server's `thread/archive` / `thread/unarchive` (the rollout moves to `<CODEX_HOME>/archived_sessions` and back, and the Codex App lists it as archived); see `docs/integrations/codex.md` ("Archive"). A runtime does it only when it declares `caps.archive` (`docs/integrations/runtimes.md`); none does yet: Paseo's and DSH's bridges archive only as their `close` (Paseo's archive stops the agent and only a re-import brings it back; the DSH plugin has no unarchive), and Antigravity's "archive" is a list in its bridge, not Antigravity's own. Claude Code (no archive for local sessions; the Claude desktop app's archive is the app's private record), Orca, opencode (its archive column is only in its database, which Persona does not write) and pi have no archive Persona drives. A Codex thread archived in Codex leaves the node's list (the same rule as one archived in the Codex App); the manager's offline snapshot keeps showing it as archived and restorable. When new activity restores a session in Persona by itself, the manager asks the tool to restore it too (already restored answers done). After "Archive and close" has closed the agent, the tool is asked again at once: a Codex thread whose terminal was still open is archived in Codex once it has closed.

### Agent naming metadata

| Manager capability | Contract |
| --- | --- |
| `agent_naming.v1` | Full-user ordinary Agent renames persist manual intent in the manager before node dispatch. Older/offline managers retain the native node path; ordinary extension calls retain the existing node authorization boundary. |
| `agent_autoname` | The manager answers `POST /api/v1/sessions/{mid}/{sid}/autoname` (see "Naming an Agent on request" below). The hub relays the request only to an owner that names it and answers 501 `agent_autoname_unsupported` for an older one. |

Session rows may carry `title_source` (`manual`, `auto`, `prompt` or `runtime`), `title_manual` and cumulative
`output_tokens` (#4812). These are additive node facts, not instructions to rename a session. Absent or unknown
provenance never proves that a title was not manually chosen. The manager uses them for guarded naming,
then publishes the resulting name in the existing `title` field; no client-side renaming algorithm is needed.

### Naming an Agent on request

`POST /api/v1/sessions/{mid}/{sid}/autoname` (#7432; hello / health feature `agent_autoname`, manager capability
`agent_autoname`) names one Agent session with the model now, for an **Auto Rename** action in the Agent's menu.
The user does not type a name. It is the background naming's own call ("Automatic session names" in
[agent-work.md](../assistant/agent-work.md)): the **Sorting** model (`inbox.triage`), the same prompt, input and
validity check. Because the user asked, the background's guards do not apply: not the per-session change limit, not
"placeholder names only", not the `agent_auto_naming` switch, and a hand-written or native custom title is replaced
too. The result is an automatic name in the manager's ledger, so nothing is typed into the Agent and its tab keeps
its name; a later native rename or `POST …/rename` wins again.

- **Request**: no body (`{}` is accepted). `mid` is the computer's id and `sid` the session id of the row
  (`machine_id`, `session_id`). Full devices only. The manager waits for the model, up to 45 seconds; give the request
  a 60-second timeout.
- **Answer** `200 {"ok": true, "title": "<new title>", "title_source": "auto", "changed": true|false}`: `title` is
  what every list shows from now on; `changed` is false when the model gave the name the lists already showed. The
  manager publishes the session list before it answers, so the existing `sessions` / `sessions_delta` /
  `sessions_list` pushes carry the new `title` to every client: none reloads or renames locally (the client that
  asked may show `title` from the answer at once). A row named this way over a custom title carries
  `title_source: "auto"` and no `title_manual`.
- **One call per session**: requests for the same session that arrive while its call is out share that call and
  get the same answer. A client still disables the action while its own request is pending.
- **Errors** use the common error body (`error` in the request's language, `code`, `retryable`):

| Status | `code` | When | `retryable` |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 400 | `assistant_session` | The session is one of Persona's own conversations (the main chat included); clients hide the action on rows with `assistant: true` | false |
| 403 | `forbidden` | The device is not a full device (an answer-only device, an extension's token) | false |
| 404 | `not_found` | No such computer, or its node lists no such session | false |
| 409 | `model_not_configured` | No model is set up for **Sorting** | false |
| 409 | `no_dialogue` | The session has no user or assistant text to name it from yet | false |
| 409 | `renamed_meanwhile` | A rename in the app or the Agent finished while the model was working; the later hand-written name is kept | false |
| 501 | `agent_autoname_unsupported` | The computer's manager is older than the feature (the hub answers; nothing was asked) | false |
| 502 | `invalid_name` | The model's answer was not a usable name (empty, too long, markup, cut off) | true |
| 502 | `model_failed` | The model call failed | true |
| 502 | `dialogue_unavailable` | The session's conversation could not be read (its computer is offline or did not answer) | true |
| 503 | `assistant_offline` | The computer's manager is not connected (the hub answers) | true |
| 503 | `names_unavailable` | The saved names could not be read; nothing was changed | true |
| 503 | `canceled` | The manager stopped during the call | true |
| 504 | `timeout` | The model did not answer in time | true |
| 500 | `save_failed` | The new name could not be saved; nothing was changed | true |

Failures are logged by the manager with a static reason code and the session's ids only (`agent naming: requested
session="<mid>"/"<sid>" reason=<code>`), never the model's or the provider's words. A failed request does not count
as a background naming failure and starts no cooldown.

Clients show the action only when the feature is listed, on rows that are not `assistant` (archived rows included:
the name is kept by computer and session). The hub lists the feature only while every manager that carries Agents
is connected and names the capability.
Claude custom-title records remain protected even outside the quick metadata tail. Other runtimes without
reliable title provenance remain ineligible. Settings and the naming ledger belong to the manager; see
`docs/assistant/agent-work.md` ("Automatic session names (#4812)").

The assistant-only `agent_autoname` MCP tool is a separate, narrow caller of the same manager operation, for a
Persona conversation acting on the user's explicit request. It takes exactly `{"machine":"<machine id or name>",
"session_id":"<full session id>"}` and rejects other fields, prefixes, ordinary coding-Agent callers and Persona's
own conversations. A phone permission card confirms the write on every invocation; declining or not answering makes
no model call and changes no title. The text result is a JSON object with the same success fields, or
`{"ok":false,"code":"<the applicable code above>","retryable":true|false,"error":"<localized sentence>"}`. It has
no URL, header or token parameters and grants no standing permission. iOS uses the HTTP endpoint, not this tool.

`agent_autoname_receipt` is an assistant-only, read-only evidence lookup (`agent_naming_receipt.go`), not a new
client dependency or an execution receipt for a particular model call. Its input is only an exact machine and full
session id, plus an optional bounded `since`/`before` window `[since,before)` (both required together, at most 24 hours). It reads
only the real calling conversation's permission history through the owning manager, never another caller's cards
or arbitrary transcript text. `confirmation: found` requires one exact target match in the original two-field
`{"machine","session_id"}` card input, independent of JSON field order or layout, with complete bounded-page
coverage; the four-field evidence query is not matched against the card. The first history read and every later
page use the exclusive upper bound and the `(created_at,id)` cursor, so equal timestamps at `since` are not
mistaken for the window's end. It returns `{id,status,allow?,resolved_at?}` only; multiple matches are `ambiguous`, and no match, a
read error or partial coverage stays `unknown`. `naming` separately reports the exact target's current
`{status,requested,title?,named_at?,observed_at}` (`status` `current`, `not_found` or `unknown`). That snapshot is
not proof this request started or finished a model call and is not associated with its call id. `last_failure` is
not returned because it can belong to background naming. No `model_started`, execution-ended or `retryable` claim
is synthesized. The tool invokes no model, writes no settings, resolves no card, renames nothing and publishes no
session list. Ordinary coding Agents, extensions and work machines cannot call it.

### Health check and feature flags

`GET /api/v1/health` needs no authentication. Public sources get only:

```json
{"ok":true,"hub_id":"<hub UUID>","hub_name":"Home","tls_port":18662,"fp":"<SPKI SHA-256 base64url>"}
```

Trusted sources such as LAN / loopback also get `version` and `features`. The source is judged by the connection address, regardless of whether a token is sent; a public HTTPS health response is trimmed too. No source gets candidate addresses. When TLS is off, `tls_port` is `0` and `fp` is an empty string.

For trusted sources the health check also returns `channel` (`release` / `docker` / `dev`), `build` (UTC `YYYYMMDDHHMM`, 0 if absent), `protocol` (the App ↔ hub major version), `min_app_build` (the oldest App it can pair with, `docs/operations/hub-update.md` "Compatibility"), `commit` (the commit it was built from, `-dirty` after it with uncommitted changes, `""` when the build did not say; the assistant marks a task deployed only once this contains the task PR's merge commit, #3205), and `update.confirmed` (whether the process has finished confirming an update: true when there is no update to confirm; the watchdog waits on it). `channel` and `build` tell how this hub was built and whether it can update itself; WS `hello` carries the same fields. WS `hello` (after authentication) also carries `public_url` (hub.json's `public_url` with the trailing `/` removed; omitted if unset): hub links in assistant answers are built from it, and the App uses it to recognize "links to this hub", even when the phone reaches the hub through another address (#2696).

`hub_name` is this hub's human-readable name (hub.json's `name`, [config.md](../operations/config.md)). `hub_id` is a UUID persisted in the database's `settings`. Clients use it to tell hubs apart and to check they still reach the same instance after switching candidates. `fp` must come from a trusted QR scan or an authenticated trusted channel; never trust an arbitrary public health response to establish pinning.

The authenticated WS `hello.features` always lists server capabilities; trusted `/health` returns the same list. The hub builds it in `features()` (`server/internal/hub/extensions_link.go`): `proto.Features` (`server/internal/proto/proto.go`), then the flags the hub adds from its own state, then those the manager reports for the extensions. The full list:

- Message receipt transport (`proto.Features`): `message_send_state` (hub-received message feedback, "Message feedback (#5258)"). Its feature string is informational; the dedicated current-socket hello version establishes receipt authority.
- In `proto.Features`, by area:
  - Connection and errors: `persona_contracts_v1` (the Persona naming contract: both sides read the old and the new names, and a client keeps sending the old ones to a hub without the flag, [rolling-upgrade-compatibility.md](rolling-upgrade-compatibility.md)), `tls` (the optional TLS listener and SPKI pin), `endpoints` (`GET /api/v1/endpoints`, see "Candidate addresses" below), `client_hello`, `heartbeat`, `app_ping` (see "Client capabilities and heartbeat"), `error_codes` (a stable `code` in error bodies, see "Error body"), `request_id` (`X-Request-Id`, see "Authentication" above), `client_ops` (see "Operation receipts"), `locale` (honors `Accept-Language`, `client_hello.locale` and the device's `locale`; human-readable text follows the language, [i18n.md](i18n.md)).
  - Devices: `ws_notify` (alerts over the WebSocket, see "Notifications over the persistent connection"), `lock_test` (see "Lock screen test"), `android_update` (see "Android packages"), `desktops` (desktop client registration: `register_desktop`, the `desktops` event, "Mute phone" `NotifyPrefs.mute_while_desktop`), `desktop_unregister` (`unregister_desktop` withdraws this connection's registration without closing the socket; without it, the desktop closes the socket and reconnects before it can register again), `desktops_link` (a client that lists `desktops_link` in `?features=` or `client_hello` also gets Persona Link desktops in the `desktops` event), `runtime_cli` (`POST /api/v1/phone/runtime-cli`, and `phone_runtime_cli` kept out of the phone's tools, [runtime-cli.md](../operations/runtime-cli.md) "Reaching a real device through the hub").

`model_configuration` (models configured by purpose, see "Model providers and per-purpose configuration"); `typed_models` (a model ID the launcher's `/model` list lacks is taken by a start, `POST …/modes` and a Persona chat message's pick, IDs typed before come back as `custom: true` and `DELETE …/models/custom` forgets one, #1644; The phone sends photos only when the hub lists it.

The phone writes a meeting's 15-second segments, and the apps read lines and topics, only when the hub lists it.

The phone shows a meeting's highlights only when the hub listed it as the meeting started.
  - `meeting_echo` only while the default manager names `meeting_echo` beside `meeting_attendance` in its `manager.hello` capabilities, the same way (#5905): Persona's echo marked on a meeting's upload (`echo` on `segments` and the top-level `spoken`, the hub's own copy of the rule; echo lines kept but left out of the minutes, the summary and the follow-up; see "Recording sync"). The phone offers **On the hub** and opens the audio socket only when the hub lists it; whether the chosen transcription contribution is ready is the manager's `meeting_transcription_ready`, not this flag.
  - `recording_day` only while the default manager names it in its `manager.hello` capabilities, the same way (an extension's report cannot add it): all-day recordings and their daily recap (#4741): the upload's `kind: "day"` with `day`, `tz`, `part` and `coverage`, `POST …/segments`, `detail.recap`, `recap_state`, `recap_final` and `recap_final_at`; see "All-day recordings (#4741)". The phone uploads a day recording only to a hub that lists it, since an older hub refuses the kind.
  - `assistant_search` only while the default manager names it in its `manager.hello` capabilities, the same way (an extension's report cannot add it): `GET /api/v1/assistant/search`, the assistant's chats found by what was said in them (see "Assistant chat search (#6282)"). Without it the apps filter titles and last messages as before; a non-default manager from before it answers the route 404, which the apps take the same way.
  - `assistant_start_service_tier` only while the default manager names it in its `manager.hello` capabilities, the same way (an extension's report cannot add it): `POST /api/v1/assistant/conversations` takes a native Codex `service_tier` with its first message, acknowledged before the first turn (#6240). The web offers pre-start Fast only while using that default manager and a model whose advertised tiers include `priority`; it neither offers nor sends the field for another manager or an older hub, which would ignore it. An explicit nonempty tier sent to a manager without the capability gets 501 `assistant_service_tier_manager_outdated` before relaying, never a silent Standard start.
  - `agent_session_archives` only while every manager (the default one, each connected one and each computer's owner) is connected and names it in its `manager.hello` capabilities, and `agent_session_archive_close` only while every manager names that one too (see "Agent session archives" above).
  - `agent_autoname` only while every manager (the same set) is connected and names it in its `manager.hello` capabilities: `POST /api/v1/sessions/{mid}/{sid}/autoname`, an Agent session named by the model when the user asks (see "Naming an Agent on request" above). Without it clients do not show **Auto Rename**.

See the card APIs in the REST table and [assistant-views.md](../assistant/assistant-views.md).
- Reported by the manager for the extensions (its `extensions.report`, [extensions.md](../extensions/extensions.md) "Who owns what"): `extension_ui_stream_v1` (whenever the manager runs extensions: extension pages streamed on the app WebSocket once a client negotiates `context.stream`, [extensions.md](../extensions/extensions.md) "Source runtime"), `messaging` (while an extension has a message source, [extension-messaging.md](../extensions/extension-messaging.md)), `error_reports` (while an extension takes error reports, see "Error reports"), `source_subscriptions` (source subscriptions deliver to the Inbox and the knowledge base, #2039: the apps show their entry rows only with it; a manager from before that answers `/api/v1/subscriptions…` and sends `subscription` events without it, [subscriptions.md](../extensions/subscriptions.md) "API"), `subscription_push` (beside it: a device can hand in its own items with `POST /api/v1/subscriptions/-/push`, #3848; the iOS Shortcuts action tells an older hub apart by it, [subscriptions.md](../extensions/subscriptions.md) "Push sources"), `inbox_sources` (beside them: the pages are Inbox Sources, with the built-in sources, recommended subscriptions, Set Up with the assistant and the preview, #5278; the apps show Settings' Inbox Sources row only with it, [subscriptions.md](../extensions/subscriptions.md) "Pages"), `inbox_sources_graph` (beside them: `GET /api/v1/subscriptions/-/graph` answers with Inbox Sources as relations, #5741; the apps offer the relationship view only with it, the same "Pages"), and the `features` that the `api` contributions of enabled, running extensions declare ([extensions.md](../extensions/extensions.md) "App endpoints"). The report cannot add `agent_session_archives`, `agent_session_archive_close`, `meeting_attendance`, `meeting_conversation`, `meeting_photos`, `meeting_live_view`, `meeting_highlights`, `meeting_echo` or `meeting_transcription` or add `assistant_start_service_tier`: only the managers' hellos decide those.

A feature flag means the implementation supports it; `tls` does not mean the listener is on, so also check `tls_port` / `fp`. A new client talking to an old hub falls back to the old behavior based on the flags. `node_version` / `node_mismatch` in the machine list flag whether the hub offers to redeploy the node: it runs another build than the one its platform gets (the hub's, or, with no build of the hub's version for that platform, the newest release its manager drives: `docs/operations/node-update.md` ("Node packages")) (the personad on that computer was not deployed by this hub deployment, i.e. `deploy.sh` deployed only part of it, or it was installed on its own; the hub also logs a line when it connects), or its manager cannot drive it. Another build alone is an upgrade offer, not a fault: whether a node can be used is decided by the node handshake (`node_protocol`, `node_incompatible`; see "Node handshake"). New fields are all optional, and the App currently checks whether a field is present. When a future request would be "misunderstood by an old hub", check here first.

`ultracode` indicates support for Claude Code's independent session toggle (#3427; see "Claude Code ultracode" below). This is a hub capability: switching it on a computer with an older node can still return `409 node_outdated`.

`launcher_switch` is a hub capability too: a computer whose node has not announced the `launcher_switch` capability (or that the manager has not reported yet) answers a `launcher` with `409 node_outdated`.

`engine_switch` is one as well: a launcher of the other engine to a computer whose node has not announced `engine_switch` is refused by that node (`switch_unsupported` or `switch_other_agent`, as before #5054), nothing changed.

`POST /api/v1/machines/{id}/deploy`: the hub installs the node build for that computer's platform and kind of program (its own, left by `deploy.sh` on the hub machine at `~/.persona/bin/nodes/personad-<os>-<arch>`, or the release's, [node-update.md](../operations/node-update.md) "Node packages") on that computer over ssh (when it is going through tailcat, it is sent to the resident node through tailcat; the node replaces itself, exits and is restarted by launchd / systemd), kills the resident node (launchd restarts it with the new binary; `launchctl kickstart` over ssh does not always work) and reconnects. It looks the build up first (at most 20 s when that needs the release site), then runs in the background and returns `{ok}` (409 with a reason when it cannot start). Progress is in the machine list: `deploying` (in progress), `deploy_error` (why the last attempt failed); on success `node_mismatch` goes away. The App shows a notice in **Settings › Machines** with a **Redeploy** button.

Persona Link's active `link` / passive `service` machines, and nodes forwarded through a member hub, are updated over the existing node RPC when they support the update protocol; no SSH is needed. `node.info`'s `node_update` / `node_update_reason` report the local update capability; the machine list's `can_deploy` / `deploy_reason` say whether that entry point can be used right now (also false when there is no node build for the machine's platform anywhere: no build of the hub's own, no release to fetch one from, or none whose node this manager drives; the reason says what to do), and `deploy_phase` is `waiting_idle` / `transferring` / `restarting` / `confirming`. An old node is first upgraded once locally. Deploy jobs are stored in Postgres and support waiting for idle, verifying the install, restarting the resident process, local rollback and confirming it is back online. The detailed RPC and recovery conventions are in [node-update.md](../operations/node-update.md).

<a id="临时配对"></a>

### Temporary pairing

`POST /api/v1/auth/pair-codes` accepts two kinds of callers: **loopback source + master token** (`personad hub pair`), or **a signed-in `full` device token** (any source, #2731: the web client's **Settings › Devices › Connect New Device**).
No request body is needed; when the body carries `machine` or `add`, it generates a pairing code for a computer's Persona Link (see "Computer pairing codes" below).
Watch (`answer`), link, peer and extension credentials, the temporary pairing token itself (one code cannot generate the next), and a master token from a non-loopback source all get 403.
A `full` device can already create long-lived credentials with `POST /api/v1/auth/tokens`; what this gives is a 10-minute, single-use code, so it does not widen permissions. The hub logs a line (device name and id) when a device requests one.
Codes for the App (without `machine`) also return `qr: {size, rows}` (the QR code of the pairing link, one string of `0` / `1` per row, no quiet zone, same as `/admin`).
When the body also carries `"web": "<web URL>"` (an absolute http(s) URL with no `#` fragment and no user/password, otherwise 400), the response also includes `web_url` (`<web URL>#token=<temporary token>`: opening it signs in to the web client, and the part after `#` is not sent to the server) and its QR code `web_qr`. On success it returns HTTP 200 with:

```json
{
  "token":"<temporary token>",
  "expires_at":"<RFC3339 UTC>",
  "url":"http://hub.example.com:18660",
  "hub_id":"<hub UUID>",
  "fp":"<SPKI SHA-256 base64url>",
  "tls_port":18662,
  "alt":["https://hub.example.com:18662"],
  "pair_url":"persona://pair?..."
}
```

The response carries `Cache-Control: no-store`. The temporary token is `jp_` plus the hex encoding of 32 random bytes; the database stores only its hash. It is valid for 10 minutes and works as a full `full` Bearer for the API / WS, for compatibility with the old iOS flow that reads machines, connects WS and registers push before exchanging credentials.

It can **exchange for a device token only once** through `POST /api/v1/auth/tokens`; a second exchange returns `401 invalid_token`. After the exchange, other APIs keep working until `min(original expiry, exchange time + 2 minutes)`; then it expires, and WS connections already opened with the temporary token are canceled too. The validity and grace periods are protocol policy, not measured performance. After a new device pairs successfully, the hub tries to send a pairing notification; if push is unavailable it logs instead.

`personad hub pair` calls the local API above and prints the temporary link and QR code; the running hub must be reachable over IPv4 loopback HTTP. Only `--legacy` prints the old format with the master token offline. Existing iOS ignores the new parameters and can keep scanning the default temporary code on the LAN; it does not need `--legacy`.

The QR code keeps `url` / `token`; the extra fields follow redesign/hub-changes.md 1.3:

```text
persona://pair?url=<compatible URL>&token=<temporary token>&hub=<hub_id>&fp=<fingerprint>&tls=<TLS port>&alt=<HTTPS candidate>&alt=<HTTPS candidate>
```

This shows the structure; actual parameter values are each URL-encoded, and order does not matter.

| Parameter | Format |
| --- | --- |
| `url` | `public_url` or the local IPv6 address selected for an app QR (see below). Old apps still use this field |
| `token` | Temporary Bearer token; the master token with `--legacy` |
| `hub` | hub UUID |
| `fp` | SHA-256(SubjectPublicKeyInfo DER), base64url without padding, 43 characters; not a hash of the whole certificate |
| `tls` | TLS listen port, decimal |
| `alt` | Full HTTPS URL, repeatable; at most two, excluding `lan`. When both literal address families are available, the first IPv6 and first IPv4 candidates, IPv6 first; otherwise the first two eligible candidates in candidate order |

For an app pairing request made over loopback, a native HTTP-only Hub using its own bare hostname and listener port can use a
bracketed unique-local IPv6 address as the QR's primary URL. This applies when LAN discovery finds no private IPv4
address and all eligible IPv6 addresses share one /64. An explicit address or DNS domain in `public_url`, the
`PERSONA_PUBLIC_URL` override, or `public.advertise` takes precedence. The Hub does not write the selected URL
back to its configuration. Browser sign-in links, computer pairing, and requests relayed from a mesh member
keep their existing addresses.

Hostnames (`name` candidates) do not count as either address family because their DNS records may not support both. They remain eligible in the fallback order when one or both literal families are absent. Reserving an explicit IPv4 candidate alongside IPv6 lets IPv4-only clients attempt pairing even when earlier candidates are IPv6 addresses or an IPv6-only hostname. This selection applies to both app and computer pairing codes.

When TLS is off the QR code omits `fp` / `tls`; with no suitable candidate it omits `alt`. The API response still has the matching fields (empty string, 0 or empty array). Renewing a certificate with the same key does not change `fp`; changing the key requires restarting the hub and re-pairing devices through a trusted path. There is no `fp_next` yet.

#### Computer pairing codes (feature `machines_add`, #3735)

From the new-user onboarding plan (#287) 4.2, 5.3. Request bodies:

```
{"add": {"name": "Lin's MacBook", "os": "mac", "icon": "laptop"}}   add a new "Computer connects" (kind link) computer and get its code
{"add": {"id": "macbook", "name": "…"}}                              same, with an explicit id (`personad hub pair --machine <id> --add`)
{"add": {"name": "…", "manager": "m-3fa21c"}}                        same, the computer belonging to that manager
{"machine": "macbook"}                                               another code for an existing link computer
```

- `add.name` may be Chinese (at most 40 characters). Without `add.id`, the id is derived from the name: the ASCII letters and digits in the name (lowercased, everything else becomes `-`); if there are none, `add.os` (`mac` / `linux` / `windows`); failing that, `computer`.
  On collision with an existing id, `-2`, `-3` are appended. `add.os` only decides which install instructions the client shows; the hub does not store it. `add.icon` is `laptop` (default) / `desktop` / `server`.
- The hub uses the same function as the admin page's **Add Computer › Computer connects** to write hub.json and hand it to the manager (effective while running, no restart).
  Computers added by a **device** are pending confirmation ("Computer trust" below); those added by **loopback + master token** are confirmed.
- When a device adds the same name again and that computer is still pending and has never connected, it is reused and a new code issued (`added: false`). A master token with `add.id` that hits an existing link computer also just reissues a code.
- `add.manager` (optional, a manager's id from `GET /api/v1/managers`): the manager the computer belongs to, normally the one the client is showing. The computer is that manager's from the start, never the carrier's first (`docs/assistant/managers.md`, "Moving a machine or a source"). The manager is checked before anything is written: a refused request adds nothing, leaves no pending computer and voids no code. `{"machine"}` takes no manager: the computer keeps its own.
  - Left out (or empty): the carrier's (`assistant`), exactly as before the field, and a reused computer (above) stays with whichever manager has it.
  - `"assistant"` is a valid value and not the same as leaving it out: a new computer is the carrier's as before, and a reused one that belongs to another manager is moved back to the carrier. Any other manager named: a reused computer that belongs to another manager is moved to it first.
  - An offline manager is accepted: the computer waits in hub.json and the manager takes it over when it connects. Until then it is not listed in `GET /api/v1/machines` (the hub lists what a manager reports; the reply's `manager` says where it went), its Persona Link gets `503 assistant_offline` and tries again, and it can be confirmed only from the `computer_joining` push (`POST /api/v1/machines/{id}/confirm`) once its Persona Link has traded the code. Not confirmed within 24 hours, it is removed as any pending computer is.
- A device can only issue codes for **pending** computers (`machine` or reuse); a confirmed one returns 409 `not_pending`. Every code a device issues goes through "pending → confirmed"; re-pairing a confirmed computer is done on the admin page or on the hub machine.
  This is not a security boundary (a full device can already sign credentials for any link computer with `kind: link` on `POST /api/v1/auth/tokens`).
- When a device reissues a code for a pending computer (`machine` or reuse), the computer's existing Persona Link credentials are revoked first: whichever computer redeemed the previous code, it cannot get confirmed along with the one holding the new code.
- Success is 200 with `Cache-Control: no-store`. Besides the fields above (`token`, `expires_at`, `url`, `hub_id`, `fp`, `tls_port`, `alt`, `machine`, `pair_url`; no `qr`), it adds:

```json
{"machine": "macbook", "name": "Lin's MacBook", "trust": "pending", "added": true, "manager": "m-3fa21c",
 "pair_url": "persona://link?url=…&token=…&machine=macbook&hub=…&fp=…&tls=…",
 "command": "persona-link pair '<pair_url>'",
 "install": {"linux": "curl -fsSL <site>/install.sh | sh -s -- --node --pair '<pair_url>'"}}
```

  `trust` is `pending` or `confirmed` (always present here). `added` says whether this call added it (omitted when not). `manager` is the manager the computer belongs to now (on every computer code, `{"machine"}` too):
  the client compares it with the `add.manager` it sent and, when they differ, says which manager the computer is under. A hub from before `add.manager` ignores the field and
  leaves `manager` out of the reply: a computer it added (`added: true`) is the carrier's, and one it reused stays where it was, which need not be the carrier. A client that sent a manager and gets
  no `manager` says so: a new computer is under the carrier; for a reused one it can look it up in `GET /api/v1/machines`. No `hello.features` flag: the reply tells. `install` is present only when the hub knows which site it was published from
  (the build-time `publish.site_url`, [config.md](../operations/config.md); local builds and Docker images don't have it), and currently only has `linux`.
- Errors (`error` is localized per `Accept-Language`):

| HTTP | code | When |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 403 | `forbidden` | Not a full device: a watch, a link, a temporary identity from a pairing code, an extension; a master token from non-loopback |
| 409 | `tls_required` | The hub has no TLS and is not behind an HTTPS reverse proxy, so Persona Link cannot connect; carries `"action": "enable_tls"` |
| 409 | `mesh_member` | The device is connected to a member hub of a linked-hub group: add it on the primary hub |
| 429 | `too_many_pending` | The device is adding a new computer while 3 are already pending (reuse and reissue don't count) |
| 409 | `exists` / `not_pending` | The given id already exists (and is not a reusable link computer) / a device issuing a code for a confirmed computer |
| 404 | `not_found` | The `machine` a device sent is not a link computer in hub.json |
| 404 | `no_manager` | `add.manager` is not in the roster (or was removed meanwhile) |
| 409 | `installing` | `add.manager` is still being installed (its install code not traded yet) |
| 503 | `assistant_offline` | The reused computer is in the own list of a manager that is offline, so it cannot move to `add.manager` now |
| 503 | `owners_unknown` | The hub could not read which manager carries which computer yet (as for a move); try again |
| 503 | (any other) | The hub could not read the roster to check `add.manager` (its database did not answer); try again |
| 400 | `unknown_machine` | The `machine` sent with a master token is not a link computer in hub.json (`hub pair --machine` then suggests adding `--add`) |
| 400 | `invalid_name` / `invalid_id` / `invalid_os` / `bad_request` | Missing or too-long name / id breaks the rules / unknown os / `machine` and `add` sent together, or `web` included |

- Receipts: when a device issues a computer code, the **other** paired devices get a push "<device> made a pairing code for the computer “<name>”"; when a pending computer's Persona Link redeems the code, all devices get "A new computer, “<name>”, wants to join. Open the app to confirm it’s yours"
  (instead of the usual "New device paired"). The code-issued receipt is a security receipt and deliberately ignores the device's notification preferences, mute and "don't push while the computer is in use". If push is unavailable it logs. Both issuing (`code`) and redeeming (`redeem`) are written to `machine_audit`.
- Receipt push payload (#4199): all three carry `aps.category` and a top-level `pair`. The ids the notification buttons need go only in `pair`; the notification text contains no ids or addresses
  (when the issuing device has no name, the text says "A device", not the credential id):

  | When | `aps.category` | `pair` |
  | --- | --- | --- |
  | A device issues a code for a computer (pushed to other devices) | `pair_receipt` | `{"kind":"computer_code","device_id":"<credential id of the issuing device>","machine":"<computer id>"}` |
  | A pending computer redeemed the code (pushed to all devices) | `computer_joining` | `{"kind":"computer_joining","machine":"<computer id>"}` |
  | A new credential (new device, Persona Link of a confirmed computer) paired (pushed to all devices) | `pair_receipt` | `{"kind":"device","device_id":"<new credential id>"}` |

  Client buttons: `pair_receipt`'s **Not you? Revoke** calls `DELETE /api/v1/auth/tokens/{device_id}` for `kind: device`, and `POST /api/v1/machines/{machine}/reject` for `kind: computer_code`
  (409 `not_pending` if the computer is already confirmed, which opens the machine details). `computer_joining`'s **It's Mine** / **Not Mine** call `…/confirm` / `…/reject`. Through the push relay, `category` and `pair` are encrypted along with the rest of the plaintext
  ([push-relay.md](../operations/push-relay.md) "Encryption"), so the relay cannot see them; the notification service extension decrypts, restores the category, and keeps `pair` in `userInfo`. Old hubs don't send these two fields, and clients show a normal notification.
  iOS / Mac already register both categories (`apple/Persona/App/PairReceiptActions.swift`): the buttons require unlocking and don't open the App, and the result comes as a local notification ("Pairing revoked", "Computer confirmed", or the reason on failure).
  The action goes to the hub that sent the push, found by the push's `hub_id` (or by the key set that decrypted it). Tapping the notification itself: `computer_joining` opens **Confirm Computer**, `pair_receipt` opens **Settings › Devices**.
  The watch does not register these categories; Android and web are not done yet.

<a id="候选地址"></a>

### Candidate addresses

`GET /api/v1/endpoints` requires authentication and returns `{hub_id,tls_port,fp,endpoints}`. Each endpoint:

```json
{"url":"https://[2001:db8::1234]:18662","kind":"ipv6","port":18662,"scheme":"https","seen_at":"<RFC3339 UTC>"}
```

The address is a documentation example. `kind` is `ipv6` / `name` / `lan` / `ipv4`, sorted in that order; within a kind HTTPS comes first. `scheme` is `https` / `http`. `seen_at` is when it was collected, not proof of reachability. Candidates merge `public_url`, `public.advertise` and qualifying local addresses; public IPv4 is published only from explicit configuration. When TLS is off, automatic candidates use HTTP, and clients must not send tokens in plaintext over the public internet because of that.

WS `hello` carries the candidates too. When the address list changes, the hub sends `{"type":"endpoints","endpoints":[...]}`, only to clients that declared `endpoints` in `client_hello.features` on that connection; a change in `seen_at` alone does not trigger the event. The event is the complete candidate list and may be empty; clients should replace the old list.

### Error body

The main API's shared error handling keeps the `error` text and adds a stable `code`. `retryable` and `delivered` are **optional** and only given when they can be determined. 404 / 405 on the main router also return JSON. Separate sub-handlers such as mail, and streaming responses, follow their own protocols; don't assume they all carry the new fields.

```json
{"error":"invalid token","code":"invalid_token","retryable":false,"delivered":"none"}
```

`delivered` is `none` / `unknown` / `yes`; absent does not mean not executed. In particular, a plain timeout never gets a made-up `none`. Absent `retryable` does not mean automatic retry is OK either. Node 409 details stay flat (e.g. `draft`, `clearable`) and are not wrapped in a new `data`.

| code | Typical HTTP status | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `tls_required` | 403 | Plaintext public API rejected; `delivered: none` |
| `master_token_local_only` | 403 | The master token can't be used over the public internet; `delivered: none` |
| `invalid_token` | 401 | Credential invalid, expired, revoked, or a temporary token exchanged twice; `retryable: false`, `delivered: none` |
| `forbidden` | 403 | Permission or pairing-code source requirements not met; `retryable: false`, `delivered: none` |
| `rate_limited` | 429 | The source is banned after authentication failures; wait per `Retry-After` |
| `token_store_unavailable` | 503 | The hub could not look the credential up (its database did not answer), so this says nothing about the credential: never treat it as revoked; retry per `Retry-After`. Not counted as an authentication failure |
| `bad_request` | 400 | Bad parameter / JSON; `retryable: false` |
| `not_found` / `method_not_allowed` | 404 / 405 | Resource doesn't exist / method not supported; `retryable: false` |
| `gone` | 410 | The interaction is no longer pending, etc.; `retryable: false` |
| `conflict` | 409 | A conflict with no more specific code |
| `input_draft` / `dialog_open` / `prompt_changed` | 409 | The send or answer was explicitly refused; `retryable: false`, `delivered: none`, see below |
| `op_id_reused` | 409 | The operation ID was already used for a different device, target or parameters; don't blindly retry with a new ID |
| `agent_start_stalled` | 409 | The agent opened but its session was not identified before the start deadline (Codex), or Claude ran but never showed its input box (since #2570: `data.screen` holds the tab's last lines, and `pane` / `kept_until` say where the tab is kept open, as for `shell_waiting`). Launcher health is unchanged; no automatic task retry or detour. Uses the existing RPC error `code` and message, also carried in `start_error_code` and task `error_code`. New hubs retain generic failure handling for uncoded errors from older nodes; older hubs can show the new node's message but may still count it as a launcher failure |
| `shell_waiting` | 409 | A start's new terminal tab stopped on a question from its shell's startup files (an update prompt, `[Y/n]`, "Press Enter") before the start command was typed (#2570). Nothing ran; `delivered: none`. `data`: `line` (the question), `screen` (the tab's last 12 lines), `pane` and `kept_until` (the tab stays open until then, then closes unless an agent came up in it). Launcher health is unchanged |
| `start_line_rejected` | 409 | A start's new terminal tab did not take the typed start line twice: something before the shell's line editor ate its first characters, and the shell answered for the rest (`permission denied` for the start file, `command not found` for a cut word, a parse error, an open quote). The node types the line once more before giving up. Nothing ran; `delivered: none`; the tab is closed. `data`: `line` (the shell's answer) and `screen`. Launcher health is unchanged |
| `node_outdated` | 409 | The node doesn't support the requested feature, e.g. file upload |
| `too_large` | 413, or 409 mapped from node RPC | Request / file over the limit |
| `timeout` | 408 / 504, often 502 for node calls | Timed out; the outcome can't be judged from this code alone |
| `node_unreachable` | 502 / 503 | The node is offline or the connection dropped; when clearly offline, `retryable: true`, `delivered: none`; not necessarily so for a dropped connection |
| `no_machine` / `machine_pending` / `claude_missing` / `launcher_missing` | 409 | The main chat (and other assistant chats) can't start: no computer / the computer isn't confirmed yet / Claude Code isn't installed on that computer / launcher not found. `error` is a plain-language sentence the hub writes in the request's language (naming the computer), `detail` is the raw text (the shell's error, shown only under "Details"), `action` is the suggested action (`add_computer` / `confirm_computer` / `install_claude` / `connect_model`), plus `machine_name`, `launcher` (sometimes) and `delivered: none`. `machine_pending` is defined and appears only once pending computers ship. Design: new-user onboarding plan (#287, #3339) sections 4.6, 5.2. **A start in a new terminal tab** (`POST /api/v1/sessions`, `agent_start`, a task) whose tab's shell said it can't run the launcher (`launcher_missing`) or the claude it runs (`claude_missing`) fails within seconds with the same codes plus `where: "terminal"`, `missing` (the command or path the shell named), `kind` (`not_found` / `no_such_file` / `permission_denied`), `pane_shell` (the tab's shell; absent when the node cannot tell, and the sentence says "the default shell"), `launcher_shell` and `rc_file` (where the node lists launchers) and `line` (the shell's own line); the sentence then says the terminal's shell lacks it and where the list came from (#1642, `docs/integrations/launchers.md` "The terminal's shell is another environment"). A launcher the node does not list either is plain `launcher_missing` without `where` |
| `center_unreachable` | 503 | Connected to a member hub of a linked-hub group, and the group's primary hub is unreachable right now (carries `center: {hub_id, name}`); the member does not take over on its own; switch to another or wait for the primary to return ([mesh.md](../server/mesh.md) "Primary") |
| `internal` | 5xx | Other internal errors |

The table lists the shared handler and the main business codes; other explicit node RPC error codes are passed through too, usually mapped to 409. Clients should branch on `code`, show `error` for unknown codes, and keep the old behavior when an old hub sends only `error`.

APIs that take a JSON body all have a size limit, from 1 KiB to 32 MiB depending on the API (`decodeJSONBody` in the hub, and the managers' copies of it): the manager join (`POST /api/v1/bus/join`) 1 KiB; small settings, card choices (`…/choose`) and pair codes 4 KiB; device registration and prefs, notify and `POST /api/v1/admin/peers` 16 KiB; hub-to-hub pairing (`POST /api/v1/peer/pair`) 64 KiB; pin / mute / launchers / card answers (`…/resolve`) / connector replies 1 MiB; starting a session (`POST /api/v1/sessions`) 4 MiB; session messages, interrupts, keys and the other bodies the hub hands to a node as they are (git commit / push / pr, agent settings) 32 MiB, which is also the hub's cap on any request it forwards to a manager. Over the limit returns 413 `too_large`; the hub stops reading at the limit instead of reading it all. Malformed input is still 400. Some manager routes still read with a plain size cap and answer an oversized body with 400 instead, for example `PUT /api/v1/recordings/{id}` (16 MiB) and `POST /api/v1/task-plans/{id}/start` (1 MiB).

## Operation receipts (client_ops)

Once the server declares `client_ops`, clients may send `X-Persona-Op-Id: <UUID>` on the following write requests:

| Operation kind | Path |
| --- | --- |
| `message` | `POST /api/v1/sessions/{mid}/{sid}/messages` |
| `start` | `POST /api/v1/sessions` |
| `assistant_start` | `POST /api/v1/assistant/conversations` (hub feature `assistant_start_ops`) |
| `resolve` | `POST /api/v1/interactions/{id}/resolve` |
| `choose` | `POST /api/v1/interactions/{id}/choose` (also accepts a body `client_id`; see "Answering a question from its notification") |
| `interrupt` / `close` / `rename` / `modes` | `POST /api/v1/sessions/{mid}/{sid}/interrupt`, `/close`, `/rename`, `/modes` |

The UUID is case-insensitive. The hub builds a digest from the operation kind, path, normalized query parameters and JSON parameters, then claims the ID atomically. A repeated request reuses the receipt only for the same device, target and parameters; a conflict returns `409 {"code":"op_id_reused"}`. Message requests set `client_msg_id` to the operation UUID, overriding any value of that name in the body. Without the header or a route-specific body receipt ID, the old behavior stays, including old iOS's non-UUID `client_msg_id` and `sent_messages` dedup.

`GET /api/v1/ops/{id}` returns the record `{id,device_id,kind,target,digest,state,result,created_at,updated_at}`. `target` contains `path` / `query`. Once recorded, `result` is `{status,body,content_type?}`, where `body` is the base64 of the original HTTP response bytes. It returns 404 when the record doesn't exist or doesn't belong to the current device credential. The master token has no device ID, so its queries are not filtered by device ownership.

| `state` | Meaning and retry behavior |
| --- | --- |
| `pending` | Claimed, execution not finished; a repeated write waits for the receipt and returns `202 {"state":"pending"}` when the configured wait runs out |
| `done` | Success receipt stored; a repeated write replays the original HTTP status and body without executing again |
| `failed` | Definitely failed, receipt stored; a repeated write still replays the original result |
| `unknown` | Outcome unknown; for ordinary operations a repeated request returns `202 {"state":"unknown"}`. Query or check by hand; never treat it as success or resend automatically |

For ordinary operations, HTTP 400 / 409 are usually recorded as `failed`; other errors are recorded as `unknown` unless it can be shown they didn't execute. On startup the hub marks leftover `pending` as `unknown` and does not re-execute them. After completion it still tries to store the receipt even if the HTTP caller has disconnected; if storing fails it returns 503 with `state: unknown`. Receipts are kept for 30 days from creation. That is a retention policy; dedup beyond the window is not guaranteed.

Lark sends and Inbox replies also derive receipts from the body's `client_id`; see "Lark API" below. They reuse `client_ops` too, but an existing upstream error response is replayed as-is. Don't apply that response rule to all ordinary operations.

When a new session is started with an operation ID, the hub keeps finishing an accepted start after the caller disconnects and stores the receipt. Replaying the same ID won't start it again; an existing HTTP result is returned as-is even if marked `unknown`, and leftover operations with no result still return `202 {"state":"unknown"}`. Android persists the ID and parameters before sending, and queries the ID if the response is lost. Neither a 404 nor an unknown result proves it didn't start, so it keeps the pending-confirmation record and doesn't POST again. Only a clearly failed receipt allows editing the form and starting a new operation. Clients without the header keep the old behavior.

A new assistant conversation (`assistant_start`, #1349) works the same way: an accepted start finishes after the caller disconnects, a repeat with the same ID gets the first answer (also when it was `502 assistant_in_doubt`, recorded as `unknown`), and nothing is started twice. `503 assistant_offline` keeps no receipt (nothing reached the assistant), so the same ID can try again once it is back. iOS / Mac send one ID per first message and, on a hub with `assistant_start_ops`, try it again through a gap (no network, a timeout, the hub restarting, `202 pending`) for up to a minute; on an older hub they send no ID and don't retry gaps.

## Device connections and lock screen test

### Connection records

`GET /api/v1/devices/{id}/sessions?since=<RFC3339 UTC>` returns `{sessions,summary}`. It defaults to the last 24 hours and is clipped to at most the last 14 days; a future or invalid time returns 400. `{id}` is the device credential ID, distinct from the push registration ID and the client-reported `client_hello.device_id`. This query uses the existing general authentication and currently has no extra restriction to the calling device; the lock screen test APIs do strictly check the current device.

Each session is `{id,device_id,connected_at,disconnected_at,reason,source,heartbeat_interval}`. `id` is the numeric database ID, used only over HTTP. While the connection is still open, `disconnected_at` is null and `reason` is empty. `source` stores only the IPv4 /24 or IPv6 /64 prefix. The heartbeat interval is the current protocol configuration, not a measured send rate.

- Only WS connections with a device token create connection records; master tokens and temporary pairing tokens are not recorded.
- `reason` is `closed`, `pong_timeout`, `error`, `replaced` or `hub_stopped`. When the hub starts or stops and fixes up unfinished records, it marks them `hub_stopped` and does not assume it can recover the exact crash time.
- `summary.disconnects` counts non-`hub_stopped` disconnects in the window; parallel connections may each count. `summary.longest_gap_seconds` merges overlapping connection intervals and computes the longest offline gap, including a gap still open at query time and excluding gaps caused by hub stops. The unknown period before the first known connection is not inferred.
- Records are kept for 14 days. The connection summary reflects what the hub observed; on its own it can't prove the phone was locked or the system killed the process.

### Lock screen test

The server capability is `lock_test`. In these APIs `{id}` must equal the current device credential ID; master tokens, temporary pairing tokens and other devices' credentials cannot act on its behalf.

| Method | Path | Request and response |
| --- | --- | --- |
| POST | `/api/v1/devices/{id}/lock-tests` | `{delay_seconds?}`, default 30, 1–3600 seconds allowed; body optional. Returns the test record |
| GET | `/api/v1/devices/{id}/lock-tests/{test_id}` | Returns the current test record, 404 if missing |
| POST | `/api/v1/devices/{id}/lock-tests/{test_id}/receipt` | `{notification_shown?}`, body optional; returns the record after the first report, repeated reports keep the first result, 409 if not sent yet or no matching test |

The record is `{test_id,device_id,created_at,due_at,status,device_session_id?,sent_at?,received_at?,notification_shown?}`. `device_session_id` is the numeric ID of the connection record actually chosen. When due, the hub picks only the most recently established connection of this device that declared `client_hello.features: ["lock_test"]` and has a connection record, and sends a standalone event:

```json
{"type":"lock_test","lock_test_id":"<test ID>","lock_test_due_at":"<RFC3339 UTC>","lock_test_sent_at":"<RFC3339 UTC>","lock_test_title":"Lock screen test","lock_test_body":"Test notification received. Go back to the app to see the result."}
```

All new payload fields have the `lock_test_` prefix to avoid clashing with old iOS Envelope types. The client shows a local notification and then reports back. Absent `notification_shown` means unknown, and true doesn't prove the user saw the notification or that the device was locked at the time. The test is scheduled by the user, is not subject to ordinary notification preferences, and does not require the `ws_notify` capability.

| `status` | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `scheduled` | Stored, waiting until due |
| `sent` | A send attempt was recorded, no device report yet; not to be treated as delivered |
| `received` | The hub received the device's report |
| `unavailable` | No qualifying connection when due; not resent |
| `interrupted` | The schedule had expired when the hub restarted; not resent |

A hub restart keeps future schedules. Recording the send and writing to WS can't be done atomically, so `sent` with no report may also mean an interruption or a failed write; it is not resent automatically. Records are kept for 14 days, and the link may be empty after connection records are cleaned up. The schedule delay is configuration; scheduling precision, background survival and whether the notification actually shows were not measured.

## Android packages

Both APIs require authentication; the feature flag is `android_update`:

| Method | Path | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| GET | `/api/v1/app/android/latest` | Returns the published `latest.json` as-is, with `download_url` set to the pinned APK below; the release script writes `{package_name,version_code,version_name,min_sdk,certificate_sha256,notes,sha256,size,source_sha}`, and one taken from a release's `android.json` adds `version` and `name` |
| GET | `/api/v1/app/android/apk` | Reads the APK by the manifest's `sha256`; MIME `application/vnd.android.package-archive`, attachment name `persona.apk`, ETag is the quoted digest, supports ServeContent range and conditional requests. A GET that takes gzip (no range) gets the published gzip copy with `Content-Encoding: gzip`, `Vary: Accept-Encoding` and the ETag `"<sha256>-gzip"`; the decoded bytes are the APK |

Published files live in `apps/android/` under the hub's config directory, with APKs named `<sha256>.apk` and their gzip copies `<sha256>.apk.gz` (an APK stores its dex files uncompressed, so the copy is about half the size; without it the APK goes out as it is). They come from a publisher over SSH (`scripts/release/publish_android_apk.py`) or, on a hub with an update source, from the newest release's `android.json` (`docs/operations/hub-update.md` ("The Android app")); either way `latest.json` is written last, under `.publish.lock`. Unpublished returns 404; an invalid manifest digest returns 500. Clients should verify size and digest, keep downloads same-origin, and leave installation to the system's confirmation. Upgrades with the same package name and signature still need on-device sign-off after artifacts are published.

## Codex sources and capabilities

External Codex sessions keep using `(machine_id, session_id)`. The fixed legacy home keeps its existing raw thread IDs; threads in other canonical homes use an opaque ID of `c0de-` plus a deterministic digest. Changes in PID, endpoint or connection generation don't change the session ID. `source_thread_id` is the original thread ID; never put the opaque ID into `claude --resume`.

New optional Session fields: `source_kind` (`codex_history` / `codex_app_server` / `identity_conflict`; Agent runtime sessions are `runtime`, see "Runtime ↔ node"; Claude Code sessions outside Persona's terminals are `claude_bg` (a background session), `claude_desktop` (Claude's desktop app) and `claude_cli` (a terminal Persona does not drive), sending through the session's peer inbox when the node can use it, see `docs/integrations/claude-integration.md` "Claude outside Persona's terminals"), `source_thread_id`, `source_instance_id`, `parent_thread_id`, `read_only_reason`, `attached`, `capabilities` (six booleans: read/send/interrupt/approve/terminal/attach, and the optional `modes`, `close`, `rename`, `model`, `rewind` and `rewind_code`). Old sources lacking these fields stay compatible; new sources lacking capabilities default to refusing writes. Without the terminal capability, terminal / keys / close pane are not shown.

`capabilities.takeover` is an optional object `{running, can_resume, reason?}`; `reason` is `encrypted_context` or `unavailable`. The signed-in full-device manager route is not an assistant tool, and generic device-call APIs deny it. GET `/api/v1/machines/{mid}/codex/{sid}/takeover` returns `{token, cwd, transcript_path, continuation_prompt}` with a single-use token valid for two minutes.
