- A cursor traverses a **frozen filtered snapshot**: updates, deletions and inserts while scrolling cannot duplicate, omit or reorder rows in that snapshot. Every page returns its snapshot's same `revision` and `total`.
- Snapshot retention is five minutes, with at most 32 active views per collection. A restart, expiry or eviction returns HTTP **409**, `code: "cursor_expired"`; restart at page one. Cursors bind filters and summary mode; a mismatched/tampered cursor returns 400.
- The runtime collection includes Codex history. It uses the manager's already-decorated state, ownership, hidden/deleted-session rules and task metadata; it does not recompute business state in the hub.

#### Ranked runtime search (`sessions_search`, #7624)

The runtime collection advertises `sessions_search` independently. It searches the hub's already-indexed Agent
metadata and latest available text, including unloaded historical sessions. It does not fetch transcripts, call models,
search every past message, or search the separate personal-agent collection. Assistant conversations are excluded:
the existing `assistant_search` contract owns them. Older hubs can ignore unknown parameters, so clients must gate
on the capability and require `search_hits` in a successful response before calling the result complete.

```http
GET /api/v1/sessions?search=machine%3Astudio%20parser&summary=1&roots=1&limit=40
```

`search` accepts one nonempty, valid UTF-8 query of at most 1,024 bytes. The page size defaults to 40, with a maximum
of 100; `q`, `since`, `counts`, `with_counts`, `catalog` and exact `session_id` lookup cannot be combined with it,
even when those parameters are empty or false. Existing filtering and permission constraints still apply. Legacy
`q` remains a contiguous substring and existing list/delta ordering is unchanged.

The normal page fields are retained, with `search_hits` always present (an empty object for no matches). Its keys
are the same JSON-encoded `[machine_id, session_id]` tuples used by runtime removals. Each value is
`{score, evidence?: {role, before, match, after}}`; `role` is `user`, `agent`, `error` or `title`. Evidence contains a
bounded fragment of actual indexed text, not model-generated explanation. Its match may fall after the summary's
truncated title or preview, so a client must not discard the row by matching the compact summary again. The map
contains only identities in the returned page, not other matches or inaccessible sessions.

All whitespace-separated terms must match the same session, though different terms may match different fields.
Explicit operators use case-insensitive substring values except exact states; values within a dimension are OR,
dimensions and remaining words are AND. Unknown operators/values remain literal terms. Plain words never silently
become filters. Supported spellings follow the existing web matcher:

| Dimension | Operators |
| --- | --- |
| Computer ID/display name | `machine:`, `host:` |
| Project name/folder | `project:`, `repo:`, `cwd:`, `path:` |
| Agent runtime ID/name | `harness:`, `agent:`, `launcher:` |
| Model | `model:` |
| Unified state | `state:`, `status:`, `is:<state>`; `is:unknown` remains literal |
| Pinned session | `is:pinned`, `is:pin`; workspace pins do not imply session pins |
| Error or attention | `is:error`, `is:errors`, `is:failed`, `is:blocked` |
| Recent update | `since:`, `after:`, `updated:` with `24h`, `7d`, `30d` and existing aliases |

Time aliases retain current client behavior: `1d`, `2d`, `48h` select the 24-hour bucket; `1w` selects seven days and
`1m` thirty days. The last recognized time operator wins. This search's time window is unrelated to the legacy
`since` delta checkpoint. The shared corpus under `spec/fixtures/session-search/` checks client/server behavior.

Global ranking is title prefix 100, title substring 80, all terms in title/project/computer/space/tab/folder 60,
other indexed metadata/latest text 40, and operators-only 30. Add 5 unless the displayed state is offline. Sort by
score descending, then update time descending and composite identity ascending. This happens before paging, not
by sorting each newest-first page in the browser. `roots=1` preserves existing child-folding and folded-state rules.

The first page freezes its ranking, evidence, membership, machine-name/pin/attention context and time cutoff.
Continuations repeat the same query and filters but use that frozen result. Normal five-minute/32-view cursor limits
apply; a 409 expiry requires an explicit new search. Authorization/private-session filtering precedes decoding,
matching and totals; cursor scope includes the authorized machine set, manager and private-data policy. Runtime
search remains hub-wide for ordinary credentials unless `manager` is explicitly supplied; a sidebar Assistant choice
or an `X-Persona-Manager` header does not silently narrow it. Extension tokens remain limited to their own manager.

#### Pane/host origins (`sessions_pane_source`, #994)

`hello.features` advertises **`sessions_pane_source`** independently of `sessions_list`. Only when it is advertised may clients request:

```http
GET /api/v1/sessions?pane_source=terminal&summary=1&limit=50
GET /api/v1/sessions?pane_source=feishu&counts=1
```

Bounded runtime rows (full and summary) include **`pane_source`**, and runtime counts include a **`pane_source` map** (omitted when empty) over the complete matching set. Classification matches the clients' `sessionSource`, in this order:

1. `space_kind == "codex_app"`, `host == "paseo"`, or both `source_kind == "runtime"` and `source_instance_id == "orca"`: **`desktop`**, even if a pane is present.
2. A `botmux:` pane: **`feishu`**.
3. Any other nonempty pane: **`terminal`**. This includes recognized Orca/Herdr App terminal panes and legacy Herdr identities; an unrecognized prefix remains a legacy Herdr pane, as in the host registry.
4. No such metadata: **`unknown`**. A runtime transport alone is not evidence of a terminal origin.

`source` still filters the existing `source_kind`; neither it nor the session's separate `origin`/`origin_ref` is repurposed. Origin combines with the other supported filters and exact lookup. The filter participates in cache keys and frozen cursor bindings. An origin-only change advances the index revision, updates complete counts, and causes an upsert/removal when a row enters/leaves the filter, even if `source_kind` and `updated_at` stay unchanged. Page, count and delta snapshots retain their existing revision rules; use a matching cursor for frozen counts.

Empty, repeated, comma-separated or unrecognized origin values return **400 `invalid_query`**. Personal-agent `/api/v1/agents/sessions` rejects this runtime-only parameter (including `unknown`); it has no pane/host metadata and does not infer origin from its provider. For an extension token restricted to one manager in a multi-manager hub, aggregate origin requests must specify an authorized `machine_id`; an unsupported aggregate returns **400 `invalid_query`** instead of computing totals through the legacy ownership projection. A token authorized for the whole runtime collection needs no machine selector. Restricted aggregate requests without an origin filter retain the legacy counts projection and omit the new origin dimension; specify a machine to obtain exact origin counts.

These counts describe the hub's complete shown runtime-session collection after the explicit filters, including any assistant/other rows that the legacy collection contains. They do **not** establish preference-defined Agents membership, pins/mutes/to-do sections, retained client windows, personal-agent aggregation or new sorting rules. Machine/session identity remains the composite `(machine_id, session_id)`.

Old hubs ignore unknown query keys, so clients **must retain the old full-list/classifier fallback unless `sessions_pane_source` is advertised**. `sessions_list` alone is insufficient. No current client query, visual default or ordering changes here. Without opt-in, legacy full-list rows and behavior are unchanged; bounded requests without an origin filter retain their membership and ordering.

#### One manager's sessions (`sessions_manager`)

`hello.features` advertises **`sessions_manager`** independently of `sessions_list`. Only when it is advertised may clients send `manager` on the runtime collection:

```http
GET /api/v1/sessions?manager=m-abcdef&summary=1&limit=50
GET /api/v1/sessions?manager=m-abcdef&counts=1
GET /api/v1/sessions?manager=m-abcdef
```

- `manager=<id>` selects the sessions on the computers that manager owns (each row's `manager`, `docs/assistant/managers.md` ("Ownership")): in a page, in `total`, in the counts (every map covers that manager's sessions only), in an exact lookup and in a `since` delta. It combines with the other filters. Without the key every manager's sessions are listed, as before.
- It does not opt into the bounded API by itself: `GET /api/v1/sessions?manager=<id>` alone answers the legacy whole list, of that manager's sessions.
- Only the query names the manager here. The `X-Persona-Manager` header is not read on this route (the hub answers it itself and never routed it), so a client that sends the header with every request gets every manager's sessions unless it adds the key.
- The filter is part of cache keys and frozen cursor bindings: repeat it with a cursor, and a cursor of another manager's list returns 400. Keep it with `since`: a computer moved to another manager leaves the old manager's list as removals in its next delta and enters the new manager's as upserts, with the rows' new `manager`.
- `manager` given twice or empty returns **400 `invalid_query`**; a manager the roster does not have (one still being installed included) **404 `no_manager`**; an extension's token naming another manager than its own **403 `other_manager`**, and naming its own changes nothing.
- A manager that is offline keeps its list: its sessions are listed in state `unknown`, as without the key.
- The key filters this route only. The WebSocket `sessions` / `sessions_delta` pushes are not filtered by manager (they carry every manager's computers), so a client using `manager` drops the rows of other managers from pushes by each row's `manager`. A `sessions_list` notification can also fire for another manager's change.

Old hubs ignore unknown query keys and would answer with every manager's sessions, so clients **must filter by each row's `manager` themselves unless `sessions_manager` is advertised**. That works for the whole list only: on an old hub a bounded page's `total`, counts and `has_more` cover every manager, so a client cannot get one manager's numbers there. Personal-agent `/api/v1/agents/sessions` is routed per manager as before and does not take this key as a filter.

#### Exact runtime-session detail (`sessions_lookup`, #6054)

`hello.features` advertises **`sessions_lookup`** independently of `sessions_list`. Only when it is advertised, a client can fetch one complete runtime row without paging or scanning unrelated sessions:

```http
GET /api/v1/sessions?summary=0&limit=50&machine_id=demo&session_id=<URL-encoded exact session id>
```

- `session_id` is an exact, opaque runtime id, not a substring or slash-separated path. It opts this runtime endpoint into the bounded API even without `limit`/`summary`; it does not apply to the personal-agent endpoint.
- Supply exactly one nonempty `session_id` and one nonempty `machine_id`. Repetition, missing machine id or an empty session id returns **400**, `code: "invalid_query"`.
- The `(machine_id, session_id)` tuple resolves directly in the existing transport-index map. Other row filters still apply to that one candidate. `summary=0` (the default) returns the identical complete, decorated/shown `Session` DTO used by the collection, including `background`, `subagents`, `workflows`, `queued`, ports and all session configuration. `summary=1` and `counts=1` retain their ordinary meanings for that candidate.
- The ordinary collection envelope is unchanged: `sessions` has zero or one row, `total` is 0 or 1, `remove` is `[]`, `has_more` is false, `next_cursor` is absent, and `revision` is the current collection checkpoint. A missing, hidden or deleted session is an empty matching collection, not a 404. The existing `agents.read` scope and manager ownership restrictions apply; a foreign manager's machine still returns 403 `other_manager`.
- Exact lookup cannot be combined with `since` or `cursor` (400 `invalid_query`). An active-chat getter takes a fresh exact baseline after coalesced `sessions_list` invalidations, rather than borrowing a list-summary delta checkpoint. Its revision is not a baseline for the whole collection.
- An active-chat getter that asked for `sessions_list_changes` (below) skips that read for a hint whose `since` is the revision of its last exact answer and whose `changed` does not name its `[machine_id, session_id]`: the answer would be the same row, and it now stands at the hint's `revision`. Any other hint (no `since`/`changed`, another `since`, its id listed) reads as before. The web does this (`web/src/lib/runtime-session.ts` `SessionDetailLoader.hint`, #6685).
- Older hubs ignore unknown query keys: sending `session_id` to one can silently return an unrelated first page of 50 sessions. Clients **must gate on `sessions_lookup`**, never assume `sessions_list` implies it. If absent, retain the older detail/full-list fallback. Requests without `session_id` and unknown parameters otherwise keep their existing behavior.

The direct lookup/count path does not build, scan or sort unrelated session views, even on a missing id, new filter or changed revision. Runtime index initialization remains a one-off full-collection cost; upstream full-list reports still update the index normally. `BenchmarkExactLookup` measures uncached found/missing requests against 1, 8,000 and 32,000 rows separately from initialization.

#### Summary rows

Runtime summaries keep the existing snake_case names and decode as a `Session` with optional detail fields absent. They contain:

- Identity/ownership: `machine_id`, `session_id`, `manager`; pane/host origin `pane_source` and `host`; source/runtime and hierarchy fields (`source_kind`, `source_thread_id`, `source_instance_id`, `parent_thread_id`, `parent_session_id`, `root_session_id`, `is_subagent`).
- Display/grouping: `title`, `cwd`, `workspace_cwd`, `repo_root`, `worktree`, `branch`, `agent`, `agent_label`, `agent_surface`, `agent_name`; space, parent-space, slot, pane, tab and workspace identifiers/names/indices; `todo {id,title}`.
- State/freshness: `state`, `status`, `updated_at`, `state_since`, `seen_at`, `pending_interactions`, `rev`, `quiet`, `awaits_reply`, `background_working`, `background_waiting`, `starting`, `awaiting_first_message`, `start_error`, turn-error fields.
- Session hierarchy (see "Session hierarchy" below): `folded_under`, `folded_as`, `children`, `started_at`, `asking_parent_session_id`.
- Row content/progress: `last_text`, `activity`, `activity_at`, `model`, `effort`, context-token/window counts; bounded `work` (phase/on/line/wait/then/wake/attempts/agent/deferred), `plan`, `goal`, and `loop` timing with its prompt omitted.
- Routing/action safety: `capabilities`, `attached`, `can_fork`, `read_only_reason`, `started_by_persona`, `assistant`, `archived`, `space`, `origin`, `origin_ref`, and an assistant chat's `model_pick` (clients that replace a chat with its summary row keep it, #5033).
- Additional scalar summaries: **`waiting`** (loop, running background tasks/subagents/workflows or an eligible hub wake), **`background_count`**, **`running_subagents`**, **`running_workflows`**. Counts of zero may be omitted; `waiting` is always a boolean. A summary-aware client uses these rather than inferring “none running” from missing arrays.

- Compact background progress (#3588): **`background_tasks_count`** is the independent count of live background entries other than `kind: workflow` and `kind: agent` (Bash commands, Monitor and other jobs). It is always present on a new summary, including **0**. **`workflow_progress`**, when present, is the newest running workflow, using the existing Workflow shape: `task_id`, `name`, `summary`, `status`, `running`, `phase`, `phase_index`, `phase_count`, `agents_started`, `agents_done`, `agents_running`, `started_at`. It has no `agents`, `phases`, `phase_stats`, tools, command, output or error content. Name/summary/phase are bounded to 256/180/120 Unicode characters. A disappeared projection clears the old run; omitted scalar counts on a summary mean zero, not a partial update. Legacy workflows/subagents reported only as background entries contribute to their respective running counts, not `background_tasks_count`.

Titles and to-do titles are capped at 256 Unicode characters; previews, error lines, work/plan/goal text at 180 (a `start_error` with a `start_error_code` at 600: the hub's sentence, its remedy last); activity/loop reason at 120. Summaries omit `background`, `subagents`, `workflows`, `queued`, ports and chat-only configuration. Do **not** replace an open chat's complete detail state with an incomplete row summary; fetch its existing `info`/`items` routes. A new client needs a summary-aware decoder/waiting rule, not just a query change.

Personal-agent rows are already compact: their summaries retain the existing entire row (`id`, `source`, `sessionKey`, `accountId`, `provider`, `title`, `kind`, `parentSessionKey`, `canSend`, `unreadCount`, `rankTimeMs`, avatar presence/version). Their bridge contract exposes only unread counts, not runtime execution state: unreadCount > 0 maps to `unread`, otherwise `idle`; no `working`/`needs_you` state is invented.

#### Counts without downloading sessions

```http
GET /api/v1/sessions?counts=1
GET /api/v1/sessions?counts=1&machine_id=demo&state=working
GET /api/v1/agents/sessions?counts=1&source=demo
```

```json
{
  "total": 8000,
  "machine": {"demo": 8000},
  "project": {"/demo/app": 8000},
  "group": {"space-a": 8000},
  "state": {"working": 2000, "needs_you": 2000, "unread": 2000, "idle": 2000},
  "pane_source": {"terminal": 4000, "desktop": 2000, "feishu": 1000, "unknown": 1000},
  "todo": {"todo_3f2a9c1d0b7e4a65": 3, "": 7997},
  "background_waiting": 120,
  "revision": "<opaque checkpoint>"
}
```

`background_waiting` (#6045, omitted when 0) is how many of the `working` ones only wait in the background (`Session.background_waiting`); they stay in `state.working` for older apps, and a client that shows them apart takes them out of its Working count.

Each map counts the complete filtered membership by that dimension; missing attributes use the empty-string key. `limit` does not truncate counts. With a matching `cursor`, counts refer to that frozen view; without one they refer to the current collection. `since`, if supplied, is validated but does not turn counts into counts of changes. Read counts separately when a group expands, rather than deriving totals from loaded pages. The runtime `pane_source` map uses the explicit four origins above, including `unknown`; the personal-agent collection omits this dimension. The maps do not contain preference-defined custom sections, per-user pins/mutes or computed repository trees.

#### Counts with the page (`sessions_page_counts`, #4858)

`hello.features` advertises **`sessions_page_counts`** independently of `sessions_list`. Only when it is advertised, a runtime page read (a first page or a `since` page) may add `with_counts=1`; the response is the ordinary page plus a `counts` object, the value `?counts=1` with the same filters returns (current membership: `since`, `cursor` and `limit` do not change it):

```http
GET /api/v1/sessions?summary=1&limit=50&since=<checkpoint>&with_counts=1
```

- A refresh that needs both rows and counts takes one request instead of two. The web runtime list and a filtered Agents list ask for them on the first page of each refresh (only that page of a multi-page delta) and fall back to the separate `counts=1` read when the answer has no valid `counts`.
- `with_counts` takes the same boolean values as `counts`; anything else is 400 `invalid_query`. Without it the page is unchanged. An extension token's manager-limited view gets that manager's counts, as with `counts=1`.
- Older hubs ignore the key and answer with the page alone: clients send it only when the feature is advertised, and still handle a page without `counts`.
- **`agents_page_counts`** (#6496) says the same of the personal-agent endpoint: a paged `GET /api/v1/agents/sessions` (a first page or a `since` page) takes `with_counts=1` and answers with the page plus what `?counts=1` with the same filters returns, from one refresh of the sources. The web personal list and a filtered personal list use it the same way.

#### Session hierarchy (`sessions_hierarchy`, #5120)

Some sessions are started by another session and arrive as rows of their own: a Codex subagent (`thread_spawn`) and an Agent another Paseo Agent created. A client can show such a child as a card in its parent's chat instead of a row, the parent's row carrying the children's state. The other Agents in a host tab fold the same way under the tab's lead (tab teams, below). The server says which row each child or worker folds under, so every client folds the same way:

- **Child and parent.** A child is a row with `is_subagent`, `parent_session_id`, `asking_parent_session_id`, or a `root_session_id` other than its own `session_id`. Its parent is the listed row on the same machine that `parent_session_id` names, else the one `asking_parent_session_id` names, else `root_session_id`'s. The manager walks up while the parent is itself a child with a listed parent; the row it stops at is the child's **`folded_under`**. A child with no listed parent (an orphan: its parent archived or not listed) and a row whose ancestors go round in a cycle have no `folded_under` and stay rows of their own. Archived Agents and a review's reviewers are not in the list the manager folds.
- **Tab teams (#5180).** In a host tab with several Agents (rows of the same `space_kind`, `space_id` and `slot_id`, both ids set; a herdr tab), the **lead** is the Agent in the tab's first pane (`pane_index` 0, the pane the others were split from): a listed row there that is no child and not `offline`. Every other listed Agent in that tab that is no child and not `offline` is one of its **workers**: its parent is the lead, so it gets `folded_under` (the lead) and **`folded_as: "worker"`**. A child keeps its own parent (a worker's child folds under the lead, the topmost listed ancestor, with no `folded_as`). A tab has no lead, and folds nothing by this rule, when its first pane is a shell or not known (`pane_index` absent), when that Agent is offline or a child, or when more than one row claims the first pane; its Agents stay peers. A stopped (`offline`) pane is no worker and stays a row of its own. Assistant rows are in no team.
- **Drawn under, not folded (`parent_agent_id`, #5935).** A row may name in **`parent_agent_id`** a listed row on the same machine it is drawn under while staying a session of its own: its own row, state, sends, unread and every count, `roots=1` included. It is no child: the manager folds nothing by it, it gets no `folded_under` and adds nothing to a `children` rollup. The node sets it on a Claude desktop app's side session (a side chat, a /btw question, a spawned session) to the session that started it, while that one is listed too (`docs/integrations/claude-integration.md` "The desktop app's sidebar (#3304)"). A client draws such a row under its parent, a level in, when it lists both, and as a row of its own otherwise; rows whose parents loop are drawn on their own. The web nests a row under its topmost listed ancestor, one level in, each group where its most recently active member is (`lib/side-sessions.ts`).
- **Fold only under a row you have.** The hub can still hide the row a child names in `folded_under` (a session deleted from the lists, `DELETE /api/v1/sessions/{mid}/{sid}`). A client folds a row only under a parent it actually lists on the same machine, and shows any other child as a row of its own; the paged list does the same (below).
- **Rollup.** The row children fold under carries **`children`** `{"total", "working", "needs_you", "workers"}`: all of them, whatever their depth, counted by their own `state` (`working` and `needs_you` omitted when 0); **`workers`** is how many of them are its tab's workers (`folded_as: "worker"`), counted in `total` too, omitted when 0. The manager computes both on each complete list, after the states; a single row sent on its own keeps what the last complete list said.
- **Folded state.** A row with children shows one state for itself and them (Go `proto.Session.FoldedState`, web `foldedState`): `needs_you` when it or a child needs the user; else `working` when a child works, unless the row is `unread` or `idle` with `awaits_reply` (its own result or question comes first); else its own `state`. The row's `state` stays its own.
- **`asking_parent_session_id`.** A runtime child that waits for the user (`status: blocked`) is listed without `is_subagent`, `parent_session_id` and `root_session_id` (#4494): the apps that fold every child away by those fields (iOS, Android, older web) would otherwise hide a session that needs the user and leave it out of their counts. The node names its parent in `asking_parent_session_id` meanwhile, so the clients that fold by `folded_under` keep the card, and its question, in the parent's chat. Once it is answered the parent fields come back and the key goes.
- **`started_at`** is when the session began, for a child card's running time: a Codex rollout's first line, a runtime row's `started_at` (the Paseo bridge sends the Agent's created time). Absent where the node does not know it.
- **Cards.** An interaction (`GET /api/v1/interactions`, the `interaction` push) carries **`folded_under`**, the asking session's, and its **`folded_as`** when that session is a tab's worker: a client shows the card in that session's chat.
- **Counts that stay.** Folding changes no other count: a child is still counted where it was (the fleet, the Live Activity, a Codex subagent's or a runtime child's subtask rules), and so is a tab's worker, which no subtask rule covers: the fleet and the Live Activity count it on its own, `roots=1` under its lead. The two definitions differ on purpose. The fleet and the Live Activity count by `IsSubtask`: a Codex subagent and a runtime child are counted under their parent, except a runtime child that waits for the user, which counts on its own (Needs you) while it waits. `roots=1` counts by `folded_under`: that waiting child is folded under its parent too (through `asking_parent_session_id`), so the parent is counted once, in Needs you by its folded state, and the child is not.

Every field is additive and omitted when empty, on full rows, summaries, `sessions` / `session` / `sessions_delta` pushes and pages; a client that ignores them sees no change. On the paged runtime list, when `hello.features` advertises **`sessions_hierarchy`**:

```http
GET /api/v1/sessions?summary=1&limit=50&roots=1&with_counts=1
GET /api/v1/sessions?summary=1&limit=50&machine_id=demo&parent_session_id=<sid>
```

- `roots=1` leaves out of the rows, `total` and every count map the rows whose `folded_under` names a row the hub lists for the same machine (a child whose parent the hub hides, a deleted one, stays a root). The `state` filter and the `state` map use the folded state of the rest; `background_waiting` counts a row only when none of its children works or needs the user.
- `parent_session_id=<sid>` with `machine_id` lists the rows folded under that session, all depths, with their own states; `counts=1` and `with_counts=1` count the same rows.
- Both combine with the other filters and are bound into cursors, cache keys and `since` deltas like them: repeat them with a cursor (a cursor of another view returns 400), and a row that becomes folded or unfolded leaves or enters the view as a removal or an upsert in the next delta.
- `roots` takes the boolean values of `counts`; repeated or malformed values, an empty `parent_session_id`, one without `machine_id` and `roots=1` together with `parent_session_id` (the rows folded under a session are never roots) return **400 `invalid_query`**.

Older hubs ignore both keys and answer with every row, so clients send them only when `sessions_hierarchy` is advertised.

#### Projects and spaces (`sessions_catalog`, #994)

The `project` filter and the `project` count map go by a directory's path, so one repository checked out on two computers is two projects, and a path means nothing without its computer. The `group` map has the same limit: space ids are machine-local and say nothing a person reads. When `hello.features` advertises **`sessions_catalog`**, the runtime collection answers both:

```http
GET /api/v1/sessions?catalog=1
GET /api/v1/sessions?catalog=1&state=needs_you&q=release&roots=1
GET /api/v1/sessions?summary=1&limit=50&place=%5B%22mac%22%2C%22%2FUsers%2Fme%2Fcode%2Fapp%22%5D&place=%5B%22pc%22%2C%22C%3A%5C%5Ccode%5C%5Capp%22%5D
GET /api/v1/sessions?counts=1&space=%5B%22mac%22%2C%22w1%22%5D
```

```json
{
  "revision": "<opaque checkpoint>",
  "total": 5,
  "projects": [
    {"id": "git:git.example.com/team/app", "name": "app", "origin": "git.example.com/team/app", "total": 3, "needs_you": 1,
     "places": [{"machine_id": "mac", "path": "/Users/me/code/app", "total": 2, "needs_you": 1},
                {"machine_id": "pc", "path": "C:\\code\\app", "total": 1}]},
    {"id": "dir:notes", "name": "notes", "total": 2,
     "places": [{"machine_id": "mac", "path": "/Users/me/notes", "total": 1},
                {"machine_id": "pc", "path": "D:\\work\\Notes", "total": 1}]}
  ],
  "spaces": [{"machine_id": "mac", "id": "w1", "name": "Release", "total": 2, "needs_you": 1},
             {"machine_id": "pc", "id": "", "name": "", "total": 3}]
}
```

- **Membership.** `catalog=1` counts the same filtered rows as `counts=1` with the same keys (`state`, `machine_id`, `project`, `group`, `source`, `provider`, `q`, `pane_source`, `roots`, `parent_session_id`, `manager`, `place`, `space`), at the current `revision`: `total` is their number, every row is in exactly one project and one space entry, and each `total` is over them. A project, a place and a space also say how many of their rows need the user (`needs_you`, omitted when 0), by the state the `state` filter goes by: the folded state with `roots=1`. A client that folds a group shows that number on its heading from this one read. `limit` and `since` do not change it (`since` is validated); a `cursor` is ignored, the catalog being of the current list. An extension token's manager-limited view has its own computers only, and its projects all go by their folder's name: what repository a directory holds is the Git routes' answer, which take full credentials, so an extension is not told it and no computer is asked for it.
- **A place** is one directory on one computer: `path` is the rows' project attribute there (`repo_root`, else `workspace_cwd`, else `cwd`), the value the `project` filter takes with that `machine_id`. The rows without one are the last project, with an empty `id` and `name` and a place with an empty `path` for each of their computers.
- **A project** is a repository wherever it is checked out. The hub asks each place's computer what the directory holds (the node's `git.status` with `identity_only`, the same answer the Git routes give) and remembers it. Directories whose computers name the same network remote are one project: `id` is `git:` and the remote lowercased, `origin` the remote as the computer spelled it (`host/path`, never credentials; a non-default SSH account as a digest), `name` its last segment. A directory with no repository, no remote or only a local-path remote, and one whose computer has not said (offline since the hub started, a node from before `identity_only`), goes by its folder's name: `id` is `dir:` and the name lowercased, so `Notes` and `notes` are one project. The folder is the path's last segment by its computer's own separator: a path that starts with a drive letter or a UNC share is a Windows computer's, read by backslashes and slashes; any other by slashes only. A project's name and origin are as its first place has them.
- **`pending`** (omitted when false): some places' computers were still being asked when the answer was written (the hub waits about 1.5 s). Those places go by their folder's name in this answer; read again a moment later. The hub asks a computer about a directory once, uses the answer for 30 minutes, and tries again after a minute when the computer could not be reached; nothing a page, a count or a push is built from waits for it.
- **A space** is one computer's: `id` is the rows' group attribute there (`space_id`, else `workspace_id`), the value the `group` filter takes with that `machine_id`; `name` is the rows' `space_name` for it, the id when they have none. A computer's rows in no space are an entry with an empty `id` and `name`.
- **Order.** `projects` by `total` descending, then name (ignoring case), then `id`; a project's `places` by `total` descending, then `machine_id`, then `path`; `spaces` by `total` descending, then name, then `machine_id`, then `id`. The entries with an empty `id` come after all the others. `projects` and `spaces` are `[]`, never null.
- **`place`** selects the rows at any of the given places, the way to list or count a project that has several: pass each of its `places` as `["<machine_id>","<path>"]`. **`space`** selects the rows in any of the given spaces the same way, as `["<machine_id>","<id>"]`. An empty path or id selects that computer's rows without one, as the catalog's last entries list them. Each combines with every other filter (a place and a `machine_id` that excludes it select nothing; `place` with `space` selects the rows that match both), applies to pages, `counts=1`, `with_counts=1`, `since` deltas and `catalog=1`, and is bound into cursors and cache keys as a set: repeat the same pairs with a cursor in any order; a cursor of other pairs returns 400. A value that is not a JSON array of exactly two strings, an empty machine id, or more than 64 values of one key returns **400 `invalid_query`**.
- `catalog` takes the boolean values of `counts`; repeated or malformed values return **400 `invalid_query`**.

Older hubs ignore these keys: `catalog=1` then answers an ordinary page, and `place` and `space` filter nothing. Clients send them only when `sessions_catalog` is advertised, and keep grouping by the `project` and `group` count maps otherwise. The personal-agent collection has none of them.

#### Sessions by to-do (`sessions_todo`, #6662)

`hello.features` advertises **`sessions_todo`**. Only then does a runtime page or counts read take **`todo=<id>`**, the sessions on that open to-do, or **`todo=none`**, the sessions on none; and the counts have a **`todo`** map, each open to-do's sessions by its id and the sessions on none under `""`. A session's to-do is `Session.todo`, which the default manager sets for an active link only (a done to-do is `completed_todo`), so the hub needs no list of open to-dos: `none` covers a done to-do's sessions too. To-do ids are `todo_<hex>`, never `none`. `todo` combines with the other filters and binds a cursor as they do; empty or repeated values return **400 `invalid_query`**.

The web's paged Agents list draws **By to-do** with it (`docs/web/web.md` "By to-do"): a section per open to-do read with `todo=<id>`, the sessions on none with `todo=none`, every number from one counts read. Older hubs ignore `todo` and list every session, so clients send it only when `sessions_todo` is advertised, and read the complete list for By to-do otherwise.

#### Quick filters (`sessions_quick_filters`, #6662)

`hello.features` advertises **`sessions_quick_filters`**. Only then does a runtime page or counts read take **`waiting=0|1`** and **`exclude_pane_source=<origin>`**. The web's paged Agents list draws the complete list's quick filters with them (`docs/web/web.md` "Paging hubs"): Needs you `state=needs_you`, Unread `state=unread`, Working `state=working&waiting=0`, Waiting in the background `state=working&waiting=1`, Lark group `pane_source=feishu`, Terminal `pane_source=terminal`, their numbers from one counts read (Working is `state.working` less `background_waiting`); hiding botmux adds `exclude_pane_source=feishu` to every read. Older hubs ignore both keys, so clients send them only when the feature is advertised and otherwise keep the state chips.

#### Incremental recovery

```http
GET /api/v1/sessions?summary=1&limit=50&since=<URL-encoded checkpoint>
```

The page has the same envelope. `sessions` contains the latest copies of changed/new matching rows; `remove` includes deleted rows and rows leaving the filter. Multiple changes to one identity collapse to its final state. For runtime rows, each removal is a **JSON tuple encoded as a string**, e.g. `"[\"demo\",\"session/with/slashes\"]"`; decode it as `[machine_id, session_id]`, never split on `/`. Personal-agent removals are their existing opaque `id` strings.

Retained deltas cover at most 128 revisions and 16,384 changed identities, evicting whole revisions. A restart or an older checkpoint returns HTTP **409**, `code: "revision_expired"`; obtain a fresh baseline, never silently treat it as a successful empty delta. Frozen delta cursors remain valid even if the underlying journal is subsequently evicted.

Client sequence:

1. Request the first summary page and counts; render immediately and fetch further pages only when needed. Keep page cursors distinct from the delta checkpoint.
2. For a complete local baseline, finish all frozen pages before advancing its checkpoint. If only a window is loaded, retain `total`/counts separately; an incoming delta may contain rows outside that window and must not be interpreted as an instruction to materialize every row.
3. After changes, fetch `since` with identical filters/summary, follow all delta pages, apply upserts/removals, and **only after the last page** advance to the returned target `revision`. Changes arriving meanwhile belong to the next delta.
4. On 409, reset and reload; on a changed filter, obtain a new first page. A counts checkpoint alone is not a row baseline.

#### Lightweight WebSocket negotiation

`hello.features` advertises **`sessions_list`**. A new runtime-list client requests `?features=sessions_list` (may list other features too). When present, it takes precedence over `sessions_delta`:

- On connect/reconnect the hub sends **no full `sessions` snapshot**, including no hidden Codex-history backlog. It sends `{"type":"sessions_list","revision":"<checkpoint>"}` once and again when the indexed collection changes.
- This small event is an **invalidation hint**, not a delta payload or authoritative baseline. Coalesce bursts, then call the HTTP `since`/counts API with the client's saved checkpoint. Do not advance the checkpoint merely by receiving the event. Reconnect always receives a current hint; HTTP epoch checks cover restart recovery.
- Existing subscribed chat items, interactions, machines and terminal streams are unchanged. Personal-agent `agents` events remain unchanged; on those events use the personal-agent collection's own HTTP checkpoint, not the runtime checkpoint.
- Older hubs do not advertise the feature; fall back to their existing full-list/delta behavior.
- **Which rows changed (`sessions_list_changes`, #6685).** A client that also lists `sessions_list_changes` in `?features=` gets, on a hint that follows a change of the index, `since` (the revision before the change) and `changed` (the ids changed after `since` up to `revision`, sorted, the same `["<machine_id>","<session_id>"]` tuples `remove` holds): `{"type":"sessions_list","revision":"<r2>","since":"<r1>","changed":[["demo","s1"]]}`. `changed` may list rows a client's filters leave out, and a change made in between by another pass; it is never missing a row changed in that range. The hub leaves both out when it cannot say (more than 64 ids, `since` no longer in the change journal) and on hints with no starting point (connect, a hub-wide notice); an extension's token never gets them. Consecutive hints chain (`since` of one is `revision` of the one before) only while nothing changed unannounced; a client trusts `changed` only from a `since` it holds, and reads otherwise. Hubs that do not know the feature ignore it and send plain hints.
- A view that needs every row keeps a **complete copy** instead of reading the query-free list per hint (#3759: that was a 373 KB list a few times a minute per client while agents worked): complete pages (`summary=0&limit=200`, no filters, all frozen pages) as its baseline, then `since` reads of complete rows, with new rows joining the copy. It reads complete pages again only on first use, `revision_expired`, a changed hub or an explicit refresh. A hint whose `revision` equals the client's checkpoint needs no read: the token includes the index epoch, so a restarted hub never repeats one. The web's pins / saved-grouping fallback and per-assistant lists (`web/src/lib/complete-sessions.ts`) and the iOS Agents list's complete fallback (grouping, filters, search, pins or mutes; `SessionListModel.complete`) do this; Android (#3760) still reads the whole list per hint.

#### Cost and verification

The runtime origin classifier lives in `server/internal/sessionorigin`, using the host registry and a shared corpus checked against the web client. The shared transport index carries/matches the immutable origin attribute without classifying sessions. The shared transport index lives in `server/internal/sessionlist`; the runtime adapter is `server/internal/hub/sessions_list.go`, the personal-agent adapter `server/internal/agents/list.go`, and its HTTP facade `server/internal/extmgr/agents.go`.

Runtime indexing is lazy on the first paginated reader/negotiated socket, then updated by the manager's session-list reports and existing push hook. Personal-agent indexing updates when the existing 20-second source cache refreshes or its fallback poll runs; invalidation generations prevent late responses from resurrecting removed/stale data. Unchanged batches do not advance the revision. A runtime row whose encoded bytes and origin the index already holds keeps its indexed summary and full row rather than being marshalled again (`indexedRow`): an update usually changes one row, and the summary is cut from the fields those bytes encode. Rows are computed again after a batch where two rows share an id, and in the batch after it. A `sessions.revs` (and the first index build) reads the machine's kept list and takes its rows from the push's kept encodings (`indexKeptLocked`, `Machine.encodeKept`): only rows whose bytes, rev or manager changed are encoded, and the list is not copied to stamp its manager, which only a re-marshalled summary carries. There is no database migration or new JSON state file.

Filtered ordered views/counts are cached by revision (up to 64); warm pages and counts do not scan or sort the full collection. Unfiltered counters are maintained on changed records, so an unfiltered delta/count request does not scan or sort unrelated sessions even after a revision change. Filtered counts never build an ordered list merely to count matches. A new filter or changed revision builds one ordered view only when pages need it and reuses it. This moves work to updates/first cache misses; it does not claim that an upstream full-list report is O(1). Frozen views, query caches and the journal are bounded. Cold index initialization is a one-off cost and must be measured separately from warm request latency.

`TestRuntimePaneSource8000` compares all pages and complete count dimensions for mixed origins and filter combinations against a corpus independently checked by the current web classifier, including late-page Feishu rows and repeated session ids across machines. Origin-only transitions and frozen page/count/delta bindings have separate regression tests. `TestIndexRowReuseMatchesFullPath` runs the reusing runtime adapter beside the full computation over lists that change, gain, lose, repeat or reorder rows, comparing pages, summaries, counts, revisions and deltas at every step; `TestReindexKeptMatchesDecorated` drives `sessions.revs` events and compares every item and revision with the full computation over the decorated list (hidden rows, an id listed twice, a list without its bytes, a manager change). `BenchmarkReindexOneRev` and `BenchmarkIndexWholeList` measure a `sessions.revs` on a list kept with its bytes and a whole-list update, each with one changed row; `TestReindexOneRevAllocation` and `TestIndexWholeListAllocation` bound their allocation.

`TestAgents8000Measurement` and `BenchmarkAgents8000Legacy` exercise the real runtime HTTP handler with 8,000 synthetic rows (four machines, previews and task metadata), reporting JSON bytes, request CPU, allocations, retained heap and process peak RSS. `TestPersonalAgentPagedRoutes8000` checks the extension HTTP adapter and warm source-call count. Index tests traverse all 8,000 frozen rows, filtered counts, field-only changes, removals, expired cursors/checkpoints and concurrent readers/writers. One-off before/after readings and local test output belong in the linked PR/archived acceptance record, not in this evolving contract.

### Live status (`session_live`, 2026-11-05)

The status line at the bottom of the screen while Claude Code works (`✻ Frosting… (16m 15s · ↓ 22.8k tokens · thinking with xhigh effort)`) has a verb, this turn's elapsed time, output tokens and whether it's thinking, none of which is in the transcript.
The web shows it for subscribed sessions, so the node reads it from the screen and pushes it.

- Type `proto.SessionLive` (`server/internal/proto/live.go`): `verb` (without the ellipsis), `elapsed_s`, `tokens_down` (output tokens from `↓`; `↑` is input and doesn't count), `thinking` (the `thinking…` segment),
  `thought_s` (`thought for 3s`), `at` (when the node read it, RFC 3339); missing fields are omitted.
- node → hub event `session.live {session_id, live}`, where `live` is a `SessionLive` or `null`.
  - Only read while this session is watched (a client is subscribed), it's Claude (`agent == "claude"`) in a host whose screen can be read (herdr, herdr-core (Herdr App) or Orca; the latter two read plain text and parse it the same way, #3904; Codex, botmux, runtimes and the headless assistant aren't read), and the host reports `working`:
    the screen is read about once a second (for herdr, `pane.read --source visible --lines 60`) with a 3-second timeout per read, in a goroutine of its own and one read at a time per session, so it slows down neither the 250 ms transcript pushes nor another session (`node/claudestatus.go`). One ticker on the node drives every watched session (`watchPump` in `node/session_watch.go`): each tick stats the transcript and reads it only when it grew, so a watched session at rest costs a stat four times a second and no screen read.
  - Parsing: starting from the top border of the input box (the second-to-last horizontal line on screen) and going up, skip blank and indented lines (hints, to-dos, right-aligned `/goal`); the first unindented line is the status line, or there is no status line;
    so a status line quoted in body text, tool output or a user message is never taken as the current one. Any spinner character (`· ✢ ✳ ✶ ✻ ✽`…), durations `2s` / `1m 5s` / `1h 2m 3s`, token units k / M / none; segments in the parentheses may be missing or in any order,
    and hints like `esc to interrupt` are ignored.
  - Sent only when different from the last one (`at` isn't compared). When work stops, the status line disappears or the watch ends (`session.unwatch`), a `live: null` follows, but only if a non-null one was sent before. A failed screen read sends nothing and logs nothing, keeping the last value.
- hub → client `{"type":"live","machine_id","session_id","live"}`: only sent to connections subscribed to this session that declared `session_live`, either in the WebSocket URL's `?features=` (the web's `wsQuery`)
  or in `client_hello.features`. The hub doesn't cache or replay: a newly subscribed client waits for the next change (within about a second while working). Old Apps don't declare it and don't get it; other events are unchanged.
- `hello.features` currently doesn't list `session_live`: clients just declare it anyway, and an old hub that doesn't know the event simply doesn't send it.

### New session

Opening a herdr tab, running the launcher and waiting for Claude's input box takes anywhere from a few seconds to a minute (a slow `~/.zshrc`, the trust-folder dialog). The App's **Start Chat** button used to spin until Claude was ready,
and the hub also had to wait for the small model to come up with a tab name first (about 2 seconds). Now `POST /api/v1/sessions` takes `async`:

- The node only does the cheap checks (launcher name, directory exists, permission mode), records the session (`sessionState`: the chat page's history fetch returns an empty list, and the subscription waits for the transcript to appear), and returns the session right away;
  opening the tab, running the launcher, waiting for readiness and sending `prompt` happen in the background (at most 4.5 minutes: up to 3 minutes for the shell to start claude, then up to 1 minute for the input box once claude is up, #1396).
- While starting, the session is in the session list with `status: idle`, `starting: true` (not counted as a turn, not timed, no "done" push). If starting fails it becomes `offline` with `start_error`, kept for 10 minutes, and `updated_at` becomes when it failed.
  A start the node refused with a code (the new tab's shell has no such launcher, or no claude: `launcher_missing` / `claude_missing` with `where: "terminal"`, see "Errors") also has `start_error_code` and `start_error_args` (the refusal's details as strings: `launcher`, `where`, `missing`, `kind`, `pane_shell`, `launcher_shell`, `rc_file`, `line`);
  `start_error` is then the hub's sentence for that code in the user's language (naming the computer), so the App can show it as is and offer the code's remedy (`connect_model` / `install_claude`); list rows and a task's `start_error` keep it whole (up to 600 characters) rather than clipping it like other error lines. A message waiting for the start gets the same code (409). Older nodes send text only.
- Messages sent while it's starting (`session.send`) wait on the node until it's ready, then are typed in order; the hub gives these sends, and sends to sessions that aren't running and must be resumed first, 5 minutes (90 seconds normally). If starting fails, these sends get the same error, and the App's bubble switches to "resend".
- The App's first message isn't put in `prompt`; it's sent as a normal message once in the chat (shows up immediately, with send status), and `name_hint` is used for naming. Above the chat input box it shows "Starting Claude…" or the failure reason (`StartingNote`).
- A node restart loses records of sessions still starting: the session is then neither in the list nor has a transcript, and the App's send fails and can be resent.
- Codex launchers (`agent: "codex"`) don't use `async`: Codex only creates the thread and fixes the session id when it gets the first message, so the App puts the first message in `prompt` and creates synchronously,
  and the node waits until that thread appears before returning (at most 60 seconds), returning its session. With no `prompt`, a node whose Codex launchers carry `prompt_optional: true` (in `launchers.list` and the hub's launcher lists)
  opens Codex waiting for its first message and returns a row with `awaiting_first_message: true`, `status: idle` and an id of its own; the first message, sent to that row or typed in its terminal, makes it the thread,
  in the same pane (`docs/integrations/codex.md` "Starting without a first message"). Rejection `code`s: `codex_needs_prompt` (`async` given, or no `prompt` on an older node),
  `codex_launcher` (a shell function that runs Codex), `codex_resume` (a Codex session that cannot be resumed from the phone: something has it open, or there is no record of it; see `docs/integrations/codex.md` "Resuming from the phone"). See `docs/integrations/codex.md` ("Creating from the phone").

### Sending messages

#### Message feedback (#5258)

A send has three distinct boundaries: the client has local input, the hub has received the request, and the node has
accepted the input. None of these alone proves that the model has begun answering.

- Show **Sending** locally as soon as the user sends, before any network or durable-outbox work.
- Subscribe to the target session before posting the message. Trust live receipts only when the current authenticated
  `hello` has top-level `message_send_state: 1`, a transport version fixed by the hub. The feature array alone is not proof:
  older hubs merge extension feature strings and did not reserve this event name. Clear this trust on disconnect/reconnect
  and credential changes; a new connection must announce its own version. This is not a user setting, and the hub emits
  to subscribers without client negotiation. For a request with `client_msg_id`, the hub sends
  `message_send_state` with `state: processing` after basic admission and before manager parameter preparation or
  terminal/process startup. Show **Processing** immediately. The existing operation middleware may first wait on its
  database admission; this receipt is not an early HTTP success, a durable queue guarantee, or permission to resend.
- Keep this per-message state separate from `Session.status`. An already working or blocked turn must not be changed
  by a new send, and a stale session-list snapshot must not erase the pending receipt. Match the machine, session and
  message ID; ignore unrelated receipts. The existing conversation/outbox state owns draft and failure recovery.
- The final event is `delivered`, `failed` or `unknown`. `delivered` hands feedback to authoritative execution/queued
  state, not to Done; no first token is needed. `failed` removes that send's Processing overlay and exposes the existing
  HTTP error and recovery. `unknown` retains the existing delivery-check guard. Receipt alone must not enable Interrupt
  as if it cancelled a not-yet-delivered HTTP flight: the hub deliberately continues that flight after disconnection.
  Keep the existing execution/delivery gate for Stop; no pending-send cancellation API is introduced here.
  Transcript echo may arrive before the
  final HTTP response; it must not resurrect an already acknowledged bubble or end a still-running turn.
- This live event is not replayed on reconnect. A missing event does not prove failure: reconcile the original operation
  through its HTTP receipt or retry the same unchanged ID, as below. A concurrent retry joins the same send flight;
  completed HTTP replays do not broadcast an older terminal event over a newer attempt.
- A client talking to an older hub keeps its Sending/outbox feedback until the existing HTTP and transcript evidence
  arrives. No client may pretend that local enqueue alone was a hub receipt.

Apple integration uses the same event and boundaries; no Apple code changes are included in #5258. A new main
conversation started through a creation endpoint has no target session subscription yet: keep local Sending/Preparing
until that endpoint's existing result binds it, then use the ordinary session flow.

Typing into someone else's terminal is the riskiest thing this App does. Before typing into a running Agent's pane, the node reads the screen once (`server/internal/node/sendsafe.go`,
`server/internal/screen`), and in the following cases **types nothing** and returns 409:

| `code` | When | Other fields |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `dialog_open` | A dialog holds the keyboard: permission prompt, trust folder, model picker, rewind, Claude Code's own notices… (`Esc to cancel` / `Enter to confirm` at the bottom, or numbered options with a cursor under the input box) | `delivered: "none"`, `dialog` (the dialog's first line), `notice` (true when it's just a notice closed by pressing Enter) |
| `input_draft` | Claude's input box has unsent text from the computer, bash mode (`!`), a paste placeholder, or a long draft cut off by the pane | `delivered: "none"`, `draft` (the text in the input box), `clearable` (only when it's a single line) |
| `open_elsewhere` | The Claude session to resume is open somewhere else: a live claude has it open in `sessions/<pid>.json` (Claude desktop, a terminal Persona doesn't drive). Another `claude --resume` would have two processes writing the session at once | `delivered: "none"`, `pid` |
| `engine_missing` | A session is to be started or resumed, but this computer's engine (herdr) isn't running or isn't installed | `delivered: "none"`, `detail` (the engine's own error) |
| `runtime_away` | The session belongs to an Agent runtime (DSH…) that isn't connected to the node right now ("Runtime ↔ node") | `delivered: "none"` |
| `codex_not_ready` | The first message to a Codex waiting for one (`awaiting_first_message`): its input box didn't come up within 20 seconds (a model still loading, another screen open) | `delivered: "none"` |
| `codex_first_text` | The first message to a Codex waiting for one carries photos or files, or no text: Codex's first message is text only | `delivered: "none"` |
| `codex_first_unconfirmed` | The first message to a Codex waiting for one was typed, but its thread didn't appear within 45 seconds: it may still come, don't send it again | `delivered: "unknown"` |
| `codex_waiting` | Modes, the queue or forking on a Codex still waiting for its first message: they need its thread | `delivered: "none"` |
| `launcher_other_kind` | One of the assistant's conversations, and the message picks a `launcher` of the other agent kind (Claude Code vs Codex). The manager refuses it before the node is asked: a conversation keeps the agent it started on ([assistant.md](../assistant/assistant.md), #4662) | `delivered: "none"`, `conversation_agent`, `launcher`, `launcher_agent` |

- Gray suggested input (Claude's predicted next line, a new session's `Try "…"`) doesn't count as a draft: telling them apart needs a colored screen read (`pane.read` with `format: ansi`) to see SGR 2 (dim);
  in plain text the two look identical. When colors can't be read, it's always treated as a draft. The rules are ported from Ovis's `claude-input.ts` (MIT). Fixtures: `server/internal/screen/testdata`.
- herdr 0.9.4 on macOS loses an answer over 8 KB: it writes it to its socket once, and past the socket's 8192-byte buffer the rest is gone (`herdr.ErrTruncated`).
  A wide pane with Claude Code's status bar takes more than that in 60 colored lines, so its colored read always failed. The check then went on without colors, and every send to a box showing Claude's suggestion
  was refused, with Clear and Send failing again (#6039). Such a read is now made of two smaller ones (`node/hosts.go` `spliceRead`): the whole screen without colors,
  and its bottom 20 (or 10) rows with colors (herdr keeps the newest), where the box and a dialog's keys are. Dialogs are judged on the whole plain screen; box rows above the colored ones have no colors, so they count as typed.
  The two are lined up from their last row with something on it, the colored rows reaching past the blank ones at the bottom, and compared without trailing white space (herdr's plain read drops the no-break space after an empty box's `❯`). When the colored rows don't match the plain ones (the screen moved between the reads) they are read again once, then the read fails.
  When herdr can't send even the plain screen whole (a wide pane full of CJK text is past 8 KB in 30 plain rows), `spliceRead` fails rather than return fewer rows taken for the whole.
  The send check then reads the most bottom rows that fit (40, 30, 24, 16, 12; `node/hosts.go` `bottomRead`), with colored rows spliced on when the reads line up, else plain (as does the after-send check,
  `ensureSubmitted`, whenever its colored read is cut). The rows are used only when the read judged shows Claude's box or a dialog: Claude draws no box while a dialog has the keyboard, and a dialog's keys and footer end it.
  Without either, or when a newer read shows neither, the send is refused (`not_delivered`) as before (#6308).
  Judged on its bottom rows, a dialog is never a notice that Enter closes (its head may be above them): a send with `dismiss_notice` presses nothing there and is refused as `dialog_open`.
  A refusal logs whether the read had colors and the box row's styles, never its text (`screen.BoxStyle`).
- `clear_draft`: after seeing the draft in the App, the user picks **Clear and Send**, and the App sends the same message again with the `clearable` it received, under a new id
  (`client_msg_id` and op id: the refused id's receipt answers its repeats, and the same id with `clear_draft` added is `op_id_reused`, #6425);
  the node clears it with `ctrl+k ctrl+u` only if the input box **still has that same text**, then reads again to confirm it's empty before sending. Multi-line drafts can only be handled on the computer (those two keys clear one line at a time).
- `client_msg_id`: the App gives each pending message a UUID, and automatic resends (no response, resending after a network drop) reuse it. **Dedup is on the hub** (`hub/send.go`, Postgres table
  `sent_messages`, with no age-based expiry): the same id arriving while a send is in progress waits for the first one's result; already delivered returns success directly; rejected or offline (nothing typed) is forgotten and can be sent again
  (with an op id, though, the refusal is that id's receipt and answers its repeats: the apps send a refused message again under a new id, #6425);
  interrupted mid-typing (the node returned `delivered: "unknown"`, or the request reached the node but no response came back: connection dropped, timeout) returns 502 + `delivered: "unknown"`,
  and resending the same id only returns the same error, never typing it a second time. The same holds after a hub restart or node reconnect (dedup used to live only in the node process's memory, and the new process after a reconnect knew nothing;
  on 2026-10-31 a message sent during a reconnect was observed reaching the computer while the App got "rpc: connection closed"). When the user has looked at the chat, confirmed it didn't arrive and taps resend, the App uses a new id.
  If the App gives up and disconnects, the hub still waits for the node's result and records it (sending isn't canceled with the request). The node also remembers for 10 minutes itself (retries within the same connection).
- Sends to the same session go one at a time (the node's `typingLocks`): when two came in at once (double tap, two devices), the second one's screen read used to find the first still in the input box (herdr's
  `agent.prompt` pastes first and presses Enter about 300 ms later), so it was rejected as a draft and even offered **Clear and Send**, which would clear the user's own first message. When the screen read sees text typed within the last 5 seconds
  (or `[Pasted text #1 …]` for long text), it waits for it to be taken (at most 2 seconds).
- `dismiss_notice` (#2553): when the bottom is a notice that only says "Enter to continue" (followed by at most one `Esc to cancel`), with no options / cursor / checkboxes, it presses Enter once to close it first (up to 3 in a row), then checks and sends as usual.
  Confirmations, permissions, selection lists and questions all still return `dialog_open` and are never pressed automatically. The assistant's `agent_send` has a parameter of the same name, and resends with it after a rejection with `notice: true`.
- After typing, the node waits for the transcript to show the message went in (`node/sendsafe_submit.go` `ensureSubmitted`, `promptWatch`, #6428): a line written after typing began — read from where the file ended before it, with no tail limit,
  since a message with screenshots is megabytes of base64 on one line — that is a user message, or a `queue-operation` enqueue while Claude works, whose words start as the message's do (notes and chips left out; for a message of pictures only, a message of the user's with a picture, not one a tool's result carries). A transcript that shrank (written anew) confirms nothing more.
  Until 2 seconds have passed it only reads the transcript, every 100 ms, and answers as soon as the message is there (one screen read for a guide first, #1707; Claude usually writes it within a second). From 2 seconds on it looks at the input box every second, up to 15 seconds after typing, and presses Enter once when the box shows the message, or the `[Pasted text #n …]` placeholder of a long one (Claude can take seconds to take in large images before the box shows it at all;
  a single look at 2 seconds missed one, and the send answered 200 while the text sat in the box). Still in the box after that Enter at the end: the send fails with `delivered: "unknown"`.
  A single look, as before: a slash command or `!` line (never a prompt in the transcript), a session without a transcript, a pane whose screen cannot be read (botmux); a window that ends with the box showing anything else is logged and counts as sent.
- A guide Claude Code opens by itself right as a message is submitted (#5504; 2.1.318's "Teach auto mode about your environment?") takes the typed text and its Enter. The check before typing can't see it, so after the prompt's grace the node looks at the screen again: a guide at the bottom (`screen.Guide`) is declined with Esc, never Enter, and the message counts as sent only once the transcript has it.
  Otherwise it is typed once more into the emptied box; when that isn't confirmed either, or there is no transcript to tell, the send fails with `delivered: "unknown"` instead of succeeding.
- After an offline session is started with `--resume`, the screen is read first too: if Claude comes up sitting on a dialog, it returns `dialog_open` and doesn't type into the dialog.
- Codex / compatible forks only check for dialogs (numbered choices like `› 1.`), not drafts: if the input box has text, the message is appended after it. Old Apps only read the `error` field, which shows them the rejection reason.
- The path and timings are in `docs/archive/integrations/session-verify.md`.

### Going back to the configured model (#2528)

When Claude Code answers an upstream refusal with another model and keeps the session there (`model_fallback`, the record of #2289), a Persona conversation can be sent back to the model it is configured with:
`POST /api/v1/sessions/{mid}/{sid}/restore-model`, **full-access devices only** (it closes a process; answer-only devices and extension tokens get 403, `-` in `testdata/route_scopes.txt`; a `pane:` address is 400). No body is read; the hub relays only the session id to the node's `session.restore_model` and waits up to 30 s.

- Only a **headless** Persona conversation (`claude -p`) is handled: the node closes its process when it is idle (no turn, background task, compaction, control request or hook call such as a permission card in progress, and no send or compaction holding it), so the next message starts it again with the model the hub configures for the conversation (asked of the hub at that moment, `assistant.model`). No process running is fine too (`closed: false`).
- It sends no message and replays nothing; it changes no key, account, quota or route; the transcript (history, todos linked to it, the permission mode) and the refusal record stay as they are, and so does `turn_error` / `turn_error_code`.
- Answer: `{restore: "next_start", restore_to: "<configured model>", closed}`. The session then carries `model_restore` until model evidence: clients say only "the next start will use the configured model"; that it is back is for a newer reply to show, and the same request may be refused again.
- Refusals (409, `code` plus the node's words, nothing closed): `restore_busy` (working or waiting on the user; never waited for), `restore_unsupported` (a terminal / TUI session, a runtime's or Codex conversation: in a terminal the user types `/model` themselves, which Claude Code may also save as the default for new sessions), `restore_nothing` (no active fallback), `restore_unknown` (the transcript is still being read, or the hub can't name the configured model), `restore_gone` (no record). Old nodes: 409 `node_outdated`.

### Rewinding to a message (#2436)

`POST /api/v1/sessions/{mid}/{sid}/rewind`, callable **only by full-access devices** (it puts files back and deletes the conversation after that point; answer-only devices like the watch and extension tokens get 403,
`-` in `testdata/route_scopes.txt`). The body only accepts these fields; nothing else is passed to the node:

```json
{"prompt": "<that message, exactly as in the transcript>", "occurrence": 2, "prompts_after": 3, "restore": "conversation"}
```

- `prompt`: the user message to go back to; `occurrence`: counting back from the end, which **identical message** it is (1 = the last one); `prompts_after` (optional): how many user messages come after it;
  Codex uses `thread/revert {threadId, beforeTurnId}`, with `thread/rollback` on older servers that answer method-not-found.
  It verifies native user-message occurrence and position, requires an idle top-level thread, and reads back the retained
  prefix before answering. The selected input must begin a native turn. Its paginated history database supplies the
  canonical transcript because native revert keeps old rollout segments. Segment database keys and each header's `history_base` bounds preserve the retained lineage and exclude abandoned rows.

  Antigravity uses its owned ACP process's native `RevertToCascadeStep` with `conversationOnly: true`, retaining the step
  immediately before the selected explicit user input. The runtime reads back native state, reconciles the summary's
  current step count with appended replacement exports, and changes the history token even when the result has zero items.
  These two integrations support `restore: conversation`. The selected original message returns to the web composer.

  `restore`: `conversation` (rewind the conversation only) or `code_and_conversation` (put the files back too). Both Claude Code's list and the App's chat count from the end, so earlier pages not yet loaded don't matter.
- The node's `session.rewind` types `/rewind` in the session's terminal, presses ↑ to reach that message, picks the mode and presses Enter, **reading the screen before every step** (`server/internal/node/rewind.go`, `screen/rewind.go`):
  if anything in any step differs from what's expected (the text of that row in the list, its position (`prompts_after`), the whole message quoted on the confirmation page, the option names (chosen by name, not number: when there are no code changes after the message, there are only "Restore conversation", "Summarize…", "Never mind"))
  it presses Esc to leave the panel, changes nothing, and returns 409. When `code_and_conversation` hits "no code changes after this", it only rewinds the conversation, with `code_restored: false` in the result.
- Success: `{prompt, restore, code_restored, input_cleared}`. Claude puts that message back in its own input box; the node clears it (`ctrl+k ctrl+u` for one line, `ctrl+c` for several),
  and when `input_cleared: true` the App puts it in its own input box; when false (couldn't clear, e.g. the input box has other text), it only shows a note.
- Rejections (409, `code` plus an explanation, nothing changed): `dialog_open`, `input_draft` (as in "Sending messages"), `rewind_busy` (working or waiting for an answer), `rewind_unsupported` (not a Claude session in a terminal),
  `rewind_nothing` (Claude has no messages to rewind to), `rewind_mismatch` (the message isn't in the list, the position doesn't match, or the confirmation page shows something else), `rewind_failed` (the screen doesn't look the way the next step needs, or the panel didn't close after confirming).
  Old nodes return 409 `node_outdated`. If the panel doesn't close after confirming, the node presses no more keys (the rewind may already have happened, and Esc can't undo it).
- **Claude Code doesn't delete the rewound part of the transcript** (observed on 2.1.318): the file is a tree (`parentUuid`); after a rewind, the next message hangs under the message before the target, and the rewound turns are still in the file.
  When reading the transcript, the node **follows the branch that wasn't abandoned** (`transcript/branch.go`): when one `parentUuid` has two of the user's own messages under it and the earlier one **got a reply** (assistant lines grew from it), the earlier one and every line that grew from it are the abandoned branch and produce no items
  (item `seq` is still the line number in the file, so the abandoned lines become gaps). **An earlier message nobody replied to doesn't count as a rewind** (#3036): pressing Esc to cancel a message that hadn't been answered and sending again (the same words or different ones) makes Claude write the second as a sibling of the first,
  but no turn was rewound; both stay, as seen in the terminal, and the `history` token doesn't change (if it did, every client would drop its local content and re-fetch, and the interrupted turn would also disappear from the chat).
  Other forks don't count (parallel tool results, attachments hanging next to a reply, the compaction's `compact_boundary`: its `parentUuid` is null and the old chain is in `logicalParentUuid`).
  When the node's own rewind succeeds, it marks the segment right away (`File.Rewound`) without waiting for the next message. How clients find out: `history` (see "Continuity of items") gains a trailing `.r<number of abandoned branches>`, and when it changes they drop local content and re-fetch,
  the same mechanism as a rewritten file, so the web, iOS and Android need no changes (iOS's `ChatStore.apply`, Android's `reducer.history` and the web's `useTranscript` already handle it this way),
  and the hub's assistant snapshots, notifications and knowledge-base archiving also read the node's items. The token is determined only by the file content and doesn't change across node restarts.
  **A rewind done in the terminal** (`/rewind` or Esc Esc, then "Restore conversation") writes nothing either, and while the rewound prompt sits in the input box Claude writes no recap (#5396). The node sees it on the screen of a resting Claude
  (the box holds the words of the transcript's last prompt, which was answered and whose turn ended, and the conversation above the box no longer shows that prompt) and marks the segment the same way (`File.RewoundAt`), so `history` changes within a few seconds.
  If Claude then writes a message or a reply **under** the segment (the guess was wrong: the user had typed the same words again), the segment comes back: the node reads the file again and `history` changes once more (it then differs from what a freshly started node would compute, so clients re-fetch once more after a node restart).

### Matching pending messages

A message the App sends shows as a pending bubble until it appears in the transcript. Claude Code, Codex and runtimes all use their own item ids for the user's line, not
`client_msg_id`, so all three clients used to match by text alone (when the text was rewritten, the same words were sent twice, or `/compact` turned into a notice, the only fallback was "collapse 60 seconds after delivery").
Now the node recognizes that line and tags each of its items with `client_msg_id` (`server/internal/node/echo.go`), in both pushes (`items` events) and pages (`/items`):

- **When it's recorded**: when `session.send` carries `client_msg_id`, the node records the send **before** typing it:
  the session, the last transcript line before sending (new lines are read once before typing), the first 200 characters of the text (with `<persona-context>`, image captions and other additions stripped), the image count, and the time.
  Claude Code writes the line as soon as it takes the message, and the watch may push it before the send returns; recorded first, that push carries the field (it used to be recorded only after delivery, so the line's one push went without it, #4855).
  The hub is told (`session.echo`) once the send was delivered (or `delivered: "unknown"`, possibly delivered); a send that surely wasn't is forgotten.
  Runtime sessions have no local transcript, so the "last line" is the seq the node had pushed up to, or only the time if there isn't one.
- **How it matches**: in send order, each takes the first not-yet-claimed **user line** after its send whose text matches: text under 12 characters (whitespace removed) must be identical,
  otherwise the first 12 characters are compared (pages truncate long text, and Claude turns images into `[Image #1]`); an image-only message matches a line with no text; a bare command (`/model`) matches
  the one completed with arguments in the terminal (`/model opus`); `/compact` matches the "Compact context" notice it turns into. User lines include the `queued` one absorbed mid-turn,
  and exclude ones from other sessions (`from`) and background task notifications. Lines more than 5 seconds before the send, or more than 2 hours after it, don't count (Codex only writes queued messages at the end of a turn);
  if nothing matches within 2 hours, it stops looking.
- **A new conversation's first message**: `assistant.send` with `client_msg_id` and no `session_id` or `new_session_id` is recorded once the conversation's id is known (the warm spare's, or a new one), as sent when it was typed and after nothing, and its first user line is matched as above. The hub keeps the ties of sends only, so after a node restart that line carries no field. The manager sends none today (#5200): an app keeps a new conversation's first message pending under an id of its own and finds it by its words, so a line tagged with another id showed it twice.
- **An assistant chat on a runtime**: the node sends the runtime each message under the `client_msg_id` it came with (`session.send`, `assistant.send`), and with none when it came with none; never one of its own (#5225). A runtime may put the id on the message's line itself, and a line it tied is taken as it is: an id the node made up there kept the App's bubble pending beside the line, so the message showed twice.
- **A message split into several items**: items from the same line share the part of the id before `#` (Claude's uuid, Codex's item id), and the line's text and images all carry the field.
- **Didn't land as a user line**: apart from `/compact`, sends with no corresponding line (other commands, discarded input) aren't matched, the items carry no field, and the App falls back as before; with two identical messages
  where the first didn't land as a user line, the second one's line gets claimed by the first (the bubble just collapses early).
- **Node restart**: the node tells the hub what it recorded and matched (event `session.echo`), and the hub stores it with the send in `sent_messages.echo`; on reconnect, it returns only the last day's echoes;
