  when the node connects, the hub first hands back this machine's entries from the last day (`session.echoes`), then lists sessions and resumes pushing. So after a node restart (an ssh node restarts with the hub),
  lines already matched still carry the field, and ones not yet matched before the restart keep being matched. Without a database on the hub, it's only in the node process's memory.
- **How the App uses it**: an item with `client_msg_id` collapses the pending message with the same id (regardless of role or kind) and won't match another one by text;
  items without it are matched by text as before (old hubs, ones the node didn't recognize). iOS `PendingMessage.tied`, Android `MessageEcho.tag`, web `lib/echo.ts`.

### File preview

The foundation shared by the file page and the various previews (spreadsheets, Office, media, diff), the same across all three clients (#1292):

- **Type**: the node sets `mime` from a fixed extension table (docx / xlsx / pptx / ipynb / heic / m4a etc.; Go's built-in table varies by machine), then the system table if not found, then sniffs the first 512 bytes (HEIC, MP4 / MOV, PDF…). A `.key` that doesn't start as a zip is treated as text (a PEM key); only a zip is Keynote.
- **Fetching content**: first `GET /file?stream=1`. Text still comes paged as `text`; binary only gives `size`, `mime`, `revision`, and the content is fetched from `/file/download` as needed: media hands the URL straight to `<video>` / `<audio>` (seeking via Range), and PDF / Office / spreadsheets are fetched whole and handed to the rendering library, so large files no longer go through JSON as one base64 blob. `revision` and the download's ETag are the same value.
- **Inline and isolation**: the hub and the web share an origin, so `inline=1` only allows images, audio/video and PDF; SVG, though inline, also carries `Content-Security-Policy: sandbox`, so when opened on its own its scripts can't run as the web page. HTML isn't inlined; for preview its text is fetched and put into a sandboxed iframe (M5).
- **Thumbnails**: images (PNG / JPEG / GIF / WebP / BMP / TIFF) are decoded and scaled by the node itself, and SVG is drawn with oksvg (shapes only); everything else goes to the system: Quick Look on a Mac (`qlmanage`: PDF, Office, iWork, HEIC, video), and on other systems `pdftoppm` for PDF and `ffmpeg` for video if installed. System tools run one at a time with a 12-second timeout per run; after one timeout (Quick Look hangs on a locked Mac) they aren't called for 5 minutes and `no_thumbnail` is returned directly, so a screenful of files doesn't wait on each one. The node keeps the latest 128 in memory.

### Sending files

**+** › **Files** in the App's chat input box (for Agents and for the assistant in the chat tab): the chosen file is uploaded to a temporary directory on **the computer the session runs on** (the node's
`os.TempDir()`: usually `/tmp` on Linux, `$TMPDIR` on macOS, and also `/tmp` for an ssh node without that variable), and its absolute path is inserted at the cursor in the input box,
**without sending automatically**. The assistant runs on its own machine (the hub machine by default), so files go there. Images still go as image attachments; for videos from the photo library, see "Sending videos" below.
Share › Persona on iOS uploads shared files the same way to the target's computer and sends their paths with the message (docs/apple/ios.md "Share to Persona").

- `POST /api/v1/machines/{mid}/files?name=<original file name>`, the body is the file itself (`Content-Length` required) → `{path, name, size}`.
  Limit 200 MB (`proto.MaxUploadBytes`): over that returns 413 `code: too_large` (the App checks the size right after picking and won't upload).
- The hub forwards while reading the body: one `file.upload.chunk` per 1 MB (base64 inside one line of JSON), so the whole file never sits in memory or in a single RPC.
  When the App cancels the upload (or disconnects), the hub sends `file.upload.abort` and the node deletes the half-written file; the node also deletes it itself if no chunk arrives for 2 minutes.
- The node first writes a hidden `.persona-upload-*` file (0600), checks the byte count once everything has arrived, then renames it to `name-YYYYMMDD-HHMMSS.ext` (things like `.tar.gz` count as one extension),
  adding a random `-xxxx` for a clash within the same second. `/`, `\` and control characters in the file name are replaced with `_`, and overlong names are shortened.
- Old nodes don't know `file.upload.*`: 409 `code: node_outdated` ("personad on <machine> is too old… needs redeploying"); old hubs don't have this endpoint (404)
  and have no `file_upload` in hello's `features`: the App asks to update the hub.
- Paths with spaces or quotes are wrapped in single quotes by the App, and multiple paths are space-separated. When the input box isn't being edited, the path is inserted at the end (an unfocused TextField's reported selection is unreliable).
- If a reverse proxy sits in front, watch its request body limit (some CDNs' free tiers only allow 100 MB).
- `?dest=terminal` (paste / drag-and-drop in the web terminal, `docs/integrations/terminal.md` section 18): the node doesn't use the system temp directory but stores it in its own `uploads/terminal/<date>/<random>-<file name>`
  (0700 / 0600, cleared at node startup after 7 days), limit 50 MB (`proto.MaxTerminalUploadBytes`; over that also returns 413 `too_large`, with `limit`). Any other `dest` returns 400;
  old hubs / old nodes ignore the parameter and use the temp directory as before.
- `?dest=health` (checkup reports for the health space, `docs/assistant/health.md` ("Checkup reports")): the node stores it in the health directory's `reports/` (`name-YYYYMMDD-HHMMSS.ext`, 0700 / 0600, no expiry), with the same limit as `MaxUploadBytes`. It is the health space of the computer's manager: the built-in manager's `health/` as ever, another manager's `health-<id>/` (the hub passes `health_dir` on `file.upload.begin`, which the node echoes; a node without the `health_spaces` capability gets 409 `node_outdated` instead of a report in the wrong space).

- `GET /api/v1/machines/{mid}/health/reports`: the reports, newest first, `{"reports":[{name,title,path?,record_path?,size,modified_at}]}` (`proto.HealthReport`, #4998). `path` is the original, `record_path` the same-name `.md` record; both are read through `file` / `file/download`.
- `DELETE /api/v1/machines/{mid}/health/reports/{name}`: permanently delete a report (original and record), succeeding even if already absent; `name` must name an ordinary file under `reports/`. Both endpoints require full credentials; old nodes return 409 `node_outdated` (RPC `health.reports.list` / `health.reports.delete`). They are of the computer's manager's health space: another manager than the built-in passes its `health_dir`, which the node echoes (no capability `health_spaces`, or no echo: 409 `node_outdated`), and asks a delete only after a list of that space echoed it. The node refuses any other name, `health` included (the built-in's is named by leaving `health_dir` out).

- `?dest=dir&dir=<folder>`: into the folder the file browser shows; see the next section, "Changing files".
- `?dest=inbox` (a file sent to the computer to keep, #3065; only while the computer's file transfer switch is on, otherwise 403 `file_transfer_disabled` before any byte is sent): into the computer's **receive folder** (hub.json `machines[].inbox_dir`, default `~/Downloads/Persona`, made when missing; a `dir` from the client is ignored). The file keeps its name, a taken one becomes `name 2.ext`, nothing is replaced; mode 0644; `path` is absolute. Limit 2 GB (`proto.MaxInboxUploadBytes`). The node must echo `dest` on begin, otherwise 409 `node_outdated` (the upload is aborted). `file_inbox` in hello's `features`. See [file-transfer.md](file-transfer.md).

### Sending files between computers

Off by default: each computer has a file transfer switch, `GET` / `PUT /api/v1/machines/{mid}/file-transfer/settings` (`{"enabled": bool}` → `{enabled, inbox?}`, full devices only), kept by the manager in settings (`machine_file_transfer`) and shown on the machine object as `file_transfer: {enabled, inbox?}` (absent from an older manager: off). While it is off, `dest=inbox` uploads to it and transfers from or to it are 403 `file_transfer_disabled` (with `machine`); chat attachments, the other upload destinations and previews / downloads do not depend on it ([file-transfer.md](file-transfer.md) "The switch").

`POST /api/v1/files/transfer` copies a file from one computer into another's receive folder, without the phone downloading it (#3065, [file-transfer.md](file-transfer.md)). The manager that carries the computers does it over its node connections; the hub relays the requests to it (`devicewire.TransferRoutes`: a POST to the manager of `from.machine`, GET / DELETE to `?manager=` or the default) and its events to the apps. `file_transfer` in hello's `features`. Full paired-device credentials only (an answer-only device gets 403, extension tokens have no scope).

- `POST /api/v1/files/transfer` `{"from":{"machine","path","cwd"?},"to":{"machine","dest":"inbox"}}` (`dest` may be omitted; nothing else is accepted) → 202 `FileTransfer`, with `Location`. Before 202 the manager reads the source's size and revision and opens the upload on the target, so these come back at once: 404 unknown machine; 403 `file_transfer_disabled` (either end's switch is off); 409 `different_managers` (the two computers are different managers'); the source's own error (no such file, `read_only`…); 413 `too_large` (over 2 GB, with `limit`); 409 `node_outdated` with `machine` (the source predates `file.chunk`, or the target `dest=inbox`); 429 `busy` (8 transfers already running in the manager); 503 `assistant_offline` while the manager is away.
- `GET /api/v1/files/transfer/{id}` → `FileTransfer`; 404 `unknown_transfer` when the manager does not know it (ended over an hour ago, or it restarted).
- `DELETE /api/v1/files/transfer/{id}` → `FileTransfer`: cancels a running transfer (the target's partial file is removed; answers once that is done, at most 15 s) and leaves one that is over as it ended.
- `FileTransfer` = `{id, state: "running"|"done"|"failed"|"cancelled", from, to, name, bytes, total, error?, code?, result_path?, started_at, updated_at}`. `result_path` is the absolute path on the target once done. `code` comes with some failures: `file_changed` (the source changed while it was sent; send it again), or the target's code (`read_only`…). `error` names the machine it came from.
- WebSocket `{"type":"file_transfer","transfer":FileTransfer}`: from the manager, passed on only to full devices that declared `file_transfer` in `?features=` or `client_hello.features` (with `manager` when it is not the built-in); at the start, at the end, and at most once a second in between. Not in the event log: after reconnecting, `GET` the transfers the app is showing.
- Transfers live in the manager's memory only: a restart or redeploy loses them (the target's node removes the partial file after 2 minutes without a chunk). A client that gets 404 for a transfer it was following shows it as interrupted and offers to send it again.

### File details and links

The file page's Info sheet and its symlink marks (#5827), on the app and the web. `file_info` in hello's `features` says the hub passes `detail`.

- **Listing** (`GET /api/v1/machines/{mid}/fs`, node `fs.list`): an entry that is a symlink carries `symlink: true`, `link_target` (what the link says, as `readlink` gives it) and `link_broken: true` when what it leads to is not there or the links loop (more than 40 on the way). The link is followed only to tell a folder from a file (`dir`), and its `size` / `mtime` are the target's when that can be read, otherwise the link's own. A link into a place the read guard refuses (a key folder, iCloud Drive) is neither followed nor called broken.
- **Details** (`GET /api/v1/machines/{mid}/stat?path=<p>&cwd=&detail=1`, node `fs.stat` with `detail: true`): each answer adds `mode` (permission bits as `chmod` takes them, setuid / setgid / sticky included), `owner` and `group` (names; numbers when the system has no name), `mtime`, `ctime` (status change), `birthtime` (creation: macOS, Windows, and Linux file systems that keep it through `statx`), and for a folder `items` (its entries, counted up to 10,000; `items_more` past that). A symlink is looked at as itself first (its folder resolved, its own name not followed): `symlink`, `link_target`, `link_real` (the real path it leads to) and `link_broken`; the other fields then describe the target, or the link itself when broken (`kind: "link"`). A link into a refused place answers `kind: "missing"` with only what the link says. Windows has no `mode`, `owner`, `group` or `ctime` here; clients show no permissions for a Windows computer (`Machine.os`).
- An older node ignores `detail` and answers `{path, kind, size}` only; clients then show what the listing had and say the computer's personad needs an update for more.

### Changing files

The app's file browser (the session's Files pane, the machine page's Files row) and the web's Files panel can upload into a folder, rename, move, and move to the trash with Undo (#315; web #4883). There is no permanent delete.

- **Where writes are allowed** (`node/writeguard.go`): inside the home only. A path first passes the read guard (`pathguard.go`: links followed component by component; iCloud, key folders such as `.ssh`,
  private key names and the hub's keys are refused); the real path after following links must still be in the home (the home itself is fine); `~/.persona`, `~/.persona`, `~/Library` and the data folder `PERSONA_HOME` names (unless it is the home itself) are entirely unwritable, and so is a manager's folder anywhere (one holding a manager's `manager.json`, unless it is the home itself); nor may a client write a file named `manager.json*`.
  `../` and links pointing outside the home are judged by where they end up. A refused write is 409 `code: read_only`. Everything outside the home stays read-only.
- **Upload into a folder**: `POST /api/v1/machines/{mid}/files?name=<file name>&dest=dir&dir=<folder>[&cwd=][&conflict=]`; `dir` may be `~/…`, absolute,
  or relative to `cwd` (the session's working directory). Chunks, cancel and timeouts as in "Send files" above; the cap is 2 GB (`proto.MaxDirUploadBytes`). A missing `dir` is 400; a folder that does not exist or is not a folder, or an unknown `conflict`, is 502 `code: internal` with the node's reason.
  - The file **keeps its name** (`/`, `\`, control characters become `_`). If the file system cannot take it (`ENAMETOOLONG`; over 255 bytes on Linux or 255 characters on a Mac), the stem is cut to 180 bytes and the extension kept, as for a numbered copy; a name that is still too long after that is refused at begin. Mode 0644; the returned `path` is the folder with `~` and `cwd` resolved (absolute, links not followed) + that (possibly shortened) name. (Rename / move / trash below answer in the form the request used.) The partial `.persona-upload-*` is written in that folder and renamed when complete.
  - Name taken: without `conflict`, begin already answers 409 `code: exists` (with `name`) and no byte is sent; the app asks "Replace / Keep Both" and sends again;
    `conflict=keep` saves as `name 2.ext`, `name 3.ext`… (like Finder); `conflict=replace` overwrites and keeps the old file's mode, and still answers `exists` when the name is a folder.
    A name taken while the upload runs is not overwritten: the end answers `exists` and the partial file is removed.
  - An old node that does not know `dest=dir` (answers `unknown upload destination`, or an even older one ignores `dest`): 409 `code: node_outdated`. The hub requires begin to echo `dest`
    and aborts without the echo, so the file never lands in a temp folder quietly. `upload_dir` in the hello `features` says the hub takes these parameters.
- **Rename, move, trash, restore** (`node/fileedit.go`, `hub/fileedit.go`): `POST /api/v1/machines/{mid}/files/{rename,move,trash,restore}` with a JSON body; paths as in a listing (`~/…`, absolute, or relative to `cwd`).
  The folder an entry is in has its links followed and is checked like an upload's; the entry's own name is not followed, so a link is renamed, moved or trashed as the link. The home itself, `~/.persona`, the former state folder and `~/Library`
  (and anything in them) are 409 `read_only`, as is a name that would land there. Answers give paths in the form the request used. `file_edit` in the hello `features` says the hub has these routes.
  - `rename {path, cwd, name}` → `{path}`: in the same folder. `name` can't be empty, `.`, `..`, or contain `/` (400). A taken name is 409 `exists` (`name`) and nothing changes; changing only the case is allowed.
  - `move {paths[], cwd, dir, conflict?}` → `{moved: [{from, to}]}`: into folder `dir`. Without `conflict`, any taken name refuses the whole move with 409 `exists` before anything moves; `keep` names it `name 2.ext`…;
    `replace` first moves the file that was there to the trash (never a folder, and never by a folder: `exists`). A folder can't go into itself (502 with the reason); one already in `dir` is left as it is. Moving to another disk is not supported (502).
  - `trash {paths[], cwd}` → `{trashed: [{path, trash_id}]}`: to the system's trash (macOS `~/.Trash`; Linux `$XDG_DATA_HOME/Trash` or `~/.local/share/Trash`, with a `.trashinfo` written first, freedesktop spec), named `name 2.ext`… if the trash has one.
    Other systems: 502. `trash_id` is opaque to clients. It carries where the file went and where it came from, so Undo works after the node or hub restarts.
  - `restore {trash_ids[]}` → `{restored: [{path}]}` (Undo): puts each back where it was, checked again like any write. A name taken there meanwhile is 409 `exists`; gone from the trash is 404 `not_found`.
  - Errors: 400 for a body that can't be the request (missing `path` / `dir` / `paths`, more than 1000 paths, an unknown `conflict`); 404 `not_found` for an entry that is not there; 409 `read_only` / `exists` / `node_outdated`
    (a node from before these: `unknown method`); anything else the node refuses is 502 `internal` with its reason. One request is not atomic: a failure part-way leaves the earlier ones done (a move checks every name first, so `exists` never does).
- **New folder, text file, zip** (#5828, #5829; `node/filemake.go`, through the same `hub/fileedit.go`): `POST /api/v1/machines/{mid}/files/{mkdir,write,zip}`, each with its own hello feature (`file_mkdir`, `file_write`, `file_zip`). Writes go where uploads may (the home, as above); answers give absolute paths, as an upload's.
  - `mkdir {dir, cwd, name}` → `{path}`: a taken name is 409 `exists`; a bad name 400.
  - `write {path, cwd, text, create?, revision?, sha256?, force?}` → `{path, size, revision, mtime}`. With `create` a new file (mode 0644; a taken name is `exists`, nothing replaced). Otherwise the file at `path` is replaced only while it is the version the app opened: its `revision` (as `file?stream=1` gave it) is still the same, or its bytes still hash to `sha256` (hex SHA-256 of the text opened: touched, not changed); else 409 `file_changed` with the file's `revision` and `mtime` now, and nothing written. `force` (Overwrite Anyway, after the user chose it) skips the check. A link is written at its target. The text goes to a file beside it, renamed over it, so a reader sees the old file or the new one; its permissions are kept. Up to 4 MB (413-style `too_large` past it); the body may be 10 MB.
  - `zip {paths[], cwd, dir?, name?, operation_id?}` → `{path, name, size, files}`: the files and folders, each under its own name, zipped into `dir` as `name` (`.zip` added; a taken name becomes `name 2.zip`, as Finder names a copy), or with no `dir` into a temporary folder of the node (`$TMPDIR/persona-zips`, removed after an hour) for the app to download through `file/download`. Links are stored as links, never followed; what the read guard refuses (keys, credentials) is left out. Up to 20,000 files and 2 GB before compression (`too_large` past either); the hub waits up to 10 minutes.
  - `copy {paths[], cwd, dir, conflict?, operation_id?}` → `{copied: [{from, to}]}` (#5830, hello `file_copy`): files and folders copied into `dir`, named as `move` names them (without `conflict` any taken name refuses the whole copy before anything is copied; `keep` makes `name 2.ext`; `replace` puts the one there in the trash first and never replaces a folder). Duplicate is a copy into the same folder with `keep`. Folders are copied whole, links as links, permissions kept; what the read guard refuses is left out; a folder can't be copied into itself. The same caps as `zip`, counted before anything is written; a copy that fails part-way removes what it made of that item.
  - **Progress and Cancel** (#6113): a copy or zip may carry a fresh `operation_id` (1–128 bytes; reusing one is 409 `exists`). While it runs, `GET /api/v1/machines/{mid}/files/operations/{oid}` returns `{id, kind, state, files_done, files_total, bytes_done, bytes_total}`: `kind` is `copy` or `zip`, `state` is `running`, `done`, `failed` or `cancelled`, file counts include accepted directories and links, and bytes are source bytes before compression. A settled operation remains readable on the node for 10 minutes and older settled entries are cleaned as later operations start; an unknown or cleaned-up id is 404 `not_found`.
    The original POST is still the authority for success, `exists` and other failures; polling only paints progress. Cancelling that POST propagates its context through the hub and a manager to the node, whose copy / zip writer checks cancellation before each block and removes its partial output. When `replace` moved an existing destination to the trash first, a failed or cancelled copy puts that original back after removing the partial replacement; if restoration fails, the error says the original is still in the trash. A conflict retry is a new POST with a new id, not a reuse of the old operation. Clients reveal progress and Cancel only after an operation read succeeds; an older hub, manager or node that cannot read it keeps the previous no-row behavior rather than offering a Cancel that merely disconnects the HTTP request.
  - `chmod {path, cwd, mode}` → `{path, mode}` (#5831, hello `file_chmod`): the permission bits of a file or folder, 0–0777 only (setuid, setgid and sticky are not set from a client; past 0777 is 400); a link changes what it leads to, as `chmod` does; the home itself is `read_only`. A Windows computer answers 409 `unsupported` (clients show no permissions there). Clients ask before sending, saying what changes.
- Full paired-device credentials only: extension tokens are refused (`testdata/route_scopes.txt` says `-`).

### Sending videos

**+** › **Photos** in the input box picks both images and videos (#981; the same in Agents, assistant chats and the new-chat input box). **Videos are sent as files**, not converted to images:
through the same endpoint as "Sending files" above, uploaded to a temporary directory on the computer the session runs on (for the assistant, its machine). Unlike **Files**, the path isn't inserted into the input box;
the video shows as a card above the input box (reading → compressing if needed → uploading, with a progress bar and ✕ to cancel; when done it shows size and duration, and ✕ removes it), and goes out with the next message.

- What it looks like in the message: a blank line after the typed text, then one tag per video
  `<persona-file kind="video" path="/tmp/IMG_0001-20261103-150102.MOV" name="IMG_0001.MOV" size="25270000" duration="12.4"/>`
  (`path` is the path on that computer, `name` is the original name on the phone, `size` in bytes, `duration` in seconds). The Agent reads the path; the App parses the tag and draws a file card
  (file name, size, duration), without showing the tag itself, and the path no longer gets a file chip; the watch shows [Video]. When only a video is sent with no text, the body is "Please look at the video".
- Can't send while uploading (the send button is grayed out; in the BeautifulUI input box, tapping it shows "The video is still uploading. Send once it's done." and the text stays in the box). At most 4 at a time, sharing the picker's 4 slots with photos.
- **Upload as is, or transcode**: up to 200 MB (the hub's limit) it's **uploaded as is**: no waiting for transcoding, no quality loss, and the HEVC / H.264 MOVs the iPhone records are readable on a Mac and by ffmpeg.
  The picker uses `.current` encoding so the system doesn't transcode first for us. Only above 200 MB is it converted to **H.264 MP4** (moov first) with AVAssetExportSession,
  picking by estimate the highest of 1080p (about 76 MB/minute) → 720p (about 54) → 540p (about 35) that is estimated to fit in 180 MB (10% headroom), checking the size again after conversion
  and dropping a tier if it's over. iPhone originals are about 60 MB/minute at 1080p30 HEVC and 170 MB/minute at 4K30, so up to about 3 minutes at 1080p or about 1 minute at 4K goes as is.
- **Limit**: even compressed it must stay within 200 MB, which at 540p fits about **5 minutes** (the estimate goes by bitrate and depends little on the content). Longer ones aren't uploaded, with the message
  ""IMG_0002.MOV" is 12:34 long and still over 200 MB at 540p, so it can't be sent. Trim it in Photos first." One still in iCloud that can't be downloaded shows "Couldn't read a video".
- Android sends videos the same way (+ › Photos, the system photo picker) but does not transcode: a video over 200 MB is refused with the file limit's message (the composer section of `docs/android/android.md`).
- Tapping the card uses the system player (a full-screen AVPlayerViewController on iOS, AVKit's player on Mac): videos sent from this phone play the local copy directly (`Caches/attached-videos`,
  keeping 1 GB by most recently played, counted under "Other Caches" in **Settings › Storage**); ones sent from other devices are first downloaded from that computer (`/file/download`, progress shown on the card, tap again to stop),
  and a copy is kept afterwards too. Once the temporary file on the computer is cleaned up, it can't be played ("Can't play").

### Continuity of items

Every batch of items (WebSocket `items` events, HTTP `/items` responses, the node's `session.items`) states its position in the transcript:

- `history`: this transcript's identity (inode + crc32 of the first line + rewrite count; for a Claude session that has been rewound, add `.r<number of abandoned branches>`, see "Rewind to a message"). A change means the file was replaced / truncated and rewritten / had turns rewound; the App drops its local content and fetches again.
- `to_seq`: the last line read in this batch (including lines with no item); `from_seq`: the line this batch continues after (only present for continuation batches: resends, live pushes, `after_seq`). The batch covers lines `from_seq + 1` through `to_seq`, so `from_seq` is the continuation cursor, not the first returned item's seq.
- The App tracks `covered` (the last line it has received continuously from the start): when `from_seq <= covered`, advance `covered` to `to_seq`; when `from_seq > covered`, a batch was lost in between.
  Fill the gap with `after_seq=covered` at once, as iOS / Mac (`AppModel`) do (#4335); Android and HarmonyOS follow the same rule (#6871). A delayed resend just de-duplicates because `fill` re-reads `covered` before every page and the per-chat `filling` gate collapses concurrent fills. The web's `useTranscript` keeps its 1.5-second settling delay.
  After more than 8 pages, fetch the latest page instead. A reconnect subscription carries `since_seq=covered`.
  A catch-up read covers the gaps and `rev` moves heard when it was sent, not when it came back: one heard while it was on its way
  reads once more after it (web `RevWatch`, Android `ContinuitySync.behind`, #3601).
- **Pushes never silently drop one message** (#3036): when a subscriber's send queue (512 messages) fills up, the hub disconnects it (`too slow`) rather than dropping just that message. Dropping it would keep the tail of a long output (thousands of items) from reaching a page that fell behind,
  with the Agent already stopped and no next batch to reveal the gap. After reconnecting, the client subscribes again with `since_seq=covered`, and resends continue from there (web `useTranscript`, iOS `AppModel`, Android `ContinuitySync` all do this).
  The same applies to non-persisted pushes such as `delta` / `live` / `screen`. Subscriptions are recorded under the computer's own id; subscribing with an absorbed old id (an entry merged away in `hub.json`) still receives pushes.
- **Sub-Agent chats use the same mechanism as sessions** (#3139): subscribing to `<session>@<agent>` is a `session.watch` for it. The node opens `<session>/subagents/agent-<id>.jsonl` and, as for the main session, reads new lines every 250 milliseconds and pushes `session.items`. The rules for `history` / `from_seq` / `to_seq` / `since_seq` are the same; `session.unwatch` (page unsubscribed, disconnected) stops it. At most 16 sub-Agent chats can be followed at once; additional watches return an error, and those pages rely on the fallback fetch below.
- **The page's own fallback** (web `useTranscript`, `lib/stale-page.ts`; iOS / Mac `AgentSyncPacing.catchUpAt` the same, #3191): if the session's `rev` moved since the page's newest `items` read was sent (the session list's row or the `revs` event; a push does not settle it, since nothing says which lines a rev was for, #1179), or the session list's `updated_at` (for a sub-Agent, its entry in the parent's `subagents`) is newer than the `ts` of the latest item the page has, and no items have arrived and the rev has not moved for 4 seconds, fetch once with `after_seq=covered` (at most once every 10 seconds per session, only while the page is in the foreground; if `history` changed, refetch the whole page). The `rev` catches the last line of a burst whose push was lost: its `updated_at` is within a second of the line before, which the page holds, and that close the two times count as the same write. The node reports revs on its next tick, mostly after the items, so an open chat makes one empty read each time it goes quiet. Fetched items merge in silently; writes that yield no items (title, mode) aren't fetched repeatedly. Only after 2 consecutive fetches find items that "should have arrived by push" (or 2 consecutive fetches fail) does a small "Not live · Reload" notice appear at the top of the chat; it disappears when pushes resume.
- Old hubs don't carry these fields: the App keeps merging by id. New hub fields are simply extra keys to old Apps.

### Turn duration from actual records

A turn-end record can produce a metadata item with `role: system`, `kind: turn_duration`. It carries no display text and uses the existing HTTP history / incremental pages, WebSocket `items`, and session cache path, with no new event or top-level Envelope field. The `turn_duration` field is optional; old iOS decodes an unknown kind as `unknown` and skips its display, while decoding everything else as usual.

```json
{"id":"duration_example#0","seq":9,"ts":"2026-01-01T00:00:00Z","role":"system","kind":"turn_duration","turn_duration":{"duration_ms":12345,"source":"claude_turn_duration","parent_uuid":"reply_example"}}
```

| Source | Original record | Association fields |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `claude_turn_duration` | `durationMs` in a Claude Code line with `type: system`, `subtype: turn_duration` | `parent_uuid` preserves `parentUuid` as is, pointing to the UUID of the message that ends the turn (the part before `#` in the item id) |
| `codex_task_complete` | `duration_ms` in a Codex / compatible rollout's `event_msg` with `payload.type: task_complete` | `turn_id` preserves the native turn ID as is; if user input for the same turn has already been parsed, also carries `user_item_id`, pointing to that input's normalized item id |

Only explicitly recorded non-negative integer milliseconds with a valid association identifier are accepted. Missing, negative, non-integer, overflowing values or mismatched known turn IDs produce no duration item. `0` is a valid recorded value. No value is filled from timestamps, the difference between `started_at` / `completed_at`, or a timeout, and durations of compaction, thinking, tools or subtasks are never treated as whole-turn duration.

Android uses the associated message to locate a user turn or background wake-up segment in loaded history, and the work row shows "Took N seconds" (milliseconds rounded down). It stays hidden if the associated message isn't loaded or the association crosses a new user turn / wake-up / recap boundary; association is retried after paging fills the gap. When a new turn has no record of its own, the status row stays blank rather than reusing the previous turn's duration. A missing field / item means no usable actual record, not zero duration; old nodes or caches may also lack this information. Folded work preserves duration metadata items; expanding folds, reconnect resends and cache restoration use the same association rules.

### Token usage on items

An item can carry `usage` (`proto.TokenUsage`, #5426): what the model requests it stands for used, so a client sums a
turn's usage (and, with the catalog's prices, its cost) from the items it already has. It travels in pages, pushes and
fold expansions like the rest of the item; old nodes send none, and clients that do not read it ignore the key.

```json
{"id":"a1#0","seq":12,"ts":"2026-01-01T10:00:00Z","role":"assistant","kind":"thinking","text":"…","model":"claude-opus-5-5",
 "usage":[{"model":"claude-opus-5-5","in":3,"out":412,"cache_read":40210,"cache_write":1180,"cache_write_1h":1180,"fast":true}]}
```

| Field | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `model` | The model the transcript names: Claude Code's `message.model` (never `<synthetic>`), a Codex turn's `turn_context` model; absent when it does not say |
| `in` | Input not read from the cache: Claude `input_tokens`; Codex `input_tokens - cached_input_tokens` (never below 0), as the usage meter counts it |
| `out` | Output; Codex's includes reasoning |
| `cache_read` | Claude `cache_read_input_tokens`; Codex `cached_input_tokens` |
| `cache_write` | Claude `cache_creation_input_tokens`, every lifetime; Codex none |
| `cache_write_1h` | Of `cache_write`, what was written for an hour (`cache_creation.ephemeral_1h_input_tokens`), priced higher than the 5-minute writes |
| `fast` | The requests ran at Claude Code's fast speed (`usage.speed` `fast`) |
| `id` | Only on an agent's report: `agent:<agent id>`, a sub-Agent's, each of its nested sub-Agents' and each agent of a workflow run's. Entries with the same `id` and `model` are one agent's: a client counts them once across the chat (the largest of each field), as an agent can be reported on more than one item (its hand-back and its notice; a nested background sub-Agent's own notice to the session as well as its launcher's report) |

Zero counts are left out. Where it rides:

- **Claude Code**: each API request (`message.id`) once, on the first item its reply lines made. Every content block of a
  reply is a line of its own repeating the request's usage; a line that made no item (a thinking block with nothing
  shown) leaves it to the request's next line, and a line without a message id is a request of its own. Claude Code up to
  2.1.306 wrote the output so far on a reply's earlier blocks: a later line of the request whose counts grew carries what
  grew, so a request's entries add up to its last usage. None on Claude Code's own lines for a failed request
  (`<synthetic>`, `isApiErrorMessage`), on usage that is all zeros (a gateway's on a turn's other replies), or on the
  sidechain lines of a session's transcript. A sub-Agent's own chat (`<session>@<agent>`, its transcript read on its
  own) carries its requests' usage this way, except for a fork's copy of the reply that launched it, before the fork's
  prompt (its first user line): that request is the launcher's. A line carries the same whether it comes in a push, a
  page or a page of a big file opened by its end.
- **Codex**: the turn's requests summed as the usage meter counts them (a `token_count` is a new request only when
  `total_token_usage.total_tokens` grew; rate-limit updates repeat it), on the `turn_duration` item its `task_complete`
  makes, or on the "已中断" notice of a turn the user stopped. An older Codex's `task_complete` without `duration_ms`
  makes no `turn_duration` item, so that turn's usage is not reported (a known limit).
- **A finished sub-Agent**: an item whose `task` is `{kind: "agent", task_id, status}` with `status` `completed`,
  `failed`, `killed`, `stopped` or `ended` (a foreground Agent call's result, a background agent's completion notice or
  hand-back) carries what the sub-Agent's own transcript (`<session>/subagents/agent-<id>.jsonl`) used under
  `id: "agent:<id>"`, and what each of its nested sub-Agents' (their metas' `parentAgentId`, recursively) used under
  that one's own `agent:<nested id>`, one entry per model and speed per agent. A fork's transcript starts with a copy of
  the reply that launched it: that request is its launcher's, not counted. A team's in-process teammate (its meta's
  `taskKind` `in_process_teammate`) is left out, its spawn result and as a nested sub-Agent alike: a long-lived worker
  with its own transcript, whose usage is not the turn that spawned it.
- **A finished workflow run**: an item whose `task` is `{kind: "workflow", task_id, status}` in one of those statuses
  (the run's report) carries what each agent of its run used
  (`<session>/subagents/workflows/<run id>/agent-<id>.jsonl`, the attempts a retry replaced included), each under its
  own `agent:<id>`. The run is the one whose state file (`<session>/workflows/<run id>.json`, written as the run ends)
  names the report's task (`taskId`); without one, the report carries none.
- **Folds**: `fold.usage` (see "Folded work").

The node adds the agents' usage to pages and pushes of Claude Code transcripts, reading each agent's file once and then
only what it gained. A turn's usage is the sum over its items, folds' `fold.usage` included; prices per one million
tokens come from the built-in catalog (`POST /api/v1/launchers/catalog`, `price`).

### Tool outcomes

A `tool_result` item can carry `outcome` (`proto.ToolOutcome`): what the call came to, read by the node while it parses
the transcript, so clients need not guess from `text` and `is_error` (#2912). The node reads it from the runtime's own
record of the call (Claude Code's `toolUseResult` and the line's `toolDenialKind`; a Codex command's `exit_code`,
`duration` and `status`) and from the fixed words a Claude result opens with. It is additive: every field is optional,
absent means the record did not say, old nodes send none, and clients that do not read it ignore the key. It travels in
pages, pushes and `/items/{iid}/full` like the rest of the item; folds carry no outcomes.

```json
{"id":"r1#0","seq":42,"ts":"2026-01-01T10:00:00Z","role":"user","kind":"tool_result","tool_use_id":"toolu_1","is_error":true,
 "text":"Exit code 1\n…","full_size":9120,
 "outcome":{"status":"failed","exit_code":1,"tail":"--- FAIL: TestX (0.01s)\nFAIL\tpkg/x\t0.012s"}}
```

| Field | Meaning | Where it comes from |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `status` | One of the statuses below; set on every result the node parses | See below |
| `exit_code` | The command's exit code | Codex `exit_code` (0 included); a failed Claude Bash result's opening `Exit code N` |
| `duration_ms` | How long the call ran, when recorded | Codex `duration` (`{secs, nanos}`); Claude WebFetch `durationMs`. Never derived from timestamps |
| `tail` | The output's last lines, only when the page cut `text` (it keeps the first 4 KB) | At most 30 lines and 2 KB, never repeating the page's text: it picks up where that stops when it fits (so a short overflow loses no line), else from a whole line; not for a Read's file content |
| `persisted` | `{path, size?}`: Claude Code saved an output too big for the model to a file on the agent's machine; `text` has only its preview | `persistedOutputPath` / `persistedOutputSize`, or the path in the `<persisted-output>` preview |
| `patch`, `patch_cut` | An Edit's or Write's change as unified diff hunks (`@@ -12,7 +12,8 @@`, the file's real line numbers) for `files[0]`, at most 8 KB of whole lines; `patch_cut` when lines were left out (each hunk header counts the lines kept) | Claude Code's `structuredPatch` |
| `files` | `[{path, adds?, dels?, created?}]`: lines added and deleted over the whole change; `created` for a new file (its lines are the adds) | `structuredPatch`; Write `type: create` and its content's line count (the content itself is not copied) |
| `git` | `commit {sha, branch?, kind?}` (committed, amended, cherry-picked), `push {branch?}`, `pr {number?, url?, action?}` (created, edited, closed…), `branch {ref?, action?}` (merged, rebased), as recorded | Claude Code's `gitOperation` |
| `read` | `{start?, lines?, total?, unchanged?}`: the part of the file a Read returned, or `unchanged` when it returned nothing because the file had not changed since the last Read | Read's `file.{startLine, numLines, totalLines}`, `type: file_unchanged`, or the result's "Wasted call — file unchanged since your last Read" |
| `answers` | AskUserQuestion's answers, question → answer (at most 16, each cut to 1 KB) | `answers` |

| `status` | Claude Code | Codex |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `ok` | Anything below does not apply | `completed` with exit code 0 |
| `failed` | `is_error` (with `exit_code` when the result opens with `Exit code N`) | `failed` or a nonzero exit code |
| `no_match` | `returnCodeInterpretation: "No matches found"` (a search that found nothing; not an error) | — |
| `denied` | `toolDenialKind` `user-rejected`, `permission-rule` (a rule, the permission mode or a hook) or `automode-*`; older lines: an error opening with Claude Code's rejection or permission words, or a `PreToolUse:` hook error | `declined` |
| `blocked` | An error opening with `<tool_use_error>` (input that failed validation, a guard) or the worktree isolation refusal: the call did not run | — |
| `interrupted` | `toolDenialKind` `interrupted` / `cancelled`, `interrupted: true`, or `[Request interrupted by user for tool use]` | — |
| `timed_out` | `timedOutAfterMs`: the command outran its timeout and Claude Code moved it to the background | — |
| `background` | `backgroundTaskId`: the command goes on in the background; its task notice reports the end | — |

Decoding rules: `toolUseResult` is read through a narrow struct that takes any value (a failed call records a string, an
MCP call its content blocks); a value or field of an unexpected type leaves that part unread and never drops the line.
Its large fields (`originalFile`, `stdout`, a Read's `content`, a Write's `content`) are never copied. `toolDenialKind`
takes any value too: anything but a string is no kind, and the status comes from the words. A line holding
several `tool_result` blocks takes no record (Claude Code writes one result per line with its record). A tool writes its
own result text, so statuses read from words (any line without `toolDenialKind`) are for display only. A client that
starts drawing outcomes must bump its item cache version: items cached from older pages have none.

### Folded work

The tool calls, thinking and intermediate Codex commentary of a turn are normally folded into one line in the chat ("Tools 502 · Thinking 81"). But in one long Codex session, the page for the last two turns had 1412 items and 1.08 MB,
with only 6 actual replies: on a weak network the top of the chat page kept spinning. When a request carries `fold_work` (HTTP `fold_work=1`, `fold_work: true` when subscribing), pages read backward from the end
(`turns` / `before_seq` / the last two turns resent on subscribe) replace each run of consecutive work (paired tool_use + tool_result, with the tool's images, thinking, and Codex commentary)
with one item of `kind: fold` (`transcript.FoldWork`):

- `id` is `fold:` + the id of the run's first item, and `seq` / `ts` are also the first item's; `fold.through_seq` / `through_id` are the last item, `until` is the last item's time;
  `items` is the item count, `tools` the number of tool calls, `thoughts` the number of thoughts with text (the App never shows empty thoughts anyway).
- `fold.errors` is how many of the run's tool results were errors (`is_error`, as the runtime reports it), and `fold.tool_names` the tools the run called,
  each once in the order first called, at most 10 (`proto.FoldToolNamesMax`); `[]` for a run of thoughts only. They let a reader that does not open folds,
  such as an extension looking for where a session went wrong (`docs/extensions/extensions.md` "Folded work"), pick the run to open. A fold from an
  older node has neither (`tool_names` absent): unknown, not zero. The apps ignore both.
- `fold.tasks` is an optional array of ordered task-list snapshots. It only includes successful TodoWrite / TaskCreate / TaskUpdate / TaskList results from this run,
  and carries no raw tool input or output; it is omitted when there is no usable snapshot. Results that are missing, have `is_error: true`, have `success: false`, or have a non-null `error` are not counted;
  a malformed list does not clear earlier tasks. Old iOS ignores this nested field; the fold's existing counts, range and expansion stay the same.
  Each successful result keeps one snapshot and its replacement boundary, applied in the order the results appear in the transcript, so a partial update does not lose task state already loaded:
  - `entries`: the task array. Each entry has an `id` (`todo:<index>` or `task:<tool task ID>`) and optional `subject`, `description`, `status`.
    Status is `pending` / `in_progress` / `completed` / `unknown`; `deleted` means the task is removed.
  - `replace: "todo"`: a full TodoWrite list; existing `todo:` entries are removed first. An empty array means clear.
    `replace: "task"`: a full TaskList list; `task:` entries not in the new list are removed, and existing entries keep the description and status the new list doesn't provide. An empty array means clear.
    Omitting `replace` means an incremental TaskCreate / TaskUpdate result; fields not provided keep their old values. A task with no old title shows "Task #ID", with unknown status.
    TaskCreate also carries `fallback_status: "pending"`, used only when neither the result nor the old task has a status.
  - `source_item_id`, `source_tool_use_id`, `source_seq`: the item ID, tool call ID and seq of the original tool call, used by "View related record" to locate it.
    Android can rebuild progress without expanding; to view the record it first expands the containing work row, then fetches the original records by range and scrolls to it. Later real results keep updating by the original rules.

  For example: `"tasks":[{"replace":"todo","entries":[{"id":"todo:0","subject":"Check the form","status":"in_progress"}],"source_item_id":"entry_tool#0","source_tool_use_id":"call_example","source_seq":3}]`.
- `fold.images` is an optional array: the images this run of work looked at (`transcript.ViewedImages`); rules are in "Images viewed this turn" below. Omitted when there are none.
  Old clients ignore this field.
- `fold.latest_thinking` optionally carries the run's newest nonempty thinking item so a live work row can preview the agent's narration on first load.
  It contains only the original `id`, `seq`, `ts`, `role`, `kind`, `text` and optional `full_size`. Text is limited to 512 Unicode characters, including an ellipsis when clipped;
  `full_size` preserves the original byte count (including any earlier clipping). It carries no tool, image or other payload, and is omitted when there is no thought with words.
  The original item remains inside the fold: counts, range and expansion are unchanged. Clients that do not use this preview ignore it.
- `fold.changes` is the files this run's successful edits changed (`transcript.foldChanges`, #5157), in the order first edited: `path` as the
  edit named it, cleaned (`path.Clean`: no `./`, `../` or doubled slashes, so one file is one entry), `add` / `del` the lines added and removed, summed over the run's edits of that file, and `exact`, false when an edit's input
  was clipped for good (its counts would be a guess, and the apps leave them out). An edit is an Edit, Write or MultiEdit call whose result is in
  the run and is not an error; a Codex file change is the Edit with its `diff` (headers not counted; without hunks the whole file, added, or
  removed when `change` is `delete`). Lines are counted as the web counts an edit's line diff: Myers' diff of the old and new text, a final
  newline ending the last line on a side whose other side is empty or ends in a newline too (a Write of `"a\nb\n"` is 2 lines; `"foo"` becoming
  `"foo\n"` is 1 added), and everything removed and added past 60,000 lines or 6,000 edits (`web/src/lib/compare.ts`). The list is
  always there, `[]` when the run edited nothing, so an app tells that from a fold an older node made, which has no list and leaves the edits
  unknown. The web's changed-files card counts a folded run by it, so the card is the same before and after a reload; the cases both read
  are in `spec/fixtures/fold-changes/cases.json`. Old clients ignore it.
- `fold.usage` is what the folded items used (their `usage`, "Token usage on items"): entries without an `id` summed per
  `model` and `fast`, entries with one as they are. Omitted when none of them carried usage, and from older nodes. Old
  clients ignore it.
- Not folded: user messages, final replies (text), notifications, recaps; on the latest page, the newest Codex commentary when no final reply follows it, so a running turn's current answer stays visible. Once a final reply follows, earlier commentary is folded as narration and remains ordinary text when opened, not thinking. Historical pages fold all their narration because a final reply may be on a later page;
  a tool_use whose result is not on this page (still running) and a tool_result whose tool_use is not on this page
  (the App has to pair them with the other half that comes later / came earlier); short runs under 3 items and under 4 KB (expanding costs another round trip; not worth it).
- When the App expands a work row it fetches the run with `from_seq=<fold.seq>&through_seq=<fold.through_seq>` (about 1000 items per page; on `more`, continue from the last item's seq + 1),
  merges it in and drops the fold. When a fold is merged in, local tool / thinking / assistant text items within its range (by seq + block index) are replaced by it.
- Resends via `after_seq` and live pushes are never folded: they continue from what the App already has, and may contain tool calls the App is waiting on.
- A page like that 1412-item / 1.08 MB one becomes a dozen or so items and a few KB after folding (`TestFoldedFirstPageOfALongSession`).

### Images viewed this turn

The App and web show an "Images viewed this turn" row under a turn's reply (#1543, #1540). The images come from tool calls in that turn's work, and both sources are aggregated by the same rules:
unfolded work is read from the items themselves, folded work from `fold.images` (once a work row is expanded, the fold is replaced by the real items and the aggregate stays the same).

- What counts: images carried in results (items with `kind: image` and a `tool_use_id`: images read by Read, computer_state screenshots, browser_look screenshots,
  images returned by other MCP tools). A Read of an image file (png / jpg / jpeg / gif / webp / heic / heif / bmp / tif / tiff) whose result carries no image
  (the image was too large to keep, or Codex's view_image, which the transcript maps to Read) also counts as one entry, with only the path. Images the user sent this turn don't count (they are in the user bubble);
  failed Reads, non-image files and calls without a result yet don't count.
- Order and dedup: in order of first appearance; the same path appears only once. Entries without a path are matched by mime + size + width/height (looking at an unchanged screen again counts as one image);
  when none of these are present, by image item.
- Each `fold.images` entry:

  | Field | Description |
  | --- | --- |
  | `item_id` | id of the image item; fetch the image with `GET /api/v1/sessions/{mid}/{sid}/items/{item_id}/image`. Path-only entries don't have it |
  | `tool_use_id`, `tool` | the call that viewed the image and its tool name (verbatim, e.g. `Read`, `mcp__persona__computer_state`) |
  | `source` | `read` (Read), `screenshot` (MCP `computer_*`), `browser` (MCP `browser_*`), `mcp` (other MCP tools), `tool` (anything else) |
  | `path` | the file Read read (`file_path`); thumbnail via `GET /api/v1/machines/{mid}/file/thumb`, full image via `file/download` |
  | `machine` | `screenshot` / `browser`: the machine named in the call (id or name), shown as "Screenshot · <machine name>" |
  | `mime`, `size`, `width`, `height` | image type, byte count (approximate: base64 length × 3 / 4), pixel width/height; same as the lazy-loaded `image`, used to reserve space before the image arrives |

  For example: `"images":[{"item_id":"entry_tool#1","tool_use_id":"call_a","tool":"Read","source":"read","path":"/work/design.png","mime":"image/png","size":48213,"width":1280,"height":800},{"tool_use_id":"call_b","tool":"Read","source":"read","path":"/work/banner.jpg"}]`.

### Terminal stream

The live view of the Terminal tab (`docs/integrations/terminal.md`). The node uses `herdr terminal session observe` to mirror the grid herdr has drawn, at the pane's own size.
Each frame is a chunk of VT bytes: a `full` frame is the whole screen (starts with `ESC[2J`); the others only redraw cells that changed, and end with the cursor position and visibility. The App just applies them in order to a `cols × rows`
grid. The grid always equals the pane size on the computer; the phone's size is never sent back.

- `epoch` identifies a stream: the node picks a new one every time it (re)opens observe, and the first frame is always `full`. The node reopens when the pane resizes, herdr is interrupted, or the deltas after the full frame exceed 256 KB.
  Within one `epoch`, `seq` increases from 1 without gaps.
- For each watched terminal the hub keeps "the latest full frame + the deltas after it". `terminal_subscribe` carries the `epoch` and last `seq` the App has:
  if it is still the same stream and the kept frames connect, only the later frames are sent; otherwise replay starts from the full frame. New frames are then pushed live.
- If the App receives a frame whose `seq` isn't contiguous (something was lost), or the `epoch` changed but the frame isn't `full`, it drops its local grid and sends `terminal_subscribe` again (without epoch).
- On `error`: the hub has dropped this stream. On `unsupported`, fall back to polling `/screen`; otherwise subscribe again after a few seconds. After the WebSocket drops and reconnects, subscribe again (with epoch / seq to resume).
- The first App to subscribe makes the hub send `terminal.watch`; the last one to unsubscribe (or disconnect) makes it send `terminal.unwatch`. Old Apps don't send these messages and keep polling `/screen`.
- Pane addresses (`features` has `terminal_panes`, `docs/integrations/terminal.md` section 19): a pane with no Agent has no session id, so the `session_id` of `terminal_subscribe` / `terminal_input` / `terminal_unsubscribe`
  can be `pane:<pane id>` (the `terminal` given by `/machines/{mid}/panes`); `GET …/sessions/{mid}/pane:…/screen` (the polling fallback) and `screen/before` accept it too. **Only `full` devices can use it**: an `answer` device subscribing (even view-only)
  gets `error: forbidden…`, and HTTP screen reads return 403. No other `session.*` accepts this address.
- Phone takeover (`features` has `terminal_control`, `docs/integrations/terminal.md` section 11): when the subscription carries `control`, the grid is the phone's size; the frame format is unchanged.
  Keys and new sizes go through `terminal_input`. On leaving (unsubscribe / disconnect) the pane goes back to the computer's size, and if others are still watching it switches back to mirroring (new epoch).


## File auto-refresh (#2439)

The web's file panel and Git panel refresh automatically while open (`web/src/lib/fs-live.ts`; the same for the iOS / Mac file and Git pages, `apple/Persona/App/FsLive.swift`, #3089; `server/internal/hub/fswatch.go`, `server/internal/node/fswatch.go`):

- The page sends `fs_watch` (message table above), **one per session directory, replacing the whole set**. Within a page, the file panel's and the Git panel's needs are merged in the page. When the page is hidden it sends an empty set; when it comes back it sends again and refreshes once.
- The hub merges the sets from all pages and calls the node's `fs.watch`, **replacing the whole set**; after the node reconnects, the hub resends once. A page connection dropping, a panel closing or a page switch all release it; when the last page goes away the node stops its watch loop (no goroutine left behind). Only full-access devices can send `fs_watch`.
- The node **polls instead of using inotify / fsnotify**: fsnotify isn't in `go.mod`, Linux inotify isn't recursive, and behavior differs across systems. It only watches the folders the page has open (one `ReadDir` every 2 seconds; the signature is the entry count plus name + type + size + mtime of the entries `fs.list` shows, which for a folder over 2000 entries are the first 2000 in its order), and Git directories run `git status --porcelain=v2` every 5 seconds plus the size and mtime of the changed files listed (editing an already-modified file again leaves the `status` text unchanged, but its size and mtime change). It pushes `fs.changed` only on change; nothing is sent when nothing changed.
- After the web receives `fs_changed` it waits 200 ms (restarting the timer if more arrive) and merges them into one refresh: it only rereads the folders that changed; Git status and open diffs refresh in place, with no loading animation.
- The node first passes every path in `fs.watch` through `pathguard` (the same check as `fs.list`). A rejected path simply can't be read and its signature is `err`; its contents are never read.

## Node handshake

The manager ↔ node protocol (the `node.*`, `sessions.*`, `session.*`… RPC over ssh, Persona Link, tailcat or a member hub) carries a version and capabilities, so a device and a manager built from different commits work together. The constants live in `server/internal/nodeproto` (a pure contract package that imports nothing).

- After `engine.use` (when there is a stored engine), the manager's first call is `node.info`. Besides what the node is, it answers `protocol` (the node protocol it speaks, an integer), `protocol_min` (the oldest manager protocol it still answers), `program` and `executable` (`personad` or `persona-node`, and the file it runs from: an update brings the same kind of program to that file; older nodes leave both out and run personad, [link.md](../operations/link.md) "The device's program") and `capabilities` (stable names: `sessions`, `model_configuration`, `assistant_service_tier`, `node_update`, `engines`, `machine_uid`, `herdr_server`, `plugin_node_call`, `ultracode`, `health_spaces`, `preview`, `secret_run`, `clipboard`, `secret_env`, `launcher_switch`, `model_http`, `engine_switch`, `model_run`, `launcher_switch_now`, `launcher_switch_idle`, `pane_cwd`, `node_update_idle`, `pane_new_space`, `session_skills_v1`, `mcp_wait_v1`; `secret_env` only from a resident node, attached or Persona Link). A name is never renamed or reused; a node drops one only together with a protocol bump.
- The protocol version rises only for a change an older peer cannot follow (a method whose params or results change meaning). Additions are new capabilities, and the manager checks the capability before using them.
- The manager drives a node when `protocol >= MinVersion`, `protocol_min <= Version` (both the manager's) and the node has every required capability (today `sessions`). Otherwise the node is **incompatible**: it stays connected and shows in the machine list, but is not configured, listed or watched, and every call except `ping`, `sessions.list`, `node.info` and `node.update.*` is refused with `node_outdated` (so it can still be updated). The machine list says why in `node_incompatible`: `node_protocol_old` (update the node) or `node_protocol_new` (the node needs a newer manager).
- Optional features check capabilities, not builds: a nonempty `service_tier` on a new conversation's `assistant.send` needs `assistant_service_tier` (the manager answers `node_outdated` before any thread or turn starts; an omitted tier keeps the old behavior); a model on `assistant.send` / `assistant.warm` / `session.start` / `session.send` needs `model_configuration`; `"ultracode":true` on `session.start` needs `ultracode` (a node from before the handshake has none; `false` asks for nothing and is never refused); another manager's health space (`health_dir` on `file.upload.begin` and `health.reports.*`) needs `health_spaces`; `clipboard.get` / `clipboard.set` need `clipboard` (`node.info`'s `clipboard: {supported, reason?}` says whether a clipboard is reachable there); an update over the node RPC needs `node_update` (and `node_update` in `node.info` saying it can run now), and with `node_update_idle` the manager waits until `sessions.list` answers `update_busy: false` ([node-update.md](../operations/node-update.md) "Usage"), for every Agent to be idle without it or when the field is missing; `secret.run` needs `secret_run` (without it the manager answers `node_outdated` before the card is shown); `secret.stage` and a `session.start` with `secret_ticket` need `secret_env` (the same `node_outdated`: an older node would start the Agent without the values); `launcher` on `session.modes` needs `launcher_switch` (the hub answers `node_outdated`: an older node would drop it and switch only the model); `switch_now` on `session.send` needs `launcher_switch_now` (the same `node_outdated`: an older node would type the message on the old launcher and leave the switch waiting); `session.switch` needs `launcher_switch_idle` (the same `node_outdated`); a launcher of the other engine there is taken as a switch to that engine by a node with `engine_switch` only (one without refuses it with a `switch_*` code); `model.http` needs `model_http` and `model.run` needs `model_run` (the same `node_outdated`).
- **Ordinary Agent skills.** `session_skills_v1` adds `session.skills` and validated explicit skill selections to ordinary `session.send`. Managers refuse selections with `skill_unavailable` and `delivered:none` on older nodes, while ordinary text keeps working. Catalogs are partial when local adapters cannot enumerate every source.
- **Assistant profiles.** `assistant_config_dir` adds explicit `config_dir` to `assistant.send`, `assistant.warm` and headless `session.send`. The manager refuses a nonempty selection with `node_outdated` on a node without it, including pre-handshake nodes, before any process starts. Omission keeps an old node's behavior; there is no protocol-version bump. A new node preserves old conversation profiles by saved metadata or actual transcript discovery.
- **Assistant start speed.** `assistant_service_tier` adds `service_tier` to a new conversation's `assistant.send`. The node consumes it only for a new Codex conversation, waits for `thread/settings/update` to acknowledge the advertised native tier before the first `turn/start`, and leaves effort independent. It rejects the field on an existing session or a non-Codex runtime. The one-shot request is not retained in process state, execution fingerprints, warm starts or recovery; later speed changes still use `session.speed`. A manager refuses a nonempty value with `node_outdated` on a node without the capability, including pre-handshake nodes. Omission and the protocol version are unchanged.
- **MCP nested wait correlation.** `mcp_wait_v1` in `node.info.capabilities` means the target node preserves a valid `call_id` from `computer.call` into a nested `computer.elicit`. The manager sends that id only to a target advertising the capability with a nonzero protocol version. While an older target owns the RPC, the manager publishes `unknown`, then restores the previous live state; it never mistakes that target's silent elicitation path for `computer`.
- **Backward compatibility.** A node from before the handshake leaves the three fields out (protocol 0): the manager drives it as before and reads the old `node.info` flags (`model_configuration`, `node_update`) for what it can do. A manager from before the handshake ignores the fields, and new nodes keep sending the old flags for it.
- **Resident reload handover (#5277).** `node.restarting` is an optional node-to-manager announcement. The resident drains admitted RPC replies and idle
  assistant processes before closing the current connection, and hands its attach listener/run lock through exec. The manager suspends new outbound calls and
  uses the following `state.load {restart_barrier:true}` request as a fence: `{restart_ready:true}` means every earlier registered call's reply arrived.
  `state.load {restart_barrier:false}` cancels that preparation and resumes calls. A manager from before the flag treats either as an ordinary read, so the
  protocol floor is unchanged. `node_restarting` means the operation was refused before execution and may retry; an unsent suspended call may retry too,
  but `rpc.ErrDropped` remains an ambiguous result and is never automatically replayed. Initial engine/node.info handshakes interrupted by exec retry within
  their existing bounded budget. A failed control exchange closes its physical peer, so a late announcement cannot leave a live manager suspended; an already
  published reply wins over a later connection closure. `node-update-check` adds optional `resident_handover: true`; resident uploads and ordinary reloads
  require it before installing or draining a replacement. Startup rollback to a legacy image releases, rather than inherits, the listener/run lock.
  This resident reload path retains the existing five-second reconnect grace; it is separate from slot blue-green promotion.
- **Builds.** The build string (`version`, `node_version` in the machine list) no longer decides compatibility. It is still the upgrade policy: another build sets `node_mismatch` (the **Redeploy** offer), the hub's automatic redeploy after it updates itself (`devices.update_nodes`) and a deploy's wait for the node to come back on the hub's build. `node_protocol` in the machine list is the protocol the node announced (absent: from before the handshake).

## Engines

Each machine's node drives one "engine", that is, a set of terminal hosts: `herdr` (the classic herdr command line; the default, so existing machines are unaffected),
`herdr-core` (the runtime behind the Herdr desktop app, display name "Herdr App"), `orca` (the runtime of the Orca desktop app, display name "Orca", `docs/plans/plan-orca-support.md` ("Orca source")),
and `herdr-both` (display name "herdr + Herdr App"): the node **registers both herdr and herdr-core as hosts at the same time**, and sessions from both are shown merged.
This is for the case "use herdr locally, and have Herdr App connect remotely to the same machine". With a single choice the hosts are not used together: running them at once slows each other's refresh;
side by side, refreshes run in parallel and events are isolated per host, so they don't slow each other down (implementation in `node/engine.go`, `refreshHosts` in `node/placement.go`, `node/herdrevents.go`;
trade-offs in `docs/plans/plan-orca-support.md` ("herdr-core host")).

- The user picks per machine in the App (at pairing, or Settings › Machines): `PUT /api/v1/machines/{mid}/engine`. The hub stores it in the Postgres settings, not in hub.json.
- **Host sets (#2576)**: a computer can enable several hosts side by side, any subset of `herdr`, `herdr-core`, `orca`, `tern`, `paseo` and `cindy` (or none at all),
  plus a **default host**: where sessions started or resumed from the phone go (the empty set has no default). Each single engine above is a set:
  `herdr-both` is `{herdr, herdr-core}` with herdr the default.
  - `PUT` body: `{"hosts": ["herdr", "orca"], "default": "herdr"}`. Without `default`, the first host in the order herdr, herdr-core, orca, tern, paseo, cindy;
    `"hosts": []` is the empty set. Older clients still send `{"engine": "herdr-core"}`, which stands for its set; a body with `hosts` is always a set.
    An unknown host, `herdr-both` as a member, or a default that is not enabled is a 400, and nothing is written.
  - **Storage**: the key `machine_engine_hosts` (machine id → `{hosts, default}`) is the choice. `machine_engines` (machine id → single engine) is written beside it
    with the single engine closest to the set (the host itself when there is one, `herdr-both` for herdr + herdr-core, else the default host, herdr for the empty set),
    so an older hub still works after a rollback. A machine with only `machine_engines` (chosen before sets) reads as the set its engine stands for and is not
    rewritten; a machine in neither is `{herdr}`.
  - **Machine fields**: `engine` stays that single engine (older clients read it). `engine_hosts` and `engine_default` are the set and the default host (never null;
    `["herdr"]` when never chosen). `engine_suggested` (while online) is the set to preselect at pairing: the hosts the node reports available, herdr when none;
    a machine that already chose is never changed by it. `engine_sets_unsupported`: the node is online but too old for sets, and the chosen set is not one it can run
    as a single engine (herdr + Orca, say). It then runs `engine` alone, and clients say so until the node is updated.
  - **Choosing the host for a new session**: `POST /api/v1/sessions` (`session.start`) may carry `host`, one of the enabled hosts; without it, the default host.
    A host that is not enabled, or one that cannot start sessions, is refused with `engine_missing` and nothing starts. When the node is
    too old (its `node.info` has no `engine_hosts`) the hub answers `node_outdated` and does not send it: an older node would ignore `host` and start in its engine.
    Session rows carry `host` (the host they live in: the pane's kind, `paseo` for Paseo's) and `also_open_in` (the other hosts the same session is live in,
    `docs/integrations/engines.md` "Host sets").
  - **`engine.use`** carries `{engine, hosts, default}`. Older nodes read only `engine`; newer ones report `engine_hosts` (the set they run) in `node.info`,
    which is how the hub knows they take sets. The empty set is sent as `"hosts": []`, never null.
- Every time the hub connects to a node, **the first call** is `engine.use` (before `node.info`), but only for machines with a stored choice. Machines never configured get nothing,
  so the node keeps using herdr and old nodes never receive a method they don't know. When the user changes it and the machine is online, it is sent right away; `engine.use` calls for the same machine are queued, and each sends the value stored at send time.
- After connecting, the node doesn't poll or subscribe to any engine's events until the engine is settled: it receives `engine.use`, or the hub skips it and calls `sessions.list` directly (never configured / old hub).
  It waits at most 3 seconds, then starts with herdr. So a machine set to herdr-core never flashes herdr sessions on connect, and never queries herdr.
- `engine` is the stored choice. If the node rejects `engine.use` (too old), the hub logs a line, the PUT still returns 200 and the choice stays stored; it takes effect once the node is updated.
- `engines` comes from `node.info`; each entry is `{id, name, available, version?, note?}`. herdr is available = it answers, or its socket file exists, or `herdr` is on PATH. herdr-core is available = its socket answers `hello`
  (a node using herdr asks herdr-core this only once, during `node.info`, and leaves it alone otherwise). `herdr-both` is available = both of the above are available (no version).
  Orca is available = `orca-runtime.json` exists, its socket answers `status.get`,
  and the protocol version is compatible (if incompatible, `available` is false, `note` is a one-sentence reason in Chinese for the user, and `version` is still included; also asked only once during `node.info`).
  Tern is available = `tern` is found and its session daemon answers `tern inspect`; its `version` is the binary's (`tern --version`), also while
  Tern is not running.
  `version` is the version each reports; omitted if there is none. Old nodes only report the first two.
- **Named herdr sessions (#2196)**: a node on the default herdr server also drives every running named herdr session (`herdr --session <name>`) as part of
  the `herdr` host. Their pane, tab and workspace ids (`pane_id`, `tab_id`, `workspace_id`, `space_id`, `slot_id`, panes and `pane:` addresses) are
  `@<session>:<id>`, the default server's stay bare; `host` and `space_kind` stay `herdr`, and the spaces are named `<session> · <label>`. Clients treat
  the ids as opaque, as before (`docs/integrations/engines.md` "Named herdr sessions").
- `herdr_running` / `herdr_running_known` in `node.info`: whether the classic herdr server answers right now, and whether the node can tell (a machine using herdr-core
  has no such socket and sends neither). Old nodes send neither; the hub uses this to tell "not running" from "unknown" (`docs/integrations/engines.md`).
- `builtin_programs` in `node.info`: the extension programs built into personad (`["cua", "ego", "imessage", "iphone"]`, #1830 steps 5 and 6; imessage's method names are still `connector.*`; iphone, #3450, answers only `plugin.node.call`: `status`, `call`, `pair`, `forget`, `cancel`; `call` takes `IPhoneCall {device?, session?, op: status|look|do, args?, approved?, confirm?, self_apps?, self_names?, timeout_ms?}` and answers `IPhoneResult {output?, text?, image?, needs_approval?, approval_summary?, approval_id?}`, `approval_summary` being the core's approval as an object (`proto.IPhoneApproval`); a failed call is an RPC error with `data: {"sent": "no" | "unknown"}`; see `docs/extensions/iphone-pairing.md` ("The node program `iphone` (#3450)")). For nodes that report it, the hub calls them via `plugin.node.call {id, method, params}`;
  old nodes don't send it, and the hub keeps using `computer.*`, `browser.*` (new nodes still answer those). See `docs/extensions/extensions.md` ("Built-in node programs").
- `herdr.server.start` (hub → node, no params, returns `{running}`): the user tapped "Start" in the Agents list. Not bound by `herdr_autostart`;
  if it can't start, the reason is returned the same way as `engine_missing`. Old nodes don't have this method, and the hub returns 502 rather than claiming herdr can't start.
  If herdr isn't installed, a pinned version is installed first (waits up to 15 seconds; if not done, returns an "Installing herdr …" error, finishes installing in the background and then starts itself; `docs/integrations/engines.md` ("When herdr is not installed")).
- `herdr.server.status` (hub → node, no params, returns `{running, known, installing, install_error}`): `installing` means the node is installing herdr,
  `install_error` is why the last install failed (empty string if it never failed); `GET /api/v1/machines/{mid}/herdr` passes them through as is (omitted when absent).
- `usage.windows` (hub → node, no params, returns `{enabled, collected_at, accounts: [UsageAccount]}`, #2432): subscription quota windows the node gets from reading this machine's Codex rollouts and the files Claude's status line writes.
  It only reads local files and never touches credentials. When `usage_windows` in `node.configure` (hub.json `machines[].usage_windows`) is false it returns `{enabled: false, accounts: []}`. Old nodes don't have this method; the hub treats them as having no data (`docs/server/usage-windows.md`).
- Operations without a pane (new, resume session, rename) go to the set's default host (the node's `defaultHost` / `defaultKind`; classic herdr for
  herdr + Herdr App); per-pane operations (read screen, send, keys, close) are routed by the host kind of the pane id, and each host's panes are limited
  only by that host's capabilities. A session live in two hosts is listed once, in the host that owns it, and every per-pane operation goes there
  (`docs/integrations/engines.md` "Host sets").
- **`paseo` (display name "Paseo", `docs/integrations/paseo.md`) is not a terminal host**: the node registers no host and runs the Paseo bridge itself (`node/paseobridge.go`).
  The bridge is a runtime with runtime id `paseo` ("Runtime ↔ node" below), and its sessions are this machine's sessions.
  - **New session**: all handed to it. When the form's choice is a login-shell launcher, it carries `shell_launcher: true`.
  - **Resuming a Claude session that isn't running**: handed over with `session.start {resume}`; the session id stays the same. After the takeover, messages go over with `session.send` as usual.
  - **When the bridge isn't connected**, both new and resume return the error `engine_missing` and nothing is sent.
  - **Detection**: Paseo in `engines` counts as available in two cases. One: the bridge is connected; then `version` is Paseo's version. Two: the address written in `paseo.pid` in the Paseo home responds;
    in that case, if the bridge can't start, `note` gives the reason.

## hub ↔ node RPC

> Since 2026-11-04, what connects to nodes is the manager (the assistant's process, [machines.md](../server/machines.md) ("Who connects to computers")): "hub" below is the manager in production; hub calls and node events are relayed over the bus ("Computers (devices.*)" under "Bus"),
> and the protocol the node sees is unchanged, word for word.

`ssh <host> ~/.persona/bin/personad node --stdio` (on the hub machine itself a child process is started directly; it is now a child of the manager). One JSON per line on stdin/stdout.
Both sides can send requests: `{"id":"h12","method":"…","params":{}}` → `{"id":"h12","result":{}}` / `{"id":"h12","error":{"message":"…"}}`;
one-way events: `{"event":"…","params":{}}`. Ids sent by the hub start with `h`, ids sent by the node start with `n`. stderr is the node log.

Cancellation (#2597): when the caller no longer waits for a request, it sends `{"event":"rpc.cancel","params":{"id":"n12"}}` and the other side cancels handling that request. The node sends it for `mcp.call`, and the manager for `model.http` and `model.run`. For `mcp.call`: when the MCP process or hook disconnects (the assistant's turn was stopped), the hub's `approve` ends with it, the card is recorded as cancelled and withdrawn, and answering it afterward returns 410, so a write nobody is waiting for is never executed (such as sending an outdated message). Old versions that don't know this event ignore it, and handling runs to completion as usual. Extension and connector connections don't send this event.
